# The sixth moment of the Riemann zeta function

**Authors:** Alexandre de Faveri Address: EPFL SB MATH, Station 10, 1015 Lausanne, Switzerland Email address: alexandre.defaveri@epfl.ch and Mayank Pandey Address: Courant Institute of Mathematical Sciences, 251 Mercer Street, New York, NY, 10012 Email address: mayankpandey9973@gmail.com

## Abstract

We prove new large value estimates for the Riemann zeta function on the critical line. For instance, we improve the upper bound on the measure of $t\in[T,2T]$ with $|\zeta(1/2+it)|\geqslant T^{1/8}$ for the first time since Hardy–Littlewood (1923). Our results imply the first improvement since work of Heath-Brown (1978) on upper bounds for the $k$ -th moment of zeta, for every $4<k\leqslant 12$ . We show in particular that

The main ingredient is a new large value estimate for exponential sums with square-root phases, and certain perturbations. Those arise in the expansion of the short second moment of zeta.

## 1. Introduction

The Lindelöf hypothesis predicts that $|\zeta(1/2+it)|\ll_{\varepsilon}(1+|t|)^{\varepsilon}$ for all $\varepsilon>0$ . It is a consequence of the Riemann hypothesis, and can act as a substitute for it in many applications. A measure of progress towards Lindelöf is provided by upper bounds for the moments

$$ M_{k}(T):=\int_{0}^{T}|\zeta(\tfrac{1}{2}+it)|^{k}\,dt. $$

For instance, the bound $M_{k}(T)\ll_{k,\varepsilon}T^{1+\varepsilon}$ for all $k\geqslant 0$ is equivalent to the Lindelöf hypothesis. Such a bound is only known for $0\leqslant k\leqslant 4$ , but partial progress towards it is useful in applications.

The classical fourth and twelfth moment bounds11 1 In both bounds, $T^{\varepsilon}$ can be replaced with a power of $\log{T}$ . We are concerned only with the exponents of $T$ in this work, so we simplify the bounds for convenience.

$$ M_{4}(T)\ll_{\varepsilon}T^{1+\varepsilon}\qquad\text{and}\qquad M_{12}(T)\ll_{\varepsilon}T^{2+\varepsilon}, $$

due respectively to Hardy–Littlewood [9] (refined by Ingham [12]) and Heath-Brown [10], imply by interpolation that $M_{k}(T)\ll_{\varepsilon}T^{1+(k-4)/8+\varepsilon}$ for $4\leqslant k\leqslant 12$ . Those have been the best known bounds since the work of Heath-Brown [10], giving in particular $M_{6}(T)\ll_{\varepsilon}T^{5/4+\varepsilon}$ .

In this paper, we show the following improved estimate for the sixth moment of zeta.

#### Theorem 1.1 (Sixth moment bound).

For every $T\geqslant 1$ and $\varepsilon>0$ , we have

$$ \int_{0}^{T}|\zeta(\tfrac{1}{2}+it)|^{6}\,dt\ll_{\varepsilon}T^{\frac{5}{4}-\frac{1}{60}+\varepsilon}. $$

We also improve the best known upper bound for the $k$ -th moment of zeta, for every $4<k\leqslant 12$ .

#### Theorem 1.2 (General moment bound).

For each $4<k\leqslant 12$ , there exists $\delta_{k}>0$ such that if $T\geqslant 1$ and $\varepsilon>0$ , then

$$ M_{k}(T)\ll_{\varepsilon}T^{1+\frac{k-4}{8}-\delta_{k}+\varepsilon}. $$

In Theorem 10.1, we show that $\delta_{12}=\frac{520}{445121}$ is admissible. Improved moment bounds can also be obtained for $12\leqslant k<12+\nu$ for a small $\nu>0$ . We do not optimize either the savings $\delta_{k}$ or the range $\nu$ in this paper, aiming instead to simplify the presentation.

Our results on moments derive from distributional estimates for $|\zeta(\tfrac{1}{2}+it)|$ . Let $N(T,V)$ be the size of the largest $1$ -spaced subset of $\{t\in[T,2T]:|\zeta(\tfrac{1}{2}+it)|\geqslant V\}$ . The classical bounds (1) imply

$$ N(T,V)\ll_{\varepsilon}T^{\varepsilon}\min(TV^{-4},T^{2}V^{-12}). $$

The Hardy–Littlewood bound $N(T,V)\ll_{\varepsilon}T^{1+\varepsilon}V^{-4}$ is the best known (up to factors of $T^{\varepsilon}$ ) for $V\leqslant T^{1/8}$ , and the bounds in (2) intersect at $V=T^{1/8}$ . Better results are available for $V>T^{1/8}$ using exponent pairs [24], so $V=T^{1/8}$ is the critical range for known bounds on the moments $M_{k}(T)$ when $4<k\leqslant 12$ . Our main result gives an improvement in and around this critical range.

#### Theorem 1.3 (Large value estimate).

Let $T\geqslant 1$ . For any $V\in[T^{7/60},T^{5/38}]$ and $\varepsilon>0$ , we have

$$ N(T,V)\ll_{\varepsilon}T^{\frac{24}{17}+\varepsilon}V^{-\frac{128}{17}}. $$

In §9 we record further bounds for $N(T,V)$ , which are superior to Theorem 1.3 for large $V$ .

### 1.1. On the sixth and twelfth moments

The estimate $M_{12}(T)\ll_{\varepsilon}T^{2+\varepsilon}$ was proved by Heath-Brown via short second moments of zeta. The desire to improve on this bound has inspired many developments in analytic number theory, and led to several different proofs of the same result. For example, Iwaniec [15] deduced it from bounds for the fourth moment of zeta in short intervals, obtained via spectral theory of automorphic forms. Jutila [17] gave a different proof of Iwaniec’s result, bypassing the appeal to spectral theory. A textbook proof is given in [14, Chapter 8].

Both Iwaniec’s and Jutila’s methods give the same bounds for a fixed $\mathrm{GL}_{2}$ $L$ -function in place of $\zeta^{2}$ . It is worth mentioning that significantly less is known for $\mathrm{GL}_{3}$ $L$ -functions. The best known bound for the second moment in the $t$ -aspect (which should be compared to $M_{6}(T)$ ) is $T^{4/3+\varepsilon}$ , due to Dasgupta, Leung, and Young [4]. Interestingly, the bound $T^{5/4+\varepsilon}$ was recently obtained by Aggarwal, Leung, and Munshi [1] for a short second moment of length $T^{2/3}$ .

As noted earlier, the sixth moment bound of $O_{\varepsilon}(T^{5/4+\varepsilon})$ follows by interpolating the fourth and twelfth moment bounds. Expanding out with the approximate functional equation, this bound roughly amounts to showing an asymptotic with remainder $O_{\varepsilon}(X^{7/6+\varepsilon})$ for a smoothed version of

$$ \sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}h\sim X^{1/3}\end{subarray}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}n\sim X\end{subarray}}d_{3}(n)d_{3}(n+h). $$

One may interpret this $7/6$ as square-root cancellation in the $h$ -sum, over the $n$ -sums minus their expected main terms, and Theorem 1.1 should improve the exponent $7/6$ .

Finally, let us mention that sufficiently large improvements on the sixth moment bound imply improved zero density estimates for zeta; Iwaniec [16] noted that a bound $M_{6}(T)\ll T^{6/5-\delta}$ implies better zero density estimates at $\sigma=3/4$ than Huxley’s [11] classical bound. Such an improvement was recently obtained via different methods by Guth and Maynard [6].

### 1.2. Large value bounds for special exponential sums

The key ingredient behind our bounds is a new large value estimate for exponential sums with certain special phases. We refer to the survey [7] for the importance of large value problems in a broad range of subjects and discussion of their difficulty. In this paper we show the following.

#### Corollary 1.4.

Let $N,W,V\geqslant 1$ , $\eta\in\mathbb{R}$ , and $a_{n}\in\mathbb{C}$ with $|a_{n}|\leqslant 1$ . Denote $\Upsilon=1+|\eta|W$ and

$$ D_{\eta}(w):=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}N<n\leqslant 2N\end{subarray}}a_{n}e(w\phi_{\eta}(n/N))\qquad\text{for}\qquad\phi_{\eta}(x):=\sqrt{x}+\eta x^{3/2}. $$

Suppose that $N\leqslant W\leqslant N^{\frac{4}{3}}$ and that $|\eta|\leqslant cW/N^{2}$ for some sufficiently small $c>0$ . Then for $\varepsilon>0$ and any $1$ -spaced set $\mathcal{W}\subset[0,W]$ such that $|D_{\eta}(w)|\geqslant V$ for all $w\in\mathcal{W}$ , we have

$$ |\mathcal{W}|\ll_{\varepsilon}N^{\varepsilon}\biggl(\frac{N^{2}}{V^{2}}+\frac{N^{2}W^{\frac{3}{4}}\Upsilon^{\frac{1}{8}}}{V^{3}}+\frac{N^{\frac{5}{2}}W^{\frac{3}{2}}\Upsilon^{\frac{1}{4}}}{V^{5}}\biggr). $$

For reference, in the more general situation where $\phi_{\eta}$ is replaced with a smooth $\phi$ satisfying $|\phi^{\prime}|\asymp|\phi^{\prime\prime}|\asymp 1$ in a fixed neighborhood of $[1,2]$ , one can show using the large sieve [19, Corollary 2] that (4) may be replaced with

$$ |\mathcal{W}|\ll\frac{N^{2}}{V^{2}}+\frac{NW}{V^{2}}. $$

Heath-Brown’s arguments in [10] (of the type used by Halász [8] and Montgomery [21] for Dirichlet polynomials) yield that

$$ |\mathcal{W}|\ll\frac{N^{2}}{V^{2}}+\frac{N^{4}W}{V^{6}}. $$

For $N\gg W$ , the term $N^{2}/V^{2}$ is optimal, and for $N\ll W$ , the bounds (6) and (5) meet at $V\asymp N^{3/4}$ , a regime often critical for large value estimates in analytic number theory. It was so in Guth–Maynard’s [6] recent work on large values of Dirichlet polynomials, and is for us too.

For the sake of clarifying Corollary 1.4 in the special case $V\asymp N^{\frac{3}{4}}$ and $N^{1+\delta}\ll W\ll N^{\frac{5}{4}}$ , we shall isolate its conclusion when $|\eta|\ll W/N^{2+\delta}$ , for a small $\delta>0$ . In this case, it gives the bound

$$ |\mathcal{W}|\ll_{\varepsilon}N^{\varepsilon}\frac{W}{\sqrt{N}}\biggl(\frac{W}{N}\biggr)^{-\frac{1}{4}}(1+|\eta|W)^{\frac{1}{8}}\ll\frac{W}{\sqrt{N}}N^{-\frac{\delta}{8}+\varepsilon}, $$

while the mean value bound (5) yields $|\mathcal{W}|\ll W/\sqrt{N}$ . Thus our result is nontrivial in this case. Since the relevant regime for the zeta function is $|\eta|\asymp 1/N$ , Corollary 1.4 suffices for our purposes.

For applications to large values of zeta, the main advantage of considering exponential sums with our special phases is that it then suffices to beat their mean value estimate. This does not seem to be the case if one directly converts the problem to large values of Dirichlet polynomials (e.g. via the approximate functional equation), so available bounds fall short of what is needed.

That we have an $\ell^{\infty}$ bound on $(a_{n})$ rather than an $\ell^{2}$ bound is essential, otherwise the estimate $|\mathcal{W}|\ll W/\sqrt{N}$ is sharp when $\eta=0$ : we may take $\mathcal{W}=\{j\sqrt{N}:1\leqslant j\leqslant W/\sqrt{N}\}$ and $a_{n}=N^{1/4}\cdot\text{1}_{\square}(n)$ , for instance. This counterexample was noted by Guth [7, §5.5] and comes from a simplification by Alex Cohen of a related counterexample due to Fu–Guth–Maldague [5].

### 1.3. Notation

Let $e(x):=e^{2\pi ix}$ . Our Fourier transforms are $\widehat{f}(\xi):=\int_{\mathbb{R}}f(x)e(-\xi x)\,dx$ by convention. For $y\in\mathbb{R}$ , denote $\|y\|=\min\{|y-n|:n\in\mathbb{Z}\}$ . We write $f\ll g$ if there is a constant $C>0$ such that $|f|\leqslant C|g|$ . If $C$ depends on a parameter $p$ , we write $f\ll_{p}g$ . The notation $f\asymp g$ means $f\ll g\ll f$ , and $a\sim A$ denotes $A<a\leqslant 2A$ . Finally, for a finite set $\mathcal{W}\subset\mathbb{R}$ , we let

$$ \displaystyle E_{2k}(\mathcal{W};D):=\#\biggl\{(w_{1},\dots,w_{2k})\in\mathcal{W}^{2k}:\biggl|\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}i=1\end{subarray}}^{k}w_{i}-\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}i=k+1\end{subarray}}^{2k}w_{i}\biggr|\leqslant D\biggr\}. $$

### Use of AI tools

The reduction of the problem to beating the mean-value bound for exponential sums with perturbed square-root phases, and the observation that the high-energy case can be controlled as in Guth–Maynard [6], are due to the authors. Using the trace method (with third powers) as in [6], and dealing with stationary points via an extra pruning step, we initially obtained a result of the same strength as Corollary 1.4 in the case $\eta=0$ . This result did not rely on AI tools, using them only in a subsidiary capacity (e.g. to quickly compute stationary points and optimize exponents), but was only nontrivial for $|\eta|=o(1/N)$ , just barely insufficient for our desired application to large values of $|\zeta(1/2+it)|$ . We then asked ChatGPT 6 Astra to extend the range of $\eta$ in our proof, and it autonomously produced a simpler argument which is nontrivial for $|\eta|=o(W/N^{2})$ . A refinement of that argument is used in this paper.

## 2. Sketch of the proof

In this section we give a sketch of the argument in the critical case $V=T^{1/8}$ . For readability, we shall be somewhat imprecise, for instance ignoring factors of $T^{\varepsilon}$ and constant factors in phases.

By work of Heath-Brown [10], it suffices to rule out the following situation: there exist $T^{1/2}$ points $t\in[T,2T]$ which are $T^{1/4}$ -spaced22 2 We can even upgrade this spacing to $T^{1/2}$ via [15], but ignore this in the sketch for simplicity. and such that $|\zeta(1/2+it)|\geqslant T^{1/8}$ .

For $N\asymp T/V^{4}\asymp T^{1/2}$ and $W_{0}\asymp\sqrt{TN}\asymp T^{3/4}$ , Atkinson’s formula would then roughly imply the existence of a set $\mathcal{W}_{0}\subset[W_{0},2W_{0}]$ of $1$ -spaced points such that $|\mathcal{W}_{0}|\asymp W_{0}/\sqrt{N}\asymp T^{1/2}$ and

$$ \biggl|\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}n\sim N\end{subarray}}d(n)e\biggl(w\sqrt{\frac{n}{N}}+\frac{T}{w}\biggl(\frac{n}{N}\biggr)^{3/2}\biggr)\biggr|\gg N^{3/4}\qquad\text{for all }w\in\mathcal{W}_{0}. $$

Recall that $\phi_{\eta}(x)=\sqrt{x}+\eta x^{3/2}$ . We subdivide $\mathcal{W}_{0}$ into intervals of length $W=N^{1+\delta}$ , for some sufficiently small $\delta>0$ . It then suffices33 3 The subdivision into shorter intervals is needed to make $\eta$ independent of $w$ , and to remove lower order terms. to show, for any coefficients $|a_{n}|\leqslant 1$ and $\eta\in\mathbb{R}$ with $|\eta|\asymp T/W_{0}^{2}\asymp 1/N$ , that there exists no $1$ -spaced subset $\mathcal{W}\subset[W,2W]$ with $|\mathcal{W}|\gg W/\sqrt{N}$ and

$$ \biggl|\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}n\sim N\end{subarray}}a_{n}e(w\phi_{\eta}(n/N))\biggr|\gg N^{3/4}\qquad\text{for all }w\in\mathcal{W}. $$

Thus we are precisely in the position of having to beat the mean value bound on $R:=|\mathcal{W}|$ .

Our proof begins similarly to that of the Halász–Montgomery bound for Dirichlet polynomials (like in Heath-Brown’s work on the twelfth moment), with an application of duality. Precisely, for some phases $\gamma_{w}$ with $|\gamma_{w}|=1$ , we have by (8) and Cauchy–Schwarz that

$$ R^{2}N^{3/2}\ll\biggl|\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\begin{subarray}{c}n\sim N\\
w\in\mathcal{W}\end{subarray}\end{subarray}}\gamma_{w}a_{n}e(w\phi_{\eta}(n/N))\biggr|^{2}\ll N\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}n\sim N\end{subarray}}\biggl|\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}w\in\mathcal{W}\end{subarray}}\gamma_{w}e(w\phi_{\eta}(n/N))\biggr|^{2}. $$

Expanding out the square, separating out the diagonal (assuming for simplicity that the off-diagonal consists only of the generic case $|w-w^{\prime}|\asymp W$ ), and applying Poisson summation in $n$ followed by stationary phase, we have that the right-hand side above is

$$ \ll N^{2}R+\frac{N^{2}}{\sqrt{W}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}|m|\sim W/N\end{subarray}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\begin{subarray}{c}w,w^{\prime}\in\mathcal{W}\end{subarray}\end{subarray}}\gamma_{w}\overline{\gamma_{w^{\prime}}}e\biggl(\frac{(w-w^{\prime})^{2}}{4Nm}+\eta\frac{(w-w^{\prime})^{4}}{8N^{3}m^{3}}\biggr). $$

At this point we apply Hölder’s inequality, so that the above is

$$ \ll N^{2}R+\frac{N^{2}}{\sqrt{W}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}|m|\sim W/N\end{subarray}}R^{3/4}\biggl(\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}w^{\prime}\in\mathcal{W}\end{subarray}}\biggl|\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}w\in\mathcal{W}\end{subarray}}\gamma_{w}e\biggl(\frac{(w-w^{\prime})^{2}}{4Nm}+\eta\frac{(w-w^{\prime})^{4}}{8N^{3}m^{3}}\biggr)\biggr|^{4}\biggr)^{1/4}. $$

We may bound (with a $T^{\varepsilon}$ loss) the sum over $w^{\prime}\in\mathcal{W}$ by an integral over $w^{\prime}\sim W$ . Denoting $w^{\prime}=Wx$ and $\Delta_{j}:=w_{1}^{j}+w_{2}^{j}-w_{3}^{j}-w_{4}^{j}$ , this gives

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}w^{\prime}\in\mathcal{W}\end{subarray}}\biggl|\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}w\in\mathcal{W}\end{subarray}}\gamma_{w}e\biggl(\frac{(w-w^{\prime})^{2}}{4Nm}+\eta\frac{(w-w^{\prime})^{4}}{8N^{3}m^{3}}\biggr)\biggr|^{4}\ll\ W\int_{x\sim 1}\biggl|\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}w\in\mathcal{W}\end{subarray}}\gamma_{w}e\biggl(\frac{(w-Wx)^{2}}{4Nm}+\eta\frac{(w-Wx)^{4}}{8N^{3}m^{3}}\biggr)\biggr|^{4}\,dx \displaystyle\ll W\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}w_{1},w_{2},w_{3},w_{4}\in\mathcal{W}\end{subarray}}\ \biggl|\int_{x\sim 1}e\biggl(-\frac{W\Delta_{1}}{2Nm}x+\eta W\biggl[-\frac{\Delta_{1}W^{2}}{2N^{3}m^{3}}x^{3}+\frac{3\Delta_{2}W}{4N^{3}m^{3}}x^{2}-\frac{\Delta_{3}}{2N^{3}m^{3}}x\biggr]\biggr)\,dx\biggr|. $$

If $|\Delta_{1}|$ is greater than a sufficiently large multiple of $|\eta|W$ , then the first term in the phase dominates, hence the contribution of such $(w_{1},\dots,w_{4})$ is negligible. This makes critical use of the shape of our initial phases $\phi_{\eta}(x)$ . If $|\Delta_{1}|\ll|\eta|W$ , the integral is $\ll(1+|\Delta_{1}|)^{-1/2}$ (modulo some minor singular cases) by stationary phase. Thus (9) is $\ll WE_{4}(\mathcal{W};1)(1+|\eta|W)^{1/2}$ , so

$$ R^{2}N^{3/2}\ll N^{2}R+\frac{N^{2}}{\sqrt{W}}\frac{W}{N}R^{3/4}W^{1/4}E_{4}(\mathcal{W};1)^{1/4}(1+|\eta|W)^{1/8}. $$

With an argument similar to that of Guth and Maynard [6, §11], we can show that $E_{4}(\mathcal{W};1)\ll NR$ . This is the only place in the argument where we make (crucial) use of the $\ell^{\infty}$ bound $|a_{n}|\leqslant 1$ , instead of a weaker $\ell^{2}$ bound. We conclude that

$$ R\ll N^{1/2}+\frac{W}{\sqrt{N}}\biggl(\frac{W}{N}\biggr)^{-\frac{1}{8}}\ll\frac{W}{\sqrt{N}}\biggl(\frac{W}{N}\biggr)^{-\frac{1}{8}}, $$

which gives the desired improvement over the mean value bound $R\ll W/\sqrt{N}$ .

## 3. Preliminary lemmas

#### Lemma 3.1 (Stationary phase).

For any bounded interval $I\subset\mathbb{R}$ and $\psi\in C_{c}^{\infty}(\mathbb{R})$ with support contained in $I$ , we have that

$$ \int_{\mathbb{R}}\psi(x)e(\alpha x+\beta x^{2})\,dx\ll_{I}(\|\psi\|_{\infty}+\|\psi^{\prime}\|_{1})(1+|\alpha|+|\beta|)^{-1/2} $$

uniformly in $\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb{R}$ .

#### Proof.

This follows immediately from stationary phase, for example as a special case of [23, Chapter VIII, Proposition 2]. ∎

#### Lemma 3.2 (Gallagher’s lemma).

For any $f\in C^{1}(\mathbb{R})$ , $x\in\mathbb{R}$ , and integer $k\geqslant 1$ , we have

$$ |f(x)|^{2k}\ll_{k}\int_{x-1/3}^{x+1/3}\big(|f(y)|^{2k}+|f(y)|^{2k-1}|f^{\prime}(y)|\big)\,dy. $$

In particular, if $\mathcal{X}$ is a $1$ -spaced subset of an interval $[a,b]\subset\mathbb{R}$ , then

$$ \sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}x\in\mathcal{X}\end{subarray}}|f(x)|^{2k}\ll_{k}\int_{a-1/3}^{b+1/3}\big(|f(y)|^{2k}+|f^{\prime}(y)|^{2k}\big)\,dy. $$

#### Proof.

This follows from the Sobolev–Gallagher lemma [20, Lemmas 19.1 and 19.2]. ∎

## 4. Energy bounds

Let $N,V,W\geqslant 1$ and $\eta\in\mathbb{R}$ be bounded. Let $\mathcal{W}\subset[W,2W]$ be a $1$ -spaced set such that $|D_{\eta}(w)|\geqslant V$ for every $w\in\mathcal{W}$ . Denote $\xi_{n}:=\phi_{\eta}(n/N)$ and

$$ F(\alpha):=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}w\in\mathcal{W}\end{subarray}}e(w\alpha). $$

In the next three sections, $f\prec g$ denotes that $|f|\ll_{\varepsilon}(NVW)^{\varepsilon}|g|$ for any $\varepsilon>0$ . Subscripts will indicate parameters on which the implied constants may depend, as usual.

The main result of this section is the following bound.

#### Proposition 4.1 (General energy bound).

Suppose $W\leqslant N^{4/3}$ and $\eta\in\mathbb{R}$ is sufficiently small. For every integer $k\geqslant 2$ and real $1\leqslant D\leqslant W$ , we have

$$ E_{2k}(\mathcal{W};D)\prec_{k}\Big(\frac{N}{V}\Big)^{4k-4}E_{2}(\mathcal{W};D)+\frac{ND}{V^{2}}|\mathcal{W}|^{2k-1}. $$

We shall require a few preparatory lemmas before we are ready to prove Proposition 4.1.

#### Lemma 4.2 (Spacing estimate).

For $\eta\in\mathbb{R}$ sufficiently small, $0<\delta<1$ , and $\lambda\in\mathbb{R}$ , we have

$$ \#\big\{m,n\sim N:m\neq n,\,\big|\phi_{\eta}(m/N)-\phi_{\eta}(n/N)-\lambda\big|\leqslant\delta\big\}\ll\delta N^{2}+N^{2/3}. $$

#### Proof.

For $x\asymp 1$ , we record that $\phi^{\prime}_{\eta}(x)\asymp\phi_{\eta}^{\prime\prime}(x)\asymp 1$ since $\eta$ is sufficiently small. A direct computation also gives $(\phi_{\eta}^{\prime\prime}/(\phi_{\eta}^{\prime})^{2})^{\prime}(x)\asymp 1$ .

Denote $\mathcal{S}=\{(m,n)\sim N:m\neq n,\,|\phi_{\eta}(n/N)-\phi_{\eta}(m/N)-\lambda|\leqslant\delta\}$ and $\mathcal{S}_{m}=\{(m,n)\in\mathcal{S}\}$ . We have that $|\mathcal{S}_{m}|\ll 1+\delta N$ , so $|\mathcal{S}|\ll N+\delta N^{2}$ , which is sufficient for $\delta\gg 1/N$ .

Suppose that $\delta\leqslant c/N$ for the remainder of this proof, where $c>0$ is sufficiently small. By symmetry, we may assume that $\lambda\geqslant 0$ . We may also suppose that $1/N\ll\lambda\ll 1$ , for otherwise we are forced into the case $n=m$ . It remains to bound the number of $m$ for which $\mathcal{S}_{m}$ is nonempty, since the number of $n$ corresponding to each $m$ is $\ll 1+\delta N\ll 1$ .

Let $g_{\lambda}(x)=\phi_{\eta}^{-1}(\phi_{\eta}(x)+\lambda)$ . It can be checked by implicit differentiation and the mean value theorem that for $x\sim 1$ we have

$$ g_{\lambda}(x)-x\asymp g_{\lambda}^{\prime}(x)-1\asymp g_{\lambda}^{\prime\prime}(x)\asymp\lambda. $$

That $|\phi_{\eta}(n/N)-\phi_{\eta}(m/N)-\lambda|\leqslant\delta$ implies $n=Ng_{\lambda}(m/N)+O(\delta N)$ by monotonicity, so

$$ |\mathcal{S}|\ll\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}m\sim N\end{subarray}}\text{1}_{\|Ng_{\lambda}(m/N)\|\ll\delta N}=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}m\sim N\end{subarray}}\text{1}_{\|N(g_{\lambda}(m/N)-m/N)\|\ll\delta N}. $$

Note that $N(g_{\lambda}(m/N)-m/N)\asymp N\lambda$ and the corresponding values are spaced by $\gg\lambda$ for $m\sim N$ . For $\lambda\leqslant N^{-1/3}$ , the desired result follows since

$$ |\mathcal{S}|\ll(1+N\lambda)\biggl(1+\frac{\delta N}{\lambda}\biggr)\ll\delta N^{2}+\lambda N\ll\delta N^{2}+N^{2/3}. $$

Suppose that $\lambda>N^{-1/3}$ from now on. By [22, Proposition 3.3] (with $\delta$ in the reference taken to be $\delta_{1}=\delta N+(\lambda/N)^{1/3}$ by positivity) we get

$$ \sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}m\sim N\end{subarray}}\text{1}_{\|N(g_{\lambda}(m/N)-m/N)\|\ll\delta N}\ll\delta N^{2}+(\lambda/N)^{1/3}N+\sqrt{\frac{N\lambda}{\delta_{1}}}+\sqrt{\frac{N\delta_{1}}{\lambda}}. $$

It remains to check that the bound is acceptable. Note from $\lambda\ll 1$ that

$$ \sqrt{\frac{N\lambda}{\delta_{1}}}\ll\sqrt{\frac{N\lambda}{(\lambda/N)^{1/3}}}\ll N^{2/3} $$

and from $\delta\ll 1/N$ and $\lambda>N^{-1/3}$ that

$$ \sqrt{\frac{N\delta_{1}}{\lambda}}\ll\sqrt{\frac{\delta N^{2}}{\lambda}}+\sqrt{\frac{N^{2/3}}{\lambda^{2/3}}}\ll\sqrt{N/\lambda}+(N/\lambda)^{1/3}\ll N^{2/3}, $$

from which the desired result follows. ∎

#### Lemma 4.3 (Smoothing).

Let $A\geqslant 1$ and $\mathcal{S}\subset[-A,A]$ be a finite set. For $\alpha\in\mathbb{R}$ , denote

$$ C(\alpha):=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}s\in\mathcal{S}\end{subarray}}c_{s}e(s\alpha), $$

where $c_{s}\in\mathbb{C}$ . Then for any $p,\ell\geqslant 1$ we have

$$ |C(\alpha)|^{p}\ll_{p,\ell}A\int_{\mathbb{R}}|C(\xi)|^{p}\cdot\big(1+A|\xi-\alpha|\big)^{-\ell}\,d\xi. $$

#### Proof.

Let $\psi$ be a Schwartz function with $\psi(x)=1$ for $x\in[-1,1]$ . For $f(s)=\psi(s/A)e(s\alpha)$ , note that $\widehat{f}(\xi)=A\widehat{\psi}(A(\xi-\alpha))$ . Hence for any $\ell\geqslant 1$ , the decay of $\widehat{\psi}$ gives

$$ |C(\alpha)|=\Big|\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}s\in\mathcal{S}\end{subarray}}c_{s}\psi\Big(\frac{s}{A}\Big)e(s\alpha)\Big|=\Big|\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}s\in\mathcal{S}\end{subarray}}c_{s}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}A\widehat{\psi}(A(\xi-\alpha))e(\xi s)\,d\xi\Big|\ll_{\ell}A\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{|C(\xi)|}{\big(1+A|\xi-\alpha|\big)^{\ell}}\,d\xi. $$

This settles the case $p=1$ , and the general case follows from Hölder’s inequality. ∎

#### Lemma 4.4 (Fourier bound).

For any integer $k\geqslant 1$ and real $1\leqslant d\leqslant W$ , we have

$$ V^{2}E_{2k}(\mathcal{W};d)\prec_{k}d\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}m,n\sim N\\
|\xi_{m}-\xi_{n}|\prec\frac{1}{d}\end{subarray}}|F(\xi_{m}-\xi_{n})|^{2k-1}. $$

#### Proof.

Note that

$$ V^{2}E_{2k}(\mathcal{W};d)\leqslant\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}w_{1},\ldots,w_{2k}\in\mathcal{W}\end{subarray}}|D_{\eta}(w_{2k})|^{2}\cdot\text{1}\Big(\Big|\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}i=1\end{subarray}}^{k}w_{i}-\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}i=k+1\end{subarray}}^{2k}w_{i}\Big|\leqslant d\Big). $$

By Lemma 4.3 applied to $D_{\eta}(\alpha)=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}n\sim N\end{subarray}}a_{n}e(\alpha\xi_{n})$ ,

$$ \displaystyle|D_{\eta}(\alpha)|^{2}\ll_{\ell}\int_{\mathbb{R}}|D_{\eta}(\xi)|^{2}\cdot(1+|\xi-\alpha|)^{-\ell}\,d\xi\prec_{\ell}\int_{|\xi-\alpha|\prec 1}|D_{\eta}(\xi)|^{2}\,d\xi+W^{-\ell}. $$

Thus for any $\tau\in\mathbb{R}$ , since $\mathcal{W}$ is $1$ -spaced, we have

$$ \sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}w\in\mathcal{W}\\
|\tau-w|\leqslant d\end{subarray}}|D_{\eta}(w)|^{2}\prec_{\ell}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}w\in\mathcal{W}\\
|w-\tau|\leqslant d\end{subarray}}\int_{|\xi-w|\prec 1}|D_{\eta}(\xi)|^{2}\,d\xi+W^{-\ell}\prec\int_{|\xi-\tau|\prec d}|D_{\eta}(\xi)|^{2}\,d\xi+W^{-\ell}. $$

Taking $\tau=w_{1}+\cdots+w_{k}-w_{k+1}-\cdots-w_{2k-1}$ , by (11) we obtain

$$ \displaystyle V^{2}E_{2k}(\mathcal{W};d) \displaystyle\prec_{\ell}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}w_{1},\ldots,w_{2k-1}\in\mathcal{W}\end{subarray}}\int_{|s|\prec d}|D_{\eta}(\tau-s)|^{2}\,ds+W^{2k-\ell}. $$

We may ignore the error term $W^{2k-\ell}$ by taking $\ell$ sufficiently large in terms of $k$ and comparing with the diagonal in the left-hand side. The condition $|s|\prec d$ can be replaced by a non-negative bump function $g(s/d)$ by positivity, with $\widehat{g}(x)\prec_{j}(1+|x|)^{-j}$ . Opening the square yields that

$$ \displaystyle V^{2}E_{2k}(\mathcal{W};d) \displaystyle\prec_{k}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}m,n\sim N\end{subarray}}a_{m}\overline{a_{n}}\int_{\mathbb{R}}F(\xi_{m}-\xi_{n})|F(\xi_{m}-\xi_{n})|^{2(k-1)}g\Big(\frac{s}{d}\Big)e(-s(\xi_{m}-\xi_{n}))\,ds \displaystyle\prec_{k}d\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}m,n\sim N\end{subarray}}|F(\xi_{m}-\xi_{n})|^{2k-1}\big|\widehat{g}\big(d(\xi_{m}-\xi_{n})\big)\big|. $$

Here we made crucial use of the assumption $|a_{n}|\leqslant 1$ . Then the decay of $\widehat{g}$ and a trivial bound for $F$ lead to

$$ V^{2}E_{2k}(\mathcal{W};d)\prec_{k}d\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}m,n\sim N\\
|\xi_{m}-\xi_{n}|\prec\frac{1}{d}\end{subarray}}|F(\xi_{m}-\xi_{n})|^{2k-1}+dW^{-100k}. $$

The term $dW^{-100k}$ is smaller than the left-hand side, so the result follows. ∎

#### Proof of Proposition 4.1.

Separating the diagonal terms $m=n$ in Lemma 4.4 gives

$$ V^{2}E_{2k}(\mathcal{W};D)\prec_{k}ND|\mathcal{W}|^{2k-1}+D\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}m,n\sim N\\
m\neq n\\
|\xi_{m}-\xi_{n}|\prec\frac{1}{D}\end{subarray}}|F(\xi_{m}-\xi_{n})|^{2k-1}. $$

By Lemma 4.2, since $W\leqslant N^{4/3}$ we have

$$ N_{W}(\lambda):=\#\big\{m,n\sim N:m\neq n,\ |\xi_{m}-\xi_{n}-\lambda|\prec 1/W\big\}\prec\frac{N^{2}}{W}+N^{2/3}\prec\frac{N^{2}}{W}. $$

From $D\leqslant W$ , the conditions $|\xi_{m}-\xi_{n}|\prec 1/D$ and $|\xi_{m}-\xi_{n}-\lambda|\prec 1/W$ imply $|\lambda|\prec 1/D$ . Applying Lemma 4.3 to $|F|^{2k-1}$ and truncating the integrals using $|F|\leqslant|\mathcal{W}|\ll W$ , we get

$$ \displaystyle D\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}m,n\sim N\\
m\neq n\\
|\xi_{m}-\xi_{n}|\prec\frac{1}{D}\end{subarray}}|F(\xi_{m}-\xi_{n})|^{2k-1} \displaystyle\prec_{k}DW\int_{|\lambda|\prec\frac{1}{D}}|F(\lambda)|^{2k-1}N_{W}(\lambda)\,d\lambda+W^{-100} \displaystyle\prec_{k}DN^{2}\int_{|\lambda|\prec\frac{1}{D}}|F(\lambda)|^{2k-1}\,d\lambda+W^{-100}. $$

The error term $W^{-100}$ can be absorbed into the diagonal contribution, so we may ignore it.

Now observe for any integer $j\geqslant 1$ that

$$ D\int_{|\lambda|\prec\frac{1}{D}}|F(\lambda)|^{2j}\,d\lambda\prec E_{2j}(\mathcal{W};D). $$

Indeed, the condition $|\lambda|\prec\frac{1}{D}$ can be replaced by a non-negative bump function $g(D\lambda/L)$ by positivity, with $1\leqslant L\prec 1$ and $\widehat{g}$ bounded and supported in $[-1,1]$ . Hence

$$ D\int_{|\lambda|\prec\frac{1}{D}}|F(\lambda)|^{2j}\,d\lambda\leqslant D\int_{\mathbb{R}}g\Big(\frac{D\lambda}{L}\Big)|F(\lambda)|^{2j}\,d\lambda=\ L\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}w_{1},\ldots,w_{2j}\in\mathcal{W}\end{subarray}}\widehat{g}\Big(\frac{L}{D}\Big(\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}i=1\end{subarray}}^{j}w_{i}-\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}i=j+1\end{subarray}}^{2j}w_{i}\Big)\Big), $$

which is $O(LE_{2j}(\mathcal{W};D/L))$ . This yields (15) by positivity, as $L\geqslant 1$ .

Now observe from Hölder’s inequality followed by (15) that

$$ \displaystyle D\int_{|\lambda|\prec\frac{1}{D}}|F(\lambda)|^{2k-1}\,d\lambda \displaystyle\leqslant\Big(D\int_{|\lambda|\prec\frac{1}{D}}|F(\lambda)|^{2}\,d\lambda\Big)^{\frac{1}{2k-2}}\Big(D\int_{|\lambda|\prec\frac{1}{D}}|F(\lambda)|^{2k}\,d\lambda\Big)^{\frac{2k-3}{2k-2}} \displaystyle\prec E_{2}(\mathcal{W};D)^{\frac{1}{2k-2}}\cdot E_{2k}(\mathcal{W};D)^{\frac{2k-3}{2k-2}}. $$

Inserting this into (14) and (13), we obtain

$$ \displaystyle V^{2}E_{2k}(\mathcal{W};D)\prec_{k}ND|\mathcal{W}|^{2k-1}+N^{2}E_{2}(\mathcal{W};D)^{\frac{1}{2k-2}}\cdot E_{2k}(\mathcal{W};D)^{\frac{2k-3}{2k-2}}. $$

If the term $ND|\mathcal{W}|^{2k-1}$ dominates, then we are done. Otherwise, we obtain

$$ E_{2k}(\mathcal{W};D)\prec_{k}\Big(\frac{N^{2}}{V^{2}}\Big)^{2k-2}E_{2}(\mathcal{W};D), $$

as desired. ∎

## 5. General large value bound

Corollary 1.4 will follow from the more flexible large value bound below.

#### Theorem 5.1 (General large value bound).

For every integer $k\geqslant 2$ , there exists $c_{k}>0$ such that the following holds. Let $N,V,W\geqslant 1$ satisfy

$$ N\leqslant W\leqslant N^{4/3}\quad\text{and}\quad|\eta|\leqslant c_{k}W/N^{2}. $$

Let $a_{n}\in\mathbb{C}$ with $|a_{n}|\leqslant 1$ , and denote as before $\Upsilon=1+|\eta|W$ and

$$ D_{\eta}(w):=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}N<n\leqslant 2N\end{subarray}}a_{n}e(w\phi_{\eta}(n/N))\qquad\text{for}\qquad\phi_{\eta}(x):=\sqrt{x}+\eta x^{3/2}. $$

Then for any $1$ -spaced subset $\mathcal{W}$ of an interval of length $W$ such that $|D_{\eta}(w)|\geqslant V$ for all $w\in\mathcal{W}$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle|\mathcal{W}|\prec_{k}\frac{N^{2}}{V^{2}}+\frac{N^{\frac{6k-4}{2k+1}}W^{\frac{k+1}{2k+1}}}{V^{\frac{8k-4}{2k+1}}}\left(\sup_{\begin{subarray}{c}1\leqslant D\ll_{k}\Upsilon\end{subarray}}\frac{E_{2}(\mathcal{W};D)}{\sqrt{D}}\right)^{\frac{1}{2k+1}}+\frac{N^{k+\frac{1}{2}}W^{\frac{k+1}{2}}\Upsilon^{\frac{1}{4}}}{V^{2k+1}}. $$

#### Proof of Corollary 1.4 assuming Theorem 5.1.

Applying Theorem 5.1 with $k=2$ together with the bound $E_{2}(\mathcal{W};D)\leqslant(2D+1)|\mathcal{W}|$ , which follows from the $1$ -spacing of $\mathcal{W}$ , we obtain

$$ |\mathcal{W}|\prec\frac{N^{2}}{V^{2}}+\frac{N^{\frac{8}{5}}W^{\frac{3}{5}}}{V^{\frac{12}{5}}}|\mathcal{W}|^{\frac{1}{5}}\Upsilon^{\frac{1}{10}}+\frac{N^{\frac{5}{2}}W^{\frac{3}{2}}}{V^{5}}\Upsilon^{\frac{1}{4}}. $$

Rearranging, this gives the desired bound

$$ |\mathcal{W}|\prec\frac{N^{2}}{V^{2}}+\frac{N^{2}W^{\frac{3}{4}}\Upsilon^{\frac{1}{8}}}{V^{3}}+\frac{N^{\frac{5}{2}}W^{\frac{3}{2}}\Upsilon^{\frac{1}{4}}}{V^{5}}. $$

∎

w\in\mathcal{W}\end{subarray}}a_{n}\gamma_{w}e(w\phi_{\eta}(n/N))\biggr|^{2}\ll N\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}n\sim N\end{subarray}}\biggl|\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}w\in\mathcal{W}\end{subarray}}\gamma_{w}e(w\phi_{\eta}(n/N))\biggr|^{2}. $$

## 7. Atkinson’s formula

In §9, our passage from large values of $|\zeta(1/2+it)|$ to exponential sums is via Atkinson’s formula [2] for the second moment in short intervals. We state it below in the greatly simplified upper bound version due to Heath-Brown [10, Lemma 1], whose proof was simplified by Ivić [14]

#### Lemma 7.1 (Atkinson’s formula [14, Theorem 7.2]).

Let $\varepsilon>0$ and suppose that $T\geqslant 2$ and $T^{\varepsilon}\leqslant G\leqslant T^{1/2-\varepsilon}$ . Denote

$$ S_{T}(\Delta,N):=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}N\leqslant n\leqslant N+\Delta\end{subarray}}(-1)^{n}d(n)e(f(T,n)) $$

for

$$ f(T,n):=\frac{T}{\pi}\left(\sinh^{-1}\left(\sqrt{\frac{\pi n}{2T}}\right)+\sqrt{\frac{\pi n}{2T}\Big(1+\frac{\pi n}{2T}\Big)}\right). $$

Then

$$ \displaystyle\int_{T-G}^{T+G}|\zeta(\tfrac{1}{2}+it)|^{2}\,dt \displaystyle\qquad\ll_{\varepsilon}G\log T+G\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\begin{subarray}{c}T^{1/3}\leqslant N\leqslant\frac{T}{G^{2}}(\log{T})^{1+\varepsilon}\\
N=2^{m}\end{subarray}\end{subarray}}(TN)^{-1/4}\Bigg(|S_{T}(N,N)|+\int_{0}^{N}\frac{|S_{T}(\Delta,N)|}{N}\,d\Delta\Bigg). $$

Truncating the power series expansion of the phases above and splitting into small intervals, we bound the short second moment of $|\zeta(1/2+it)|$ in terms of exponential sums with the special phases that we are considering.

#### Corollary 7.2 (Phase truncation).

Let $1\leqslant N\leqslant T^{3/5}$ , $1\leqslant W\leqslant\sqrt{TN}$ , and $N^{1/2}W^{2}\leqslant T^{3/2}$ . For each $t_{0}\in[T,2T]$ , there exist coefficients $a_{n}\in\mathbb{C}$ with $|a_{n}|\leqslant 1$ such that for any $t\in\big[t_{0},t_{0}+W(T/N)^{1/2}\big]$ and $\varepsilon>0$ we have

$$ \max_{0\leqslant\Delta\leqslant N}|S_{t}(\Delta,N)|\ll_{\varepsilon}N^{\varepsilon}\max_{0\leqslant\Delta\leqslant N}\biggl|\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}N\leqslant n\leqslant N+\Delta\end{subarray}}a_{n}e\Big(w\Big[\sqrt{\frac{n}{N}}-\frac{\pi N}{12t_{0}}\Big(\frac{n}{N}\Big)^{3/2}\Big]\Big)\biggr|, $$

where $S_{t}(\Delta,N)$ is given in (40) and

$$ w:=\sqrt{\frac{2N}{\pi}}\bigl(\sqrt{t}-\sqrt{t_{0}}\bigr)\in[0,W]. $$

#### Proof.

We may assume that $T$ is sufficiently large, otherwise the result is trivial. For $|z|\leqslant\frac{1}{2}$ , a Taylor expansion gives

$$ g(z):=\big(\sinh^{-1}(z)+z\sqrt{1+z^{2}}\big)-\Big(2z+\frac{z^{3}}{3}\Big)=O(|z|^{5}) $$

and $g^{\prime}(z)=O(|z|^{4})$ . Note that $t\asymp T$ since $W\leqslant\sqrt{TN}$ , and let $N<n\leqslant 2N$ . Taking $z=\sqrt{\frac{\pi n}{2t}}\asymp\sqrt{N/T}\ll T^{-1/5}$ in (41), we obtain

$$ f(t,n)=\sqrt{\frac{2nt}{\pi}}+\frac{\sqrt{2\pi}}{12}\frac{n^{3/2}}{\sqrt{t}}+r_{t}(n) $$

with $|r_{t}(n)|+n|r_{t}^{\prime}(n)|\ll N^{5/2}T^{-3/2}\leqslant 1$ . Thus partial summation yields

$$ \max_{0\leqslant\Delta\leqslant N}|S_{t}(\Delta,N)|\ll\max_{0\leqslant\Delta\leqslant N}\biggl|\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}N\leqslant n\leqslant N+\Delta\end{subarray}}(-1)^{n}d(n)e\biggl(\sqrt{\frac{2nt}{\pi}}+\frac{\sqrt{2\pi}}{12}\frac{n^{3/2}}{\sqrt{t}}\biggr)\biggr|. $$

Next we replace $t$ with $t_{0}$ in the second term. Using

$$ \frac{1}{\sqrt{t}}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{t_{0}}}=-\frac{\sqrt{t}-\sqrt{t_{0}}}{t_{0}}+\frac{(\sqrt{t}-\sqrt{t_{0}})^{2}}{t_{0}\sqrt{t}}, $$

the phase in (42) equals

$$ \sqrt{\frac{2nt_{0}}{\pi}}+\frac{\sqrt{2\pi}}{12}\frac{n^{3/2}}{\sqrt{t_{0}}}+w\Big[\sqrt{\frac{n}{N}}-\frac{\pi N}{12t_{0}}\Big(\frac{n}{N}\Big)^{3/2}\Big]+q_{t}(n) $$

for

$$ q_{t}(n)=\frac{\sqrt{2\pi}}{12}\frac{n^{3/2}(\sqrt{t}-\sqrt{t_{0}})^{2}}{t_{0}\sqrt{t}}. $$

Since $|t-t_{0}|\ll W\big(\frac{T}{N}\big)^{1/2}$ and $t\asymp T$ , this gives

$$ |q_{t}(n)|+n|q_{t}^{\prime}(n)|\ll\frac{N^{3/2}(\sqrt{t}-\sqrt{t_{0}})^{2}}{T^{3/2}}\ll\frac{N^{1/2}W^{2}}{T^{3/2}}\leqslant 1. $$

Thus a second partial summation removes $e(q_{t}(n))$ . Taking

$$ a_{n}=(-1)^{n}d(n)e\biggl(\sqrt{\frac{2nt_{0}}{\pi}}+\frac{\sqrt{2\pi}}{12}\frac{n^{3/2}}{\sqrt{t_{0}}}\biggr), $$

which does not depend on $t$ , and rescaling via the divisor bound so that $|a_{n}|\leqslant 1$ , we obtain the claimed result. ∎

The maxima in the result above were a convenient device to quickly execute partial summation, but they need to be removed once we sum over distinct points. This is accomplished at little loss by the simple lemma below.

#### Lemma 7.3 (Removing maxima of partial sums).

Let $N,J\geqslant 1$ , $\mathcal{W}_{j}\subset\mathbb{R}$ be finite sets, $a_{j,n}\in\mathbb{C}$ , and $\xi_{j,n}\in\mathbb{R}$ . Then there exist $a^{\prime}_{j,n}\in\mathbb{C}$ with $|a^{\prime}_{j,n}|=|a_{j,n}|$ such that

$$ \sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}1\leqslant j\leqslant J\end{subarray}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}w\in\mathcal{W}_{j}\end{subarray}}\max_{0\leqslant\Delta\leqslant N}\biggl|\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}N<n\leqslant N+\Delta\end{subarray}}a_{j,n}e(w\xi_{j,n})\biggr|\ll\ \log(2N)\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}1\leqslant j\leqslant J\end{subarray}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}w\in\mathcal{W}_{j}\end{subarray}}\biggl|\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}n\sim N\end{subarray}}a^{\prime}_{j,n}e(w\xi_{j,n})\biggr|. $$

#### Proof.

We may assume that $N,\Delta\in\mathbb{Z}$ . Summing the geometric series, note that the Fourier coefficients of the indicator of $\{1,\ldots,\Delta\}$ on $\mathbb{Z}/(2N)\mathbb{Z}$ are

$$ \widehat{\text{1}}_{[1,\Delta]}(h):=\frac{1}{2N}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}a=1\end{subarray}}^{\Delta}e\Big(-\frac{ha}{2N}\Big)\ll\frac{1}{1+|h|} $$

for each $-N<h\leqslant N$ . Applying the Fourier expansion at $n-N$ gives

$$ \displaystyle\max_{0\leqslant\Delta\leqslant N}\biggl|\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}N<n\leqslant N+\Delta\end{subarray}}a_{j,n}e(w\xi_{j,n})\biggr|\ll\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}-N<h\leqslant N\end{subarray}}\frac{1}{1+|h|}\biggl|\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}n\sim N\end{subarray}}a_{j,n}e\Big(\frac{hn}{2N}\Big)e(w\xi_{j,n})\biggr|. $$

Summing over $1\leqslant j\leqslant J$ and $w\in\mathcal{W}_{j}$ , since $\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}-N<h\leqslant N\end{subarray}}(1+|h|)^{-1}\ll\log(2N)$ we obtain the conclusion with $a^{\prime}_{j,n}=a_{j,n}e\big(\frac{hn}{2N}\big)$ for some $-N<h\leqslant N$ . ∎

Let us also record the following standard result.

#### Lemma 7.4 ([13, Theorem 1.2]).

For every $t\in\mathbb{R}$ and integer $k\geqslant 1$ ,

$$ |\zeta(\tfrac{1}{2}+it)|^{k}\ll_{k}1+\log(2+|t|)\int_{t-1/3}^{t+1/3}|\zeta(\tfrac{1}{2}+iu)|^{k}\,du. $$

## 8. Refined spacing for large values of zeta

We will use the following result of Iwaniec [15] on the short fourth moment of the Riemann zeta function on average. This is unnecessary if one only wishes to obtain some power saving for the sixth moment, but improves the exponents without much extra effort.

From now on, denote $f\prec g$ when $|f|\ll_{\varepsilon}T^{\varepsilon}|g|$ for any $\varepsilon>0$ .

#### Proposition 8.1 ([15, Theorem 4]).

Let $T\geqslant 1$ and $\sqrt{T}\leqslant L\leqslant T$ . Suppose that $I_{1},\dots,I_{J}\subset[T,2T]$ are disjoint intervals, each of length $L$ . Then

$$ \sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}j\leqslant J\end{subarray}}\int_{I_{j}}|\zeta(\tfrac{1}{2}+it)|^{4}\,dt\prec JL+T\sqrt{J/L}. $$

As a corollary, we obtain the following upper bound on $E_{2}$ at any scale.

#### Corollary 8.2 ( $E_{2}$ refinement).

Suppose that $1\leqslant G\leqslant T/10$ and let $t_{1},\dots,t_{R}\in[T,2T]$ be $2G$ -spaced points such that

$$ \int_{|t-t_{j}|\leqslant G}|\zeta(\tfrac{1}{2}+it)|^{4}\,dt\geqslant V $$

for each $1\leqslant j\leqslant R$ , where $V\geqslant 1$ . Then for any $H\geqslant 1$ we have

$$ E_{2}(\{t_{1},\dots,t_{R}\};H)\prec R+\frac{RH}{V}+\frac{T\sqrt{R}}{V^{3/2}}. $$

#### Proof.

Since the intervals $[t_{j}-G,t_{j}+G]$ have disjoint interiors, the hypothesis and the fourth-moment bound give

$$ RV\leqslant\int_{T-G}^{2T+G}|\zeta(\tfrac{1}{2}+it)|^{4}\,dt\prec T. $$

If $H<G$ , then spacing gives $E_{2}(\{t_{1},\ldots,t_{R}\};H)=R$ . Furthermore, if $H\geqslant T$ , then a trivial bound and (47) imply

$$ E_{2}(\{t_{1},\ldots,t_{R}\};H)\leqslant R^{2}\prec\frac{RT}{V}\leqslant\frac{RH}{V}. $$

From now on, assume that $G\leqslant H<T$ . Partition $\mathbb{R}$ into intervals $(I_{\ell})_{\ell\in\mathbb{Z}}$ of length $H$ , and let $m_{\ell}$ denote the number of points $t_{j}$ (for $1\leqslant j\leqslant R$ ) which lie in $I_{\ell}$ . Pairs $t_{i},t_{j}$ with $|t_{i}-t_{j}|\leqslant H$ lie in the same or adjacent intervals $I_{\ell}$ , so

$$ E_{2}(\{t_{1},\ldots,t_{R}\};H)\ll\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\ell\end{subarray}}m_{\ell}^{2}. $$

By dyadic pigeonholing, there exists a scale $1\leqslant M\leqslant R$ such that denoting $J:=|\mathcal{J}|$ for $\mathcal{J}:=\{\ell\in\mathbb{Z}:M\leqslant m_{\ell}<2M\}$ , we have

$$ E_{2}(\{t_{1},\ldots,t_{R}\};H)\prec JM^{2}. $$

Note that $JM\leqslant R$ , and fix $\delta>0$ . If $MV\leqslant T^{\delta}\max(H,\sqrt{T})$ , then (47) gives

$$ JM^{2}\leqslant RM\ll\frac{RT^{\delta}}{V}\big(H+\sqrt{T}\big)\prec T^{\delta}\Big(\frac{RH}{V}+\frac{T\sqrt{R}}{V^{3/2}}\Big). $$

If instead $MV>T^{\delta}\max(H,\sqrt{T})$ , put

$$ L=\min(MVT^{-\delta},T). $$

Then $L>\max(H,\sqrt{T})$ , since $H<T$ , and clearly $L\leqslant T$ . We have

$$ JMV\ll\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\ell\in\mathcal{J}\end{subarray}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}t_{i}\in I_{\ell}\end{subarray}}\int_{|t-t_{i}|\leqslant G}|\zeta(1/2+it)|^{4}\,dt. $$

Since $G\leqslant H<L\leqslant T$ , the intervals of integration above can be covered by $O(J)$ disjoint intervals of length $L$ . Applying Proposition 8.1, we get

$$ JMV\prec JL+T\sqrt{J/L}. $$

The first term on the right-hand side is absorbed into the left-hand side, as $L\leqslant MVT^{-\delta}$ . Thus

$$ JM^{2}V^{2}\prec\frac{T^{2}}{L}\leqslant\frac{T^{2+\delta}}{MV}+T\prec\frac{T^{2+\delta}}{MV}. $$

Above we used that $MV\prec T$ , due to (47). Hence we conclude that

$$ JM^{3}\prec\frac{T^{2+\delta}}{V^{3}}. $$

Since $JM\leqslant R$ , this implies

$$ JM^{2}=\sqrt{JM}\cdot\sqrt{JM^{3}}\prec T^{\delta/2}\frac{T\sqrt{R}}{V^{3/2}}. $$

Taking $\delta>0$ arbitrarily small and collecting (48), (49), and (50) yields the desired estimate

$$ E_{2}(\{t_{1},\ldots,t_{R}\};H)\prec R+\frac{RH}{V}+\frac{T\sqrt{R}}{V^{3/2}}. $$

∎

## 9. Large value estimates for $|\zeta(1/2+it)|$

In this section, we show the following general large value estimate, whose case $k=2$ corresponds to Theorem 1.3.

#### Theorem 9.1.

Let $E_{2}(\sigma):=\frac{24-128\sigma}{17}$ and $[\sigma_{-}(2),\sigma_{+}(2)]:=\big[\frac{7}{60},\frac{5}{38}\big]$ . For integers $k\geqslant 3$ , let

$$ E_{k}(\sigma):=\frac{32k^{2}-12k-10-(192k^{2}-120k-28)\sigma}{16k^{2}+10k-17}, $$

$$ \sigma_{-}(k):=\frac{16k^{2}-22k+7}{8(16k^{2}-20k+5)},\qquad\text{and}\qquad\sigma_{+}(k):=\frac{4k-3}{30k-22}. $$

Then for any $\sigma\in[\sigma_{-}(k),\sigma_{+}(k)]$ we have

$$ N(T,T^{\sigma})\prec_{k}T^{E_{k}(\sigma)}. $$

In Figure 1, we plot the exponent $E(\sigma)$ for the best bound $N(T,T^{\sigma})\prec T^{E(\sigma)}$ obtained from Theorem 9.1 in each range, comparing it to the fourth and twelfth moment bounds.

*Figure 1. Plot of new large value exponents*

#### Proof of Theorem 9.1.

We may assume throughout the proof that $T$ is sufficiently large. Let $V=T^{\sigma}$ for $\sigma\in[\sigma_{-}(k),\sigma_{+}(k)]$ , and denote

$$ \tau:=\begin{cases}\frac{1}{2}+\sigma&\text{for }k=2,\\
4\cdot\frac{(8k-7)+(16k^{2}-46k+40)\sigma}{16k^{2}+10k-17}&\text{for }k\geqslant 3.\end{cases} $$

Suppose that $\mathcal{T}\subset[T,2T]$ is a $1$ -spaced set with $|\zeta(1/2+it)|\geqslant V$ for all $t\in\mathcal{T}$ . Write $R:=|\mathcal{T}|$ and $G:=V^{2}(\log T)^{-100}$ .

Partition $\mathbb{R}$ into intervals $(I_{\ell})_{\ell\in\mathbb{Z}}$ of length $\frac{2G}{3}$ , and let $f_{\ell}:=|\mathcal{T}\cap I_{\ell}|$ . By dyadic pigeonholing, there exists a scale $1\ll F\ll R$ such that denoting $\mathcal{L}:=\{\ell\in\mathbb{Z}:f_{\ell}\sim F\}$ , we have $|\mathcal{L}|F\succ R$ . Let $\mathcal{S}\subset[T,2T]$ be the set of leftmost points of the intervals $\overline{I_{\ell}}\cap[T,2T]$ , for $\ell\in\mathcal{L}$ whose congruence class modulo $4$ is the most abundant one among elements of $\mathcal{L}$ . Thus $\mathcal{S}$ is $2G$ -separated and $|\mathcal{S}|\succ R/F$ . By Lemma 7.4, for every $t\in\mathcal{S}$ we have

$$ \int_{|u-t|\leqslant G}|\zeta(\tfrac{1}{2}+iu)|^{2}\,du\gg\frac{FV^{2}}{\log T}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\int_{|u-t|\leqslant G}|\zeta(\tfrac{1}{2}+iu)|^{4}\,du\gg\frac{FV^{4}}{\log T}. $$

By Lemma 7.1 and further dyadic pigeonholing, there exist a scale

$$ T^{1/3}\ll N\ll\frac{T}{G^{2}}(\log T)^{2} $$

and $\mathcal{S}^{\prime}\subset\mathcal{S}$ still satisfying $|\mathcal{S}^{\prime}|\succ R/F$ such that for every $t\in\mathcal{S}^{\prime}$ we have

$$ \max_{0\leqslant\Delta\leqslant N}|S_{t}(\Delta,N)|\succ\frac{FV^{2}(TN)^{1/4}}{G}\succ F(TN)^{1/4}. $$

At this point, take

$$ W:=N^{\frac{\tau}{1-4\sigma}}(\log T)^{-1000}+N. $$

We record that $\sigma\in[\sigma_{-}(k),\sigma_{+}(k)]$ implies that

$$ N\leqslant T^{\frac{3}{5}},\qquad N\leqslant W\leqslant N^{\frac{4}{3}},\qquad N^{1/2}W^{2}\leqslant T^{3/2}. $$

In particular, also $W\leqslant\sqrt{TN}$ . Further subdividing $[T,2T]$ , we may partition $\mathcal{S}^{\prime}$ into sets

$$ \mathcal{S}_{j}\subset\biggl[t_{0,j},t_{0,j}+W\sqrt{\frac{T}{N}}\biggr]\qquad\text{with}\qquad t_{0,j}:=T+(j-1)W\sqrt{\frac{T}{N}}\asymp T $$

for $1\leqslant j\leqslant J\asymp\frac{\sqrt{TN}}{W}$ . Now, let

$$ \mathcal{W}_{j}:=\bigg\{\sqrt{\frac{2N}{\pi}}(\sqrt{t}-\sqrt{t_{0,j}}):t\in\mathcal{S}_{j}\bigg\}\subset[0,W]. $$

The mean value theorem shows that each $\mathcal{W}_{j}$ is $\gg G\sqrt{N/T}$ -spaced.

Using (56), we may apply Corollary 7.2 and Lemma 7.3 to (55), concluding that there exist coefficients $|a_{j,n}|\leqslant 1$ such that setting

$$ \eta_{j}:=-\frac{\pi N}{12t_{0,j}}\qquad\text{and}\qquad D_{\eta}^{j}(w):=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}n\sim N\end{subarray}}a_{j,n}e(w\phi_{\eta}(n/N)), $$

we have that

$$ \sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}1\leqslant j\leqslant J\end{subarray}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}w\in\mathcal{W}_{j}\end{subarray}}\big|D_{\eta_{j}}^{j}(w)\big|\succ F(TN)^{1/4}|\mathcal{S}^{\prime}|\succ R(TN)^{1/4}. $$

Dyadic pigeonholing for the size of $|D_{\eta_{j}}^{j}(w)|$ implies that there exists a scale $Z$ and subsets $\mathcal{W}_{j}^{\prime}\subset\mathcal{W}_{j}$ such that for every $1\leqslant j\leqslant J$ and $w\in\mathcal{W}_{j}^{\prime}$ we have $|D_{\eta_{j}}^{j}(w)|\sim Z$ and the bounds

$$ Z\succ F(TN)^{1/4},\quad R_{1}Z\succ R(TN)^{1/4},\qquad\text{ where }R_{1}:=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}j\end{subarray}}|\mathcal{W}_{j}^{\prime}|. $$

Partition each $\mathcal{W}_{j}^{\prime}\subset[0,W]$ into $\prec G^{-1}\sqrt{T/N}$ subsets $\mathcal{W}_{j,\ell}^{\prime}$ that are $1$ -spaced. It can be checked that

$$ \frac{|\eta_{j}|N^{2}}{W}\ll\frac{N^{3}}{TW}\prec T^{2-12\sigma-\tau}=o(1)\qquad\text{as}\qquad T\to\infty. $$

Thus we may apply Theorem 5.1, which implies that for each $1\leqslant j\leqslant J$ and $\ell$ we have

$$ |\mathcal{W}_{j,\ell}^{\prime}|\prec_{k}\frac{N^{2}}{Z^{2}}+\frac{N^{\frac{6k-4}{2k+1}}W^{\frac{k+1}{2k+1}}}{Z^{\frac{8k-4}{2k+1}}}\Bigg(\sup_{\begin{subarray}{c}1\leqslant D\ll_{k}1+\frac{NW}{T}\end{subarray}}\frac{E_{2}(\mathcal{W}_{j,\ell}^{\prime};D)}{\sqrt{D}}\Bigg)^{\frac{1}{2k+1}}+\frac{N^{k+\frac{1}{2}}W^{\frac{k+1}{2}}\big(1+\frac{NW}{T}\big)^{\frac{1}{4}}}{Z^{2k+1}}. $$

Let $\mathcal{S}^{\prime\prime}\subset\mathcal{S}^{\prime}$ consist of the original ordinates corresponding to the elements of the retained sets $\mathcal{W}^{\prime}_{j}$ . More precisely, $t\in\mathcal{S}^{\prime\prime}$ corresponds to $\sqrt{2N/\pi}\big(\sqrt{t}-\sqrt{t_{0,j}}\big)\in\mathcal{W}^{\prime}_{j}$ . Thus $|\mathcal{S}^{\prime\prime}|=R_{1}$ and

$$ \sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}j,\ell\end{subarray}}E_{2}(\mathcal{W}_{j,\ell}^{\prime};D)\ll E_{2}(\mathcal{S}^{\prime\prime};D\sqrt{T/N}). $$

By (54) and Corollary 8.2, this implies that

$$ \sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}j,\ell\end{subarray}}E_{2}(\mathcal{W}_{j,\ell}^{\prime};D)\prec R_{1}+\frac{R_{1}D\sqrt{T/N}}{FV^{4}}+\frac{T\sqrt{R_{1}}}{F^{3/2}V^{6}}. $$

Separately, the $1$ -spacing of each $\mathcal{W}^{\prime}_{j,\ell}$ also implies the bound $O(R_{1}D)$ for the above. We may absorb the middle term of (60) into the first one because $N\gg T^{1/3}$ and $\tau\leqslant\tfrac{1}{2}+\sigma\leqslant 6\sigma$ , so

$$ D\sqrt{T/N}\ll\sqrt{T/N}+W\sqrt{N/T}\prec T^{1/3}+T^{\tau-2\sigma}\prec V^{4}. $$

Therefore, we have that

$$ \sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}j,\ell\end{subarray}}E_{2}(\mathcal{W}_{j,\ell}^{\prime};D)\prec R_{1}\biggl(1+\frac{T}{F^{3/2}V^{6}\sqrt{R_{1}}}\biggr). $$

The total number of subsets $\mathcal{W}_{j,\ell}^{\prime}$ is

$$ \prec J\cdot\frac{\sqrt{T/N}}{G}\prec\frac{\sqrt{TN}}{W}\cdot\frac{\sqrt{T/N}}{G}\ll\frac{T}{GW}, $$

so combining with (59), we obtain

$$ R_{1}\prec_{k}\frac{T}{GW}\biggl[\frac{N^{2}}{Z^{2}}+\frac{N^{3-\frac{2}{k}}W^{\frac{k+1}{2k}}}{Z^{4-\frac{2}{k}}}\biggl(1+\frac{T}{F^{3/2}V^{6}\sqrt{R_{1}}}\biggr)^{\frac{1}{4k}}+\frac{N^{k+\frac{1}{2}}W^{\frac{k+1}{2}}\big(1+\frac{NW}{T}\big)^{1/4}}{Z^{2k+1}}\biggr]. $$

Rearranging to clear the power of $R_{1}$ , this gives

$$ \displaystyle R_{1}\prec_{k}\frac{T}{GW}\biggl[\frac{N^{2}}{Z^{2}}+\frac{N^{3-\frac{2}{k}}W^{\frac{k+1}{2k}}}{Z^{4-2/k}}+\frac{N^{k+\frac{1}{2}}W^{\frac{k+1}{2}}\big(1+\frac{NW}{T}\big)^{\frac{1}{4}}}{Z^{2k+1}}\biggr]+\biggl(\frac{T^{8k+2}N^{24k-16}}{G^{8k}W^{4k-4}Z^{32k-16}F^{3}V^{12}}\biggr)^{\frac{1}{8k+1}}. $$

Multiplying by $Z/(TN)^{1/4}$ and using that $R\prec ZR_{1}/(TN)^{1/4}$ and $Z\succ F(TN)^{1/4}$ , we get

$$ R\prec_{k}\frac{T^{\frac{1}{2}}N^{\frac{3}{2}}}{GW}+\frac{T^{\frac{1}{2k}}N^{2-\frac{3}{2k}}}{GW^{\frac{k-1}{2k}}}+\frac{T^{\frac{3}{4}-\frac{k}{2}}N^{\frac{k}{2}+\frac{1}{4}}W^{\frac{k-1}{2}}\big(1+\frac{NW}{T}\big)^{\frac{1}{4}}}{G}+\biggl(\frac{T^{6}N^{16k-12}}{G^{8k}W^{4k-4}V^{12}}\biggr)^{\frac{1}{8k+1}}. $$

Using that $N\prec T^{1-4\sigma}$ and $N^{\frac{\tau}{1-4\sigma}}\prec W\prec N^{\frac{\tau}{1-4\sigma}}$ , this leads to

$$ R\prec_{k}T^{2-8\sigma-\tau}+T^{2-\frac{1}{k}-(10-\frac{6}{k})\sigma-\frac{k-1}{2k}\tau}+T^{1-(2k+4)\sigma+\frac{2k-1}{4}\tau}+T^{\frac{16k-6-(80k-36)\sigma-4(k-1)\tau}{8k+1}}. $$

Our choice of $\tau$ satisfies

$$ \frac{16k-6-(80k-36)\sigma-4(k-1)\tau}{8k+1}=E_{k}(\sigma). $$

For $k\geqslant 3$ , the third exponent in (67) also equals $E_{k}(\sigma)$ , while the second is at most $E_{k}(\sigma)$ precisely when $\sigma\leqslant\sigma_{+}(k)$ ; the first is smaller throughout the stated range. For $k=2$ , the second and third exponents both equal $\frac{11}{8}-\frac{29\sigma}{4}$ , which is $\leqslant E_{2}(\sigma)$ for $\sigma\leqslant\frac{5}{38}$ . The first exponent in (67) is also smaller than the third for $\sigma\in\big[\frac{7}{60},\frac{5}{38}\big]$ . Hence we obtain the desired bound $R\prec_{k}T^{E_{k}(\sigma)}$ . ∎

## 10. Improved moment bounds

An immediate consequence of our large value estimates, combined with work of Trudgian and Yang [24], is the following improvement of the twelfth moment bound of Heath-Brown [10].

#### Theorem 10.1 (Twelfth moment bound).

For every $T\geqslant 1$ and $\varepsilon>0$ , we have

$$ \int_{0}^{T}|\zeta(\tfrac{1}{2}+it)|^{12}\,dt\ll_{\varepsilon}T^{2-\frac{520}{445121}+\varepsilon}. $$

For reference, $\frac{520}{445121}$ is slightly greater than $\frac{1}{1000}$ .

#### Proof.

Theorem 9.1 with $k=6$ states that

$$ N(T,T^{\sigma})\prec T^{\frac{1070-6164\sigma}{619}}\qquad\text{for}\qquad\tfrac{451}{3688}\leqslant\sigma\leqslant\tfrac{21}{158}. $$

Combined with [24, Lemma 5.1], using the exponent pair $\big(\frac{64}{135},\frac{122}{243}\big)$ corresponding to $m=10$ in their given sequence, we also have

$$ N(T,V)\prec TV^{-6}+T^{\frac{593}{288}}V^{-\frac{3587}{288}}. $$

Applying the subconvexity bound of Bourgain [3], it can be checked that for $\sigma_{1}=\frac{451}{3688}$ and $\sigma_{2}=\frac{58907}{445121}$ we have

$$ \displaystyle\int_{T}^{2T}|\zeta(\tfrac{1}{2}+it)|^{12}\,dt \displaystyle\prec\sup_{\begin{subarray}{c}\sigma\in\left[0,\frac{13}{84}\right]\end{subarray}}T^{12\sigma}N(T,T^{\sigma}) \displaystyle\hskip-85.35826pt\prec\max\Big(\sup_{\begin{subarray}{c}\sigma\in[0,\sigma_{1}]\end{subarray}}T^{1+8\sigma},\sup_{\begin{subarray}{c}\sigma\in[\sigma_{1},\sigma_{2}]\end{subarray}}T^{\frac{1070+1264\sigma}{619}},\sup_{\begin{subarray}{c}\sigma\in\left[\sigma_{2},\frac{13}{84}\right]\end{subarray}}T^{\max\left(1+6\sigma,\frac{593-131\sigma}{288}\right)}\Big)\prec T^{2-\frac{520}{445121}+\varepsilon}. $$

Splitting into dyadic intervals yields Theorem 10.1. ∎

The claimed improvements for all intermediate moments is now simple to deduce.

#### Proof of Theorem 1.2.

The existence of some $\delta_{k}>0$ for each $4<k\leqslant 12$ follows from interpolation between the fourth moment and the new twelfth moment bound in Theorem 10.1. ∎

#### Proof of Theorem 1.1.

Let $V_{0}=T^{7/60}$ and $V_{1}=T^{5/38}$ . Dyadically decomposing the level sets $|\zeta(1/2+it)|\geqslant V$ , using Theorem 1.3 for $V\in[V_{0},V_{1}]$ , and (2) for $V$ outside of this range, we get

$$ \int_{T}^{2T}|\zeta(\tfrac{1}{2}+it)|^{6}\,dt\ll_{\varepsilon}T^{\varepsilon}\bigl(TV_{0}^{2}+T^{\frac{24}{17}}V_{0}^{-\frac{26}{17}}+T^{2}V_{1}^{-6}\bigr)\ll_{\varepsilon}T^{\frac{37}{30}+\varepsilon}. $$

Summing over dyadic intervals gives the desired bound, since $\frac{37}{30}=\frac{5}{4}-\frac{1}{60}$ . ∎

# Higher order uniformity of the primes and cancellation of the Möbius function in shorter intervals

**Authors:** Kaisa Matomäki Address: Department of Mathematics and Statistics, University of Turku, 20014 Turku, Finland Email address: ksmato@utu.fi , Mayank Pandey Address: Courant Institute of Mathematical Sciences, 251 Mercer Street, New York, NY, 10012 Email address: mayankpandey9973@gmail.com , Javier Pliego Address: Departamento de Matemáticas, Facultad de Ciencias, Universidad Autónoma de Madrid, Ciudad Universitaria de Cantoblanco, 28049 Madrid, Spain Email address: javier.pliego@uam.es , Joni Teräväinen Address: Department of Pure Mathematics and Mathematical Statistics, University of Cambridge, Cambridge CB3 0WB, UK Email address: joni.p.teravainen@gmail.com and Mengdi Wang Address: École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne (EPFL), Lausanne, Switzerland Email address: mengdi.wang@epfl.ch

## Abstract

We prove the Gowers uniformity of the von Mangoldt function minus its Cramér model in all short intervals $[X,X+X^{3/5+\varepsilon}]$ , improving on the work of the first and fourth authors with Shao and Tao, where the exponent was $5/8$ . This also implies a local-to-global theorem for linear equations in primes in such short intervals.

We also show that the Möbius function has cancellation in all intervals $[X,X+X^{19/35+\varepsilon}]$ , improving on the work of the first and fourth authors, where the exponent was $11/20$ .

Both improvements are based on improved treatment of trilinear sums over short intervals which naturally reduces to estimating mean values of products of three Dirichlet polynomials. In a general setting, we reduce the task of estimating mean values of products of Dirichlet polynomials with given large value bounds to the task of showing that a certain piecewise linear function is positive. This reduction allows recent large value estimates to be incorporated.

Combining this general framework with the most recent large value estimates stemming from the work of Guth and Maynard, we prove a Heath-Brown–Iwaniec type estimate for type I/II sums in intervals of length $X^{19/35+\varepsilon}$ and a Baker–Harman–Pintz parallelogram type estimate for general trilinear sums in intervals of length $X^{3/5+\varepsilon}$ .

## 1. Introduction

### 1.1. Higher order uniformity results

Our first main result concerns higher order uniformity of the von Mangoldt function $\Lambda$ minus its Cramér model in all short intervals of length $X^{3/5+\varepsilon}$ . The Cramér model $\Lambda_{X}^{\sharp}$ is defined, following [10, (1.1)], by

$$ \Lambda_{X}^{\sharp}(n)\coloneqq\frac{\mathcal{P}(R)}{\varphi(\mathcal{P}(R))}\,\mathbf{1}_{(n,\mathcal{P}(R))=1},\quad\text{with }R=\exp(\log^{1/10}X)\quad\text{and}\quad\mathcal{P}(R)=\prod_{p<R}p. $$

The following theorem improves on the work of the first and fourth authors with Shao and Tao [10, Theorem 1.5(i)], where the interval length $X^{5/8+\varepsilon}$ for the Gowers uniformity of $\Lambda-\Lambda^{\sharp}$ was obtained.

#### Theorem 1.1 (Higher order uniformity of $\Lambda$ ).

Let $s\geqslant 1$ be an integer and $\varepsilon>0$ . Uniformly for $X\geqslant 3$ and

$$ X^{3/5+\varepsilon}\leqslant H\leqslant X, $$

one has11 1 See Section 1.6 for the definition of the Gowers norm

$$ \left\lVert\Lambda-\Lambda_{X}^{\sharp}\right\rVert_{U^{s}(X,X+H]}=o_{s,\varepsilon}(1). $$

By applying the inverse theorem for the Gowers norms, Theorem 1.1 reduces to showing discorrelation of the von Mangoldt function minus its model against all fixed complexity nilsequences. Such an estimate is the key technical input for proving Theorem 1.1, and since the approach via combinatorial decompositions is quite flexible, it naturally leads to a similar result for the Möbius function.

#### Theorem 1.2 (Nilsequence discorrelation).

Let $d,D\in\mathbb{N}$ , let $\varepsilon>0$ , $\delta\in(0,1/2)$ , $X\geqslant 3$ , and

$$ X^{3/5+\varepsilon}\leqslant H\leqslant X^{1-\varepsilon}. $$

Let $G/\Gamma$ be a filtered nilmanifold22 2 The symbols relating to nilsequences have the same meanings as in [10, Section 2.3]. of degree at most $d$ , dimension at most $D$ , and complexity at most $1/\delta$ , and let $F\colon G/\Gamma\to\mathbb{C}$ be a Lipschitz function of norm at most $1/\delta$ . Then, for every $A>0$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\sup_{g\in\Poly(\mathbb{Z}\to G)}\left\lvert\sum_{X<n\leqslant X+H}\mu(n)\overline{F(g(n)\Gamma)}\right\rvert^{\,*} \displaystyle\ll_{A,\varepsilon,d,D}\delta^{-O_{d,D}(1)}\frac{H}{\log^{A}X}, \displaystyle\sup_{g\in\Poly(\mathbb{Z}\to G)}\left\lvert\sum_{X<n\leqslant X+H}(\Lambda(n)-\Lambda_{X}^{\sharp}(n))\overline{F(g(n)\Gamma)}\right\rvert^{\,*} \displaystyle\ll_{A,\varepsilon,d,D}\delta^{-O_{d,D}(1)}\frac{H}{\log^{A}X}. $$

Remarks.

- (1) We could also obtain a similar improvement for the $k\geqslant 4$ case of [10, Theorem 1.1(iii)] concerning higher order uniformity of the $k$ -fold divisor function $d_{k}$ . We leave the details for the interested reader.

- (2) For the von Mangoldt function, this result improves on [10, Theorem 1.1], where one had $H\in[X^{5/8+\varepsilon},X^{1-\varepsilon}]$ .

- (3) For the Möbius function, this result improves on [10, Theorem 1.1(iv)], where the length range was the same but the savings were a small power of logarithm. The smaller savings already sufficed for proving the Gowers uniformity of $\mu$ in short intervals $(X,X+X^{3/5+\varepsilon}]$ in [10, Theorem 1.5(iii)], so we do not state this consequence here.

As in [10], we obtain an immediate corollary for polynomial phases.

#### Corollary 1.3 (Polynomial phases).

Let $\varepsilon>0$ , $d\geqslant 1$ , $A>0$ , $X\geqslant 3$ , and $X^{3/5+\varepsilon}\leqslant H\leqslant X^{1-\varepsilon}$ . For every polynomial $P\in\mathbb{R}[Y]$ of degree at most $d$ ,

$$ \left\lvert\sum_{X<n\leqslant X+H}\mu(n)e(P(n))\right\rvert\ll_{A,d,\varepsilon}\frac{H}{\log^{A}X}. $$

Moreover, we have

$$ \left\lvert\sum_{X<n\leqslant X+H}\Lambda(n)e(P(n))\right\rvert\ll_{A,d,\varepsilon}\frac{H}{\log^{A}X}, $$

unless, writing

$$ P(\lfloor X\rfloor+m)=\alpha_{0}+\alpha_{1}m+\cdots+\alpha_{d}m^{d}, $$

there exists an integer $1\leqslant q\leqslant\log^{O_{A,d,\varepsilon}(1)}X$ such that

$$ \max_{1\leqslant j\leqslant d}H^{j}\left\lVert q\alpha_{j}\right\rVert_{\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}}\leqslant\log^{O_{A,d,\varepsilon}(1)}X. $$

We also remark that, for the Möbius function and when $\deg P=1$ , an upcoming work of the third and fifth authors [12, Theorem 1.1] extends the orthogonality estimate (1.5) to the range $X^{0.58+\varepsilon}\leqslant H\leqslant X$ , albeit with a weaker error term $O(H(\log X)^{-1/3+\varepsilon})$ , thereby providing only a small logarithmic saving.

#### Proof of Corollary 1.3 assuming Theorem 1.2.

Polynomial phases are nilsequences on the filtered torus $\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}$ with filtration degree $d$ , so (1.5) follows directly from Theorem 1.2. For (1.6), write $\Lambda=(\Lambda-\Lambda_{X}^{\sharp})+\Lambda_{X}^{\sharp}$ . The first term is covered by Theorem 1.2; the second is a standard major arc calculation for the Cramér model (1.1), giving a negligible contribution unless (1.7) holds. This is the argument of [10, Corollary 1.3] with $5/8$ replaced by $3/5$ . ∎

### 1.2. Results on short sums of arithmetic functions

Using variants of the arithmetic inputs that go into our higher order uniformity results also leads to improvements in several results about untwisted short sums of multiplicatively defined sequences. In particular, we obtain cancellation for sums of the Möbius function in shorter intervals than was previously known, improving on the work of the first and fourth authors [11, Theorem 1.1], who had the exponent $11/20=0.55$ in place of $19/35\approx 0.54286$ .

#### Theorem 1.4 (Möbius sums in short intervals).

Let $\varepsilon>0$ . Uniformly for $X\geqslant 3$ and

$$ X^{19/35+\varepsilon}\leqslant H\leqslant X, $$

one has

$$ \left|\sum_{X<n\leqslant X+H}\mu(n)\right|\ll_{\varepsilon}\frac{H}{\log^{1/3-\varepsilon}X}. $$

We can similarly improve other results in [11]. Firstly, we can sharpen the exponent in a result about sums of two squares in short intervals ([11, Theorem 1.2]) from $11/20$ to $19/35$ .

#### Theorem 1.5.

Let $N_{0}(X)$ be the number of integers $\leqslant X$ that are expressible as sums of two squares of integers. Let $\varepsilon>0$ be fixed. Uniformly for $X\geqslant 3$ and $X^{19/35+\varepsilon}\leqslant H\leqslant X,$ one has

$$ N_{0}(X+H)-N_{0}(X)=\frac{CH}{\log^{1/2}X}+O\left(\frac{H}{\log^{2/3-\varepsilon}X}\right), $$

where $C=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\prod_{p\equiv 3\,(\mathrm{mod}\,4)}(1-1/p^{2})^{-1/2}$ is the Landau–Ramanujan constant.

Likewise, we can improve the exponent $\theta_{k}$ for which the expected asymptotic formula for the sum of the $k$ -fold divisor functions $d_{k}$ on short intervals of length $H\geqslant X^{\theta_{k}+\varepsilon}$ is valid. The previous best known value for $\theta_{k}$ when $k\geqslant 5$ was $\theta_{k}=11/20$ (see [11, Theorem 1.3]).

#### Theorem 1.6.

Let $\varepsilon>0$ and let $k\geqslant 5$ be an integer. Uniformly for $X\geqslant 3$ and $X^{19/35+\varepsilon}\leqslant H\leqslant X$ one has

$$ \sum_{X<n\leqslant X+H}d_{k}(n)=(X+H)P_{k-1}(\log(X+H))-XP_{k-1}(\log X)+O\big(H(\log X)^{(2/3+\varepsilon)k-1}\big), $$

where $P_{k-1}$ is an explicit polynomial of degree $k-1$ (see [14, equation (5.36) in Section II.5.4])33 3 In [11, Theorem 1.3] the main term is simplified to $HQ_{k-1}(\log X)$ where $Q_{k-1}=P_{k-1}+P_{k-1}^{\prime}$ in the current paper’s notation, but in fact this is only valid if $H/X\ll(\log X)^{1-k/3+k\varepsilon}$ , and for $H$ close to $X$ one must retain the difference above..

Lastly, we include a result concerning $E_{2}$ almost primes, that is, numbers of the shape $p_{1}p_{2}$ with $p_{1},p_{2}$ primes, improving the exponent $11/20$ in [11, Theorem 1.4].

#### Theorem 1.7.

Let $\varepsilon>0$ . Uniformly for $X\geqslant 100$ and $X^{19/35+\varepsilon}\leqslant H\leqslant X$ one has

$$ \sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}X<n\leqslant X+H\\
n\in E_{2}\end{subarray}}1=\frac{H\log\log X}{\log X}+O\Big(\frac{H\log\log\log X}{\log X}\Big). $$

### 1.3. A result on short patterns in the primes

Theorem 1.1 also yields an asymptotic local-to-global theorem for primes in short intervals, improving on [10, Theorem 1.7]. The deduction of the following theorem from Theorem 1.1 is the same as [10, Proof of Theorem 1.7 in Section 10] and we will not repeat it in this paper.

#### Theorem 1.8 (Linear equations in primes in short intervals of exponent $3/5$ ).

Let $\varepsilon>0$ and $X^{3/5+\varepsilon}\leqslant H\leqslant X^{1-\varepsilon}$ . Let $d,t\geqslant 1$ be integers and let $L\geqslant 1$ . Let $\Psi=(\psi_{1},\ldots,\psi_{t})$ be a system of affine linear forms $\psi_{i}\colon\mathbb{Z}^{d}\to\mathbb{Z}$ of the shape

$$ \psi_{i}(\mathbf{n})=\dot{\psi}_{i}\cdot\mathbf{n}+\psi_{i}(0),\qquad\dot{\psi}_{i}\in\mathbb{Z}^{d}, $$

with $0<\|\dot{\psi}_{i}\|_{\infty}\leqslant L$ and $\left\lvert\psi_{i}(0)\right\rvert\leqslant LX$ , and suppose that $\dot{\psi}_{i}$ and $\dot{\psi}_{j}$ are linearly independent over $\mathbb{Q}$ whenever $i\neq j$ . Let $K\subset(X,X+H]^{d}$ be a convex body. Extend $\Lambda$ by zero to the nonpositive integers. Then,

$$ \sum_{\mathbf{n}\in K\cap\mathbb{Z}^{d}}\prod_{i=1}^{t}\Lambda(\psi_{i}(\mathbf{n}))=\beta_{\infty}\prod_{p}\beta_{p}+o_{d,t,L,\varepsilon}(H^{d}), $$

where

$$ \beta_{\infty}=\vol\bigl(K\cap\Psi^{-1}(\mathbb{R}_{>0}^{t})\bigr) $$

and

$$ \beta_{p}=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{n}\in(\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z})^{d}}\prod_{i=1}^{t}\frac{p}{p-1}\mathbf{1}_{\psi_{i}(\mathbf{n})\not\equiv 0\pmod{p}}. $$

#### Remark 1.9.

Note that for all primes $p$ one has $\beta_{p}=1+O_{d,t,L}(p^{-2})$ . Thus the Euler product in (1.9) converges absolutely. It is zero if and only if one of the local factors $\beta_{p}$ vanishes.

### 1.4. Plan for the paper

Using Heath-Brown’s identity, the work of [10] on the case of non-abelian nilmanifolds, and a standard Perron formula argument, we reduce our main task to bounding mean values of products of Dirichlet polynomials.

In Section 2 we collect some known mean and large value results for Dirichlet polynomials. In Section 3 we reduce the task of estimating mean values of products of Dirichlet polynomials with given large value bounds to the task of showing that a piecewise linear function is positive. This reduction is directly adaptable to other contexts.

In Sections 4 and 5 we utilise the results of the two previous sections to prove new mean value estimates for products of three Dirichlet polynomials. The elementary proofs that the corresponding piecewise linear functions are positive are postponed to Section 8.

In Section 6 we prove Theorem 1.1 through nilsequence discorrelation, and in Section 7 we prove Theorem 1.4, using Ramaré’s identity.

### 1.5. Limiting cases

In the proofs of the above theorems, there are some limiting cases for the lengths of the Dirichlet polynomials arising from Heath-Brown’s identity which force one to impose the restrictions $H\geqslant X^{3/5+\varepsilon}$ and $H\geqslant X^{19/35+\varepsilon}$ respectively, preventing any further improvement (apart from possibly improving on the $+\varepsilon$ , in the spirit of Heath-Brown’s work [7]) without new arithmetic information. In the setting of Theorem 1.1, the particular case in which there are four Dirichlet polynomials of length $X^{1/4+o(1)}$ entails bounding the large value set of the polynomials “corresponding to the $7/10$ -line”, and this does not seem to be tractable whenever $H\leqslant X^{3/5}$ with the current technology available. A similar situation occurs in the context of Theorems 1.4–1.7 for the case of five Dirichlet polynomials of length $X^{1/5+o(1)}$ and the large value set of the polynomials “corresponding to the $5/7$ -line” (see Remarks 4.3 and 5.4 for a more technical discussion).

### 1.6. Notation

We use the usual Landau and Vinogradov notation $O(\cdot),o(\cdot),\ll,\gg,\asymp$ . Implied constants may depend on fixed structural parameters such as the degree of the Gowers norms, nilmanifold degree and dimension, the number of forms in a linear system, and on $\varepsilon>0$ , but not on $X$ and $H$ .

As in [10, (1.4)], for an interval $I\subset\mathbb{R}$ of length $\geqslant 1$ and a function $f$ on $I\cap\mathbb{Z}$ , define the maximal progression norm

$$ \left\lvert\sum_{n\in I\cap\mathbb{Z}}f(n)\right\rvert^{\,*}\coloneqq\sup_{P\subseteq I\cap\mathbb{Z}}\left\lvert\sum_{n\in P}f(n)\right\rvert, $$

where $P$ ranges over all arithmetic progressions contained in $I\cap\mathbb{Z}$ .

As in [10, Definition 2.1], we define the total variation norm as follows. Let $P$ be an arithmetic progression and let $f\colon P\to\mathbb{C}$ . Define

$$ \|f\|_{\mathrm{TV}(P)}\coloneqq\sup_{n\in P}|f(n)|+\sup_{\begin{subarray}{c}k\geqslant 1\\
n_{1}<\cdots<n_{k}\\
n_{1},\ldots,n_{k}\in P\end{subarray}}\sum_{j=1}^{k-1}|f(n_{j+1})-f(n_{j})|. $$

We set $\|f\|_{\mathrm{TV}(P)}=0$ when $P=\emptyset$ . If $q\geqslant 1$ is an integer, we also write

$$ \|f\|_{\mathrm{TV}(P;q)}\coloneqq\sum_{a\bmod q}\|f\|_{\mathrm{TV}(P\cap(a+q\mathbb{Z}))}. $$

For an integer $s\geqslant 1$ and a finitely supported function $f\colon\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{C}$ , define the unnormalised Gowers norm by

$$ \left\lVert f\right\rVert_{U^{s}(\mathbb{Z})}\coloneqq\left(\sum_{x,h_{1},\ldots,h_{s}\in\mathbb{Z}}\prod_{\omega\in\{0,1\}^{s}}\mathcal{C}^{|\omega|}f(x+\omega_{1}h_{1}+\cdots+\omega_{s}h_{s})\right)^{1/2^{s}}, $$

where $\mathcal{C}$ denotes complex conjugation and $|\omega|=\omega_{1}+\cdots+\omega_{s}$ . For a bounded interval $I\subset\mathbb{R}$ containing an integer and an arbitrary function $f\colon\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{C}$ , set

$$ \left\lVert f\right\rVert_{U^{s}(I)}\coloneqq\frac{\left\lVert f\mathbf{1}_{I}\right\rVert_{U^{s}(\mathbb{Z})}}{\left\lVert\mathbf{1}_{I}\right\rVert_{U^{s}(\mathbb{Z})}}. $$

Finally, we write $e(x)=e^{2\pi ix}$ for $x\in\mathbb{R}$ .

## 2. Mean and large value results for Dirichlet polynomials

In this section we collect mean and large value results for Dirichlet polynomials. Let $s\in\mathbb{C}$ . We say that a Dirichlet polynomial

$$ A(s):=\sum_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\frac{a(n)}{n^{s}} $$

has length at most $N$ if the coefficients are supported on $[1,N]$ .

#### Definition 2.1.

Let $\nu\geqslant 0$ and $T\geqslant 1$ , and let $\mathcal{T}\subseteq[T,2T]$ be a subset. Suppose that $A(s)$ is a Dirichlet polynomial whose coefficients are supported on $(X^{\beta},2X^{\beta}]$ with $\beta>0$ . We define $\mathcal{N}_{A}(\nu;\mathcal{T})$ to be the maximal cardinality of a $1$ -separated subset $\mathcal{U}\subseteq\mathcal{T}$ such that

$$ |A(1/2+it)|\geqslant X^{\beta(\frac{1}{2}-\nu)}\qquad\text{for all }t\in\mathcal{U}. $$

For example, if $|a(n)|\leqslant 1$ , then [4, Theorem 1.1] implies

$$ \mathcal{N}_{A}(\nu;[T,2T])\ll T^{o(1)}(X^{2\beta\nu}+X^{\beta(4\nu-2/5)}+TX^{\beta(4\nu-8/5)}). $$

We will bound $\mathcal{N}_{A}(\nu;\mathcal{T})$ by $X^{\mathcal{K}(\beta,\nu;\tau)+o(1)}$ , where the function $\mathcal{K}(\beta,\nu;\tau)$ is defined as follows.

#### Definition 2.2.

We define the functions $\mathcal{K},\mathcal{K}_{0}\colon\mathbb{R}_{+}\times\mathbb{R}_{\geqslant 0}\times(0,1]\to\mathbb{R}$ via

$$ \mathcal{K}_{0}(\beta,\nu;\tau):=\min\left\{\tau+\beta(6\nu-2),\max\left\{\tau+\beta\left(4\nu-\frac{8}{5}\right),\frac{\tau}{2}+\beta(4\nu-1)\right\},\tau+\beta(2\nu-1)\right\}, $$

and

$$ \mathcal{K}(\beta,\nu;\tau):=\min\left\{\tau,\max\left\{2\beta\nu,\mathcal{K}_{0}(\beta,\nu;\tau)\right\}\right\}. $$

To provide some intuition, we point out that the three terms in $\mathcal{K}_{0}(\beta,\nu;\tau)$ arise from the Halász–Montgomery–Huxley large values estimates, the Chen–Gupta–Li large values estimates [2] (that refine Guth–Maynard’s bound), and the diagonal contribution in the second moment estimate, respectively.

#### Lemma 2.3 (Large values estimates).

Let $B\geqslant 1$ be fixed. Let $\beta>0$ , $X\geqslant 3$ , and

$$ A(s)=\sum_{X^{\beta}<n\leqslant 2X^{\beta}}a(n)n^{-s},\qquad|a(n)|\leqslant d_{B}(n)\log^{B}X. $$

Let $T=X^{\tau}$ with $\tau\in(0,1]$ . Then the following statements hold:

- (i) For every $\nu\geqslant 0$ and every fixed $k\in\mathbb{N}$ , we have (2.1)

$$ \mathcal{N}_{A}(\nu;[T,2T])\ll X^{\mathcal{K}(\beta k,\nu;\tau)+o(1)}. $$

- (ii) There is a constant $C=C(B)>0$ such that the following holds. Let

$$ a(n)=\mathbf{1}_{n\in I}\chi(n)\log^{r}n, $$

where $I\subseteq(X^{\beta},2X^{\beta}]$ is an interval, $\chi$ is a Dirichlet character of modulus $\ll\log^{B}X$ and $r\in\{0,1\}$ . Let $\mathcal{T}\subseteq[T,2T]$ be such that (2.2)

$$ |A(1/2+it)|\geqslant\frac{X^{\beta/2}}{T}\log^{C}X $$

for every $t\in\mathcal{T}$ . Then, if $\tau>1/\sqrt{\log X}$ , for every $\nu\geqslant 0$ we have (2.3)

$$ \mathcal{N}_{A}(\nu;\mathcal{T})\ll X^{\tau+2\beta(2\nu-1)+o(1)}. $$

#### Proof.

Proof of (i). We first note that it suffices to prove

$$ \mathcal{N}_{A}(\nu;[T,2T])\ll X^{\mathcal{K}(\beta,\nu;\tau)+o(1)}. $$

Indeed, let $k\in\mathbb{N}$ be fixed and write

$$ A(s)^{k}=\sum_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\frac{c_{k}(n)}{n^{s}}. $$

The coefficients are supported on $N^{k}<n\leqslant 2^{k}N^{k}$ , where $N=X^{\beta}$ , and satisfy

$$ |c_{k}(n)|\leqslant d_{Bk}(n)\log^{Bk}X. $$

Split

$$ A(s)^{k}=\sum_{\ell=0}^{k-1}A_{k,\ell}(s),\qquad A_{k,\ell}(s)=\sum_{2^{\ell}N^{k}<n\leqslant 2^{\ell+1}N^{k}}\frac{c_{k}(n)}{n^{s}}. $$

Let $\mathcal{U}\subseteq[T,2T]$ be a $1$ -separated set on which

$$ |A(1/2+it)|\geqslant X^{\beta(1/2-\nu)}. $$

Then, for every $t\in\mathcal{U}$ , at least one $\ell\in\{0,\ldots,k-1\}$ satisfies

$$ |A_{k,\ell}(1/2+it)|\geqslant\frac{1}{k}X^{k\beta(1/2-\nu)}. $$

We partition $\mathcal{U}$ according to the least such $\ell$ . Since $2^{\ell+1}N^{k}=X^{k\beta+O_{k}(1/\log X)}$ , applying (2.4) to each $A_{k,\ell}$ , with the parameters changed by $O_{B,k,\beta,\nu}(1/\log X)$ , gives

$$ \#\mathcal{U}\ll_{B,k}X^{\mathcal{K}(k\beta,\nu;\tau)+o(1)}, $$

where we used that $\mathcal{K}$ is piecewise linear. This proves the reduction to (2.4).

We now turn to the proof of (2.4). Recall that $T=X^{\tau}$ . If $\mathcal{K}(\beta,\nu;\tau)=\tau$ , then $X^{\mathcal{K}(\beta,\nu;\tau)}=X^{\tau}=T$ and the claim is trivial. We may therefore assume henceforth that

$$ \mathcal{K}(\beta,\nu;\tau)=\max\left\{2\beta\nu,\mathcal{K}_{0}(\beta,\nu;\tau)\right\}\leqslant\tau. $$

Set $N=X^{\beta}$ and $V=N^{1/2-\nu}$ , and let $\mathcal{U}\subseteq[T,2T]$ be any $1$ -separated set such that

$$ |A(1/2+it)|\geqslant V\qquad\text{for }t\in\mathcal{U}. $$

Write

$$ G\coloneqq\sum_{N<n\leqslant 2N}\frac{|a(n)|^{2}}{n}\ll\log^{2B}XN^{-1}\sum_{N<n\leqslant 2N}d_{B}(n)^{2}\ll\log^{O_{B}(1)}X. $$

By the second moment large values theorem [8, Theorem 9.7], one has

$$ \#\mathcal{U}\ll(N+T)GV^{-2}\log(2N)\ll(X^{2\beta\nu}+X^{\tau+\beta(2\nu-1)})X^{o(1)}. $$

By Huxley’s large values estimate in the form of [8, Corollary 9.9], one has

$$ \#\mathcal{U}\ll\left(GNV^{-2}+G^{3}NTV^{-6}\right)\log^{6}(2T)\ll(X^{2\beta\nu}+X^{\tau+\beta(6\nu-2)})X^{o(1)}. $$

Next we apply the large value results of Guth and Maynard [4], together with the refinement due to Chen, Gupta, and Li [2]. Let $C_{B}$ be sufficiently large and set

$$ A^{\ast}(it)\coloneqq N^{1/2-C_{B}/\log\log N}A(1/2+it)=\sum_{N<n\leqslant 2N}b(n)n^{-it}, $$

where

$$ b(n)=\frac{a(n)}{N^{C_{B}/\log\log N}}\left(\frac{N}{n}\right)^{1/2}. $$

The standard bound for the divisor function shows that if $C_{B}$ is large enough, then $|b(n)|\leqslant 1$ for all $n$ . Moreover, for $t\in\mathcal{U}$ ,

$$ |A^{\ast}(it)|\geqslant V^{\ast},\qquad V^{\ast}\coloneqq N^{1-\nu-C_{B}/\log\log N}. $$

Suppose first that $\beta\geqslant 5\tau/6$ . Then, for all sufficiently large $X$ ,

$$ N=X^{\beta}\geqslant(2T)^{2/3}. $$

We may therefore apply [2, Theorem 1.1], with $q=q_{1}=1$ and height $2T$ , to the points $-t$ with $t\in\mathcal{U}$ . It gives

$$ \#\mathcal{U}\ll(2T)^{o(1)}\left(N^{2}(V^{\ast})^{-2}+(2T)^{1/2}N^{3}(V^{\ast})^{-4}+2TN^{2}(V^{\ast})^{-4}+2TN^{12/5}(V^{\ast})^{-4}\right). $$

The third term is dominated by the fourth. Since $V^{\ast}=N^{1-\nu+o(1)}$ , we obtain

$$ \#\mathcal{U}\ll\left(X^{2\beta\nu}+X^{\tau/2+\beta(4\nu-1)}+X^{\tau+4\beta\nu-8\beta/5}\right)X^{o(1)}. $$

If instead $\beta\leqslant 5\tau/6$ , we have from [4, Theorem 1.1] with $V=N^{1-\nu+o(1)}$ that

$$ \#\mathcal{U}\ll\big(X^{2\beta\nu}+X^{\tau+\beta(4\nu-8/5)}+X^{\beta(4\nu-2/5)}\big)X^{o(1)}. $$

Noting that $\beta(4\nu-2/5)\leqslant\tau/2+4\beta\nu-\beta$ whenever $\beta\leqslant 5\tau/6$ , we can also conclude estimate (2.8) in this case.

Now (2.4) follows by comparing the estimates (2.6), (2.7), and (2.8) with (2.5) and the definition of $\mathcal{K}_{0}(\beta,\nu;\tau)$ .

Proof of (ii). Now we assume that $a(n)=\mathbf{1}_{n\in I}\chi(n)\log^{r}n$ for some Dirichlet character $\chi$ of modulus $\ll\log^{O(1)}X$ , some interval $I\subseteq(X^{\beta},2X^{\beta}]$ , and some $r\in\{0,1\}$ .

Write $N=X^{\beta}$ . Perron’s formula and the fourth moment estimate for Dirichlet $L$ -functions give that there is a constant $C_{0}=C_{0}(B)>0$ such that, for every $1$ -separated set $\mathcal{U}\subseteq[T,2T]$ ,

$$ \sum_{t\in\mathcal{U}}|A(1/2+it)|^{4}\ll\left(T+\#\mathcal{U}\left(\frac{1}{T^{2}}+\frac{N^{2}}{T^{4}}\right)\right)\log^{C_{0}}X; $$

this follows from the proof of [1, Lemma 9] and partial summation to remove the coefficients $\log^{r}n$ .

Let $\nu\geqslant 0$ be arbitrary. Let $\mathcal{U}$ be a $1$ -separated subset of

$$ \left\{t\in\mathcal{T}:|A(1/2+it)|\geqslant N^{1/2-\nu}\right\}. $$

We choose the constant $C=C(B)$ in (2.2) so that $4C>C_{0}+10$ . If $\nu\geqslant 1/2$ , the trivial bound $\#\mathcal{U}\ll T$ for a $1$ -separated subset of $[T,2T]$ gives

$$ \mathcal{N}_{A}(\nu;\mathcal{T})\ll T\leqslant X^{\tau+2\beta(2\nu-1)}, $$

so we may suppose that $\nu<1/2$ .

The definition of $\mathcal{U}$ and (2.9) give

$$ \displaystyle\#\mathcal{U} \displaystyle\ll N^{4\nu-2}T\log^{C_{0}}X+\#\mathcal{U}\left(N^{4\nu-2}T^{-2}+N^{4\nu}T^{-4}\right)\log^{C_{0}}X. $$

Since $\nu<1/2$ and $\tau>1/\sqrt{\log X}$ , we have

$$ N^{4\nu-2}T^{-2}\log^{C_{0}}X=o(1). $$

Now, let $\nu_{1}$ be defined by

$$ N^{1/2-\nu_{1}}=\frac{N^{1/2}}{T}\log^{C}X. $$

The hypothesis $\tau>1/\sqrt{\log X}$ gives, for all sufficiently large $X$ ,

$$ \nu_{1}=\frac{\tau\log X-C\log\log X}{\beta\log X}>0. $$

If $\nu_{1}\leqslant\nu$ , assumption (2.2) shows that every $t\in\mathcal{T}$ belongs to the level sets corresponding to both $\nu_{1}$ and $\nu$ . Hence

$$ \mathcal{N}_{A}(\nu;\mathcal{T})=\mathcal{N}_{A}(\nu_{1};\mathcal{T}), $$

and it is enough to prove (2.3) with $\nu_{1}$ in place of $\nu$ . We may therefore replace $\nu$ by $\nu_{1}$ in this case and hence assume that $\nu\leqslant\nu_{1}$ . It follows that

$$ N^{4\nu}T^{-4}\leqslant N^{4\nu_{1}}T^{-4}=\frac{1}{\log^{4C}X}. $$

Combining with (2.10) and (2.11) we obtain

$$ \#\mathcal{U}\ll N^{4\nu-2}T\log^{C_{0}}X+o(\#\mathcal{U})=X^{\tau+2\beta(2\nu-1)+o(1)}+o(\#\mathcal{U}), $$

and (2.3) follows. This completes the proof of the lemma. ∎

We shall also require the following second moment estimate for sparse sets in Section 3.

#### Lemma 2.4 (Sparse mean square).

Let $N,T\geqslant 2$ and

$$ A(s)=\sum_{N<n\leqslant 2N}a(n)n^{-s} $$

with $a(n)\in\mathbb{C}$ . Let $\mathcal{U}\subset[-T,T]$ be $1$ -separated. Then, for $\eta\in(0,1/2]$ ,

$$ \sum_{t\in\mathcal{U}}|A(it)|^{2}\ll_{\eta}\left(N+|\mathcal{U}|\cdot T^{\frac{9}{2}\cdot\eta^{3/2}}N^{1-\eta}\log^{2/3}T\right)\sum_{N<n\leqslant 2N}|a(n)|^{2}. $$

#### Proof.

The proof is a slight variant of the proof of the Halász–Montgomery mean value theorem (see e.g. [8, Theorem 9.6]). For a similar variant for prime-supported Dirichlet polynomials, see [9, Lemma 4.4].

By the duality principle (see e.g. [8, Section 7.1]), it suffices to show that, for any complex coefficients $c(t)$ , one has

$$ \sum_{N<n\leqslant 2N}\left|\sum_{t\in\mathcal{U}}c(t)n^{-it}\right|^{2}\ll\left(N+|\mathcal{U}|T^{\frac{9}{2}\eta^{3/2}}N^{1-\eta}\log^{2/3}T\right)\sum_{t\in\mathcal{U}}|c(t)|^{2}. $$

Let $w$ be a smooth non-negative compactly supported function such that $w(x)=1$ for $x\in[1,2]$ . Its Mellin transform

$$ \widetilde{w}(z)=\int_{0}^{\infty}w(x)x^{z-1}\,\textnormal{d}x $$

satisfies, for $1/2\leqslant\sigma\leqslant 2$ ,

$$ \widetilde{w}(\sigma+it)\ll(1+|t|)^{-10}. $$

By inserting this smooth weight $w$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{N<n\leqslant 2N}\left|\sum_{t\in\mathcal{U}}c(t)n^{-it}\right|^{2}\leqslant\sum_{n}w\left(\frac{n}{N}\right)\left|\sum_{t\in\mathcal{U}}c(t)n^{-it}\right|^{2}=\sum_{t_{1},t_{2}\in\mathcal{U}}c(t_{1})\overline{c(t_{2})}\sum_{n}w\left(\frac{n}{N}\right)n^{-i(t_{1}-t_{2})}. $$

For the inner summation, Mellin inversion on a line $c>1$ gives

$$ w\left(\frac{n}{N}\right)=\frac{1}{2\pi i}\int_{c-i\infty}^{c+i\infty}\widetilde{w}(z)N^{z}n^{-z}\,\textnormal{d}z. $$

Hence

$$ \sum_{n}w\left(\frac{n}{N}\right)n^{-i(t_{1}-t_{2})}=\frac{1}{2\pi i}\int_{c-i\infty}^{c+i\infty}\widetilde{w}(z)N^{z}\zeta(z+i(t_{1}-t_{2}))\,\textnormal{d}z. $$

Moving the contour to $\operatorname{Re}(z)=1-\eta$ crosses a pole at $z=1+i(t_{2}-t_{1})$ . This gives

$$ \sum_{n}w\left(\frac{n}{N}\right)n^{-i(t_{1}-t_{2})}=\widetilde{w}(1+i(t_{2}-t_{1}))N^{1+i(t_{2}-t_{1})}+\frac{1}{2\pi i}\int_{1-\eta-i\infty}^{1-\eta+i\infty}\widetilde{w}(z)N^{z}\zeta(z+i(t_{1}-t_{2}))\,\textnormal{d}z. $$
