We bound the integral using (2.13) and a result of Ford [3, Theorem 1], which for $|t|\geqslant 3$ and $\sigma\in[1/2,1]$ gives

$$ |\zeta(\sigma+it)|\leqslant 100(|t|+1)^{\frac{9}{2}(1-\sigma)^{3/2}}\log^{2/3}(|t|+2). $$

For $|t|\leqslant 3$ , we instead use $|\zeta(1-\eta+it)|\ll_{\eta}1$ . This leads to

$$ \displaystyle\left|\int_{1-\eta-i\infty}^{1-\eta+i\infty}\widetilde{w}(z)N^{z}\zeta(z+i(t_{1}-t_{2}))\,\textnormal{d}z\right| \displaystyle\leqslant N^{1-\eta}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}|\widetilde{w}(1-\eta+iu)||\zeta(1-\eta+i(u+t_{1}-t_{2}))|\,\,\textnormal{d}u \displaystyle\ll_{\eta}N^{1-\eta}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{(|u+t_{1}-t_{2}|+1)^{\frac{9}{2}\eta^{3/2}}\log^{2/3}(|u+t_{1}-t_{2}|+2)}{(1+|u|)^{10}}\,\,\textnormal{d}u \displaystyle\ll_{\eta}N^{1-\eta}(1+|t_{1}|+|t_{2}|)^{\frac{9}{2}\eta^{3/2}}\log^{2/3}(2+|t_{1}|+|t_{2}|). $$

Thus, one concludes from (2.14) and the above estimates that

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{N<n\leqslant 2N}\left|\sum_{t\in\mathcal{U}}c(t)n^{-it}\right|^{2} \displaystyle\ll N\sum_{t_{1},t_{2}\in\mathcal{U}}|c(t_{1})\overline{c(t_{2})}|\cdot|\widetilde{w}(1+i(t_{2}-t_{1}))| \displaystyle+N^{1-\eta}\sum_{t_{1},t_{2}\in\mathcal{U}}|c(t_{1})\overline{c(t_{2})}|(1+|t_{1}|+|t_{2}|)^{\frac{9}{2}\eta^{3/2}}\log^{2/3}(2+|t_{1}|+|t_{2}|). $$

The claim (2.12) now follows from the inequality $|c(t_{1})\overline{c(t_{2})}|\leqslant(|c(t_{1})|^{2}+|c(t_{2})|^{2})/2$ , the rapid decay of $\widetilde{w}$ (see (2.13)) and the assumption that $\mathcal{U}$ is $1$ -separated. ∎

## 3. Bounding Dirichlet polynomial mean values via a one-variable check

The following simple lemma allows us to reduce a multivariable check to a one-variable check. There and later we use the convention that the infimum of an empty set is $\infty$ .

#### Lemma 3.1.

Let $\tau>0$ , $\varepsilon_{0}>0$ , $J\in\mathbb{N}$ and $I\subseteq\mathbb{R}_{\geqslant 0}$ . For each $j\in\{1,\dotsc,J\}$ , let $\beta_{j}\geqslant 0$ , let $H_{j}\colon I\to[0,\tau],$ and define

$$ P_{j}(t)=\inf\{\beta_{j}y\colon y\in I,H_{j}(y)\geqslant t\}. $$

Assume that

$$ \sum_{j=1}^{J}P_{j}(t)>t+\varepsilon_{0}\qquad\text{ for all }t\in[0,\tau]. $$

Then, for arbitrary $y_{1},\dotsc,y_{J}\in I$ one has

$$ \min_{j\in\{1,\dotsc,J\}}H_{j}(y_{j})<\sum_{j=1}^{J}\beta_{j}y_{j}-\varepsilon_{0}. $$

#### Proof.

We argue by contradiction and assume that (3.2) fails. Thus there exist $y_{1},\dotsc,y_{J}\in I$ and $t_{0}\in\mathbb{R}$ such that

$$ \min_{j\in\{1,\dotsc,J\}}H_{j}(y_{j})\geqslant t_{0}\geqslant\sum_{j=1}^{J}\beta_{j}y_{j}-\varepsilon_{0}. $$

By the range of $H_{j}$ , we can assume that $t_{0}\in[0,\tau].$ For each $j\in\{1,\dotsc,J\}$ , by the definition of $P_{j}(t)$ , the inequality $H_{j}(y_{j})\geqslant t_{0}$ implies that $P_{j}(t_{0})\leqslant\beta_{j}y_{j}$ . Thus

$$ t_{0}\geqslant\sum_{j=1}^{J}\beta_{j}y_{j}-\varepsilon_{0}\geqslant\sum_{j=1}^{J}P_{j}(t_{0})-\varepsilon_{0}. $$

Consequently, the assumption (3.1) fails, and the claim follows. ∎

The following proposition reduces the task of bounding a mean value of a product of Dirichlet polynomials using large value estimates to a one-variable check. In the following two sections we shall prove two applications of Proposition 3.2 and the estimates in Section 2. These applications are tailored for our needs, and one could similarly prove variants of these results for other needs.

#### Proposition 3.2.

Let $\varepsilon>0$ be small but fixed and let $B\geqslant 1$ . Let $X\geqslant 2,\,T=X^{\tau}$ with $\tau\in(0,1/2)$ and let $\mathcal{T}\subseteq[T,2T]$ . Let $J\geqslant 3$ be a fixed integer and let $\beta_{j}\geqslant\varepsilon$ for $j=1,\dotsc,J$ be numbers satisfying $\beta_{1}+\dotsb+\beta_{J}=1$ . For $1\leqslant j\leqslant J$ , let

$$ A_{j}(s)=\sum_{X^{\beta_{j}}<n\leqslant 2X^{\beta_{j}}}a_{j}(n)n^{-s}, $$

be a Dirichlet polynomial for which $a_{j}(n)\ll d_{B}(n)\log^{B}X$ for all $n$ . Suppose that there exists $j_{0}\in\{1,\dotsc,J\}$ such that

$$ \sup_{t\in\mathcal{T}}\big|A_{j_{0}}(1/2+it)\big|\ll_{C}\frac{X^{\beta_{j_{0}}/2}}{\log^{C}X} $$

for every $C\geqslant 1.$

For each $1\leqslant j\leqslant J$ , suppose that the function $H_{j}\colon\mathbb{R}_{\geqslant 0}\to[0,\tau]$ is such that

$$ \mathcal{N}_{A_{j}}(\nu;\mathcal{T})\leqslant X^{H_{j}(\nu)+\varepsilon^{20}} $$

for all $\nu\in[\varepsilon^{6},\varepsilon^{-1}]$ . Define the functions $P_{j}\colon[0,\tau]\to[0,\infty]$ via

$$ P_{j}(t)=\inf\{\beta_{j}\nu\colon\nu\in[\varepsilon^{6},\varepsilon^{-1}],H_{j}(\nu)\geqslant t\}. $$

Assume that

$$ \sum_{j=1}^{J}P_{j}(t)>t+\varepsilon^{10}\qquad\text{ for every }t\in[0,\tau]. $$

Then

$$ \int_{\mathcal{T}}|A_{1}(1/2+it)A_{2}(1/2+it)\dotsm A_{J}(1/2+it)|\,\textnormal{d}t\ll_{\varepsilon,A,B}\frac{X^{1/2}}{\log^{A}X} $$

for every $A>0$ .

#### Remark 3.3.

By Lemma 2.3, for $\nu\in[\varepsilon^{6},\varepsilon^{-1}]$ we may take

$$ H_{j}(\nu)=\min_{1\leqslant k\leqslant K_{\varepsilon}}\mathcal{K}(k\beta_{j},\nu;\tau),\qquad K_{\varepsilon}=\lceil\varepsilon^{-7}\rceil. $$

Note that using larger $k$ would not be helpful. Indeed, if $k>K_{\varepsilon}$ , then $2k\beta_{j}\nu\geqslant 2>\tau$ , and hence $\mathcal{K}(k\beta_{j},\nu;\tau)=\tau$ , so such $k$ cannot decrease the displayed minimum.

#### Proof.

By a standard reduction, it suffices to show that, for any $1$ -separated subset $\mathcal{U}\subseteq\mathcal{T}$ we have, for any $A\geqslant 1$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{t\in\mathcal{U}}|A_{1}(1/2+it)\dotsm A_{J}(1/2+it)|\ll_{\varepsilon,A,B}\frac{X^{1/2}}{\log^{A}X} $$

We split $\mathcal{U}=\mathcal{U}_{1}\sqcup\mathcal{U}_{2}\sqcup\mathcal{U}_{3}$ , where $\mathcal{U}_{1}$ consists of those $t\in\mathcal{U}$ for which there exists $j_{1}\in\{1,\dotsc,J\}$ such that $|A_{j_{1}}(1/2+it)|\leqslant X^{-1/2}$ , $\mathcal{U}_{2}$ consists of those $t\in\mathcal{U}\setminus\mathcal{U}_{1}$ for which there exists $j_{2}\in\{1,\dotsc,J\}$ such that $|A_{j_{2}}(1/2+it)|\geqslant X^{\beta_{j_{2}}(1/2-\varepsilon^{6})}$ , and finally, we set $\mathcal{U}_{3}=\mathcal{U}\setminus(\mathcal{U}_{1}\cup\mathcal{U}_{2})$ . It suffices to show that, for each $k\in\{1,2,3\}$ , we have

$$ S_{k}:=\sum_{t\in\mathcal{U}_{k}}|A_{1}(1/2+it)A_{2}(1/2+it)\dotsm A_{J}(1/2+it)|\ll_{\varepsilon,A,B}\frac{X^{1/2}}{\log^{A}X} $$

for every $A\geqslant 1$ .

Estimation of $S_{1}.$ For $j\in\{1,\dotsc,J\}$ , let $\mathcal{U}_{1,j}$ consist of those $t\in\mathcal{U}_{1}$ for which $j$ is the least index satisfying

$$ |A_{j}(1/2+it)|\leqslant X^{-1/2}. $$

Then $\mathcal{U}_{1}=\bigsqcup_{j=1}^{J}\mathcal{U}_{1,j}$ . For $t\in\mathcal{U}_{1,j}$ we use for $\ell\neq j$ the crude estimate

$$ |A_{\ell}(1/2+it)|\leqslant\sum_{X^{\beta_{\ell}}<n\leqslant 2X^{\beta_{\ell}}}\frac{|a_{\ell}(n)|}{n^{1/2}}\ll X^{\beta_{\ell}/2+o(1)}. $$

Combining this estimate with the fact that $\beta_{1}+\cdots+\beta_{J}=1$ and $\beta_{j}\geqslant\varepsilon$ , we then deduce that the contribution of $\mathcal{U}_{1,j}$ to $S_{1}$ is

$$ \#\mathcal{U}_{1,j}\cdot\frac{1}{X^{1/2}}\cdot X^{(1-\beta_{j})/2+o(1)}\leqslant\#\mathcal{U}_{1,j}\cdot X^{-\varepsilon/2+o(1)}. $$

Since $\#\mathcal{U}\ll X^{\tau}\leqslant X^{1/2}$ , we obtain, for all sufficiently large $X$ and any $A\geqslant 1$ , that

$$ S_{1}\ll\#\mathcal{U}_{1}\cdot X^{-\varepsilon/2+o(1)}\ll_{\varepsilon,A}\frac{X^{1/2}}{\log^{A}X}. $$

Estimation of $S_{2}$ . Let us first bound $\#\mathcal{U}_{2}$ . For $j\in\{1,\dotsc,J\}$ , let $\mathcal{U}_{2,j}$ consist of those $t\in\mathcal{U}_{2}$ for which $j$ is the least index satisfying

$$ |A_{j}(1/2+it)|\geqslant X^{\beta_{j}(1/2-\varepsilon^{6})}. $$

Then $\mathcal{U}_{2}=\bigsqcup_{j=1}^{J}\mathcal{U}_{2,j}$ . Let $j\in\{1,\dotsc,J\}$ . Choose $k_{j}\in\mathbb{N}$ so that $k_{j}\beta_{j}\in[1,2]$ . Lemma 2.3, applied to $\mathcal{U}_{2,j}$ with $k=k_{j}$ and $\nu=\varepsilon^{6}$ , gives

$$ \#\mathcal{U}_{2,j}\ll X^{\min\{\tau,\max\{2k_{j}\beta_{j}\varepsilon^{6},\mathcal{K}_{0}(k_{j}\beta_{j},\varepsilon^{6};\tau)\}\}+o(1)}. $$

Since

$$ \mathcal{K}_{0}(k_{j}\beta_{j},\varepsilon^{6};\tau)\leqslant\tau+k_{j}\beta_{j}(2\varepsilon^{6}-1)\leqslant\tau+2\varepsilon^{6}-1<0, $$

we obtain

$$ \#\mathcal{U}_{2}\ll\sum_{j=1}^{J}X^{2k_{j}\beta_{j}\varepsilon^{6}+o(1)}\ll_{\varepsilon}X^{4\varepsilon^{6}+o(1)}. $$

To estimate $S_{2}$ , we next partition $\{1,\dotsc,J\}=\{j_{0}\}\sqcup\mathcal{J}_{1}\sqcup\mathcal{J}_{2}$ , where $\mathcal{J}_{1}$ and $\mathcal{J}_{2}$ are non-empty, and, for $k\in\{1,2\}$ , set

$$ M_{k}=\prod_{j\in\mathcal{J}_{k}}X^{\beta_{j}},\qquad B_{k}(s)=\prod_{j\in\mathcal{J}_{k}}A_{j}(s)=\sum_{M_{k}<n\leqslant 2^{|\mathcal{J}_{k}|}M_{k}}\frac{b_{k}(n)}{n^{s}}. $$

Splitting each $B_{k}(s)$ into $O_{\varepsilon}(1)$ dyadic Dirichlet polynomials and applying Lemma 2.4 with $\eta=\varepsilon^{4}$ to each of them, we obtain

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{t\in\mathcal{U}_{2}}|B_{k}(1/2+it)|^{2} \displaystyle\ll\left(M_{k}+|\mathcal{U}_{2}|T^{\frac{9}{2}\varepsilon^{6}}M_{k}^{1-\varepsilon^{4}}\right)\log^{O_{B,\varepsilon}(1)}X \displaystyle\ll M_{k}\left(1+X^{10\varepsilon^{6}-\varepsilon^{5}}\right)\log^{O_{B,\varepsilon}(1)}X\ll M_{k}\log^{O_{B,\varepsilon}(1)}X $$

once $\varepsilon$ is sufficiently small. Thus, by the pointwise bound for $A_{j_{0}}(1/2+it)$ and the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality, we obtain, for any $C\geqslant 1$ ,

$$ S_{2}\ll_{B,C}\frac{X^{\beta_{j_{0}}/2}}{\log^{C}X}(M_{1}M_{2})^{1/2}\log^{O(1)}X. $$

This is $\ll X^{1/2}/\log^{A}X$ for any $A\geqslant 1$ .

Estimation of $S_{3}$ . We split into level sets according to the sizes of $|A_{j}(1/2+it)|$ .

For $j\in\{1,\dotsc,J\}$ , we define

$$ \nu_{j,\ell}=\min\left\{\varepsilon^{-1},\varepsilon^{6}+\frac{\ell\log 2}{\beta_{j}\log X}\right\},\qquad 0\leqslant\ell\leqslant L_{j} $$

with

$$ L_{j}=\left\lceil\frac{\beta_{j}(\varepsilon^{-1}-\varepsilon^{6})\log X}{\log 2}\right\rceil. $$

Now

$$ \beta_{j}\left(\frac{1}{2}-\nu_{j,0}\right)=\beta_{j}\left(\frac{1}{2}-\varepsilon^{6}\right),\quad\beta_{j}\left(\frac{1}{2}-\nu_{j,L_{j}}\right)\leqslant\beta_{j}\left(\frac{1}{2}-\varepsilon^{-1}\right)\leqslant-\frac{1}{2}. $$

Thus, for every $t\in\mathcal{U}_{3}$ and every $j$ , there is an $\ell_{j}\in\{0,\ldots,L_{j}-1\}$ such that

$$ X^{\beta_{j}(1/2-\nu_{j,\ell_{j}+1})}<|A_{j}(1/2+it)|\leqslant X^{\beta_{j}(1/2-\nu_{j,\ell_{j}})}. $$

Partitioning $\mathcal{U}_{3}$ according to $(\ell_{1},\ldots,\ell_{J})$ , and using

$$ 0\leqslant\beta_{j}(\nu_{j,\ell_{j}+1}-\nu_{j,\ell_{j}})\leqslant\frac{\log 2}{\log X}, $$

we obtain

$$ S_{3}\ll 2^{J}\log^{J}X\max_{\ell_{1},\ldots,\ell_{J}}X^{\sum_{j=1}^{J}\beta_{j}(\frac{1}{2}-\nu_{j,\ell_{j}+1})}\min_{j}\mathcal{N}_{A_{j}}(\nu_{j,\ell_{j}+1};\mathcal{U}_{3}). $$

In particular by assumption (3.3), we have $S_{3}\ll X^{1/2}\log^{-A}X$ if

$$ \min_{j\in\{1,\dotsc,J\}}H_{j}(\nu_{j})\leqslant\beta_{1}\nu_{1}+\dotsb+\beta_{J}\nu_{J}-\varepsilon^{10}\quad\text{for every $\nu_{1},\dotsc,\nu_{J}\in[\varepsilon^{6},\varepsilon^{-1}]$}. $$

By Lemma 3.1, this happens if, for every $t\in[0,\tau]$ , we have

$$ \sum_{j=1}^{J}P_{j}(t)>t+\varepsilon^{10}, $$

and the claim follows. ∎

## 4. A Heath-Brown–Iwaniec type trilinear estimate

We now prove a trilinear estimate for Dirichlet polynomials in the spirit of the work of Heath-Brown and Iwaniec [6, Lemma 2].

#### Lemma 4.1 (Heath-Brown–Iwaniec trilinear estimates).

Let $\varepsilon>0$ and $B\geqslant 1$ . Set $T_{0}\coloneqq\exp(\log^{1/4}X)$ and let

$$ T_{1}=X^{\tau_{1}},\qquad\tau_{1}:=\frac{16}{35}-\varepsilon. $$

Let $\beta_{1},\beta_{2},\beta_{3}\in[\varepsilon,\tau_{1}]$ be such that $\beta_{1}+\beta_{2}+\beta_{3}=1$ . For $j\in\{1,2,3\}$ , let

$$ A_{j}(s)=\sum_{X^{\beta_{j}}<n\leqslant 2X^{\beta_{j}}}a_{j}(n)n^{-s}, $$

where $|a_{j}(n)|\ll d_{B}(n)\log^{B}X$ . Assume further that $a_{1}(n)=\mathbf{1}_{n\in I}\chi(n)\log^{r}n$ for some interval $I\subseteq(X^{\beta_{1}},2X^{\beta_{1}}]$ , some $r\in\{0,1\}$ , and some Dirichlet character $\chi$ of modulus $\ll\log^{B}X$ .

Then

$$ \int_{T_{0}}^{T_{1}}|A_{1}(1/2+it)A_{2}(1/2+it)A_{3}(1/2+it)|\,\textnormal{d}t\ll_{A,B}\frac{X^{1/2}}{\log^{A}X} $$

for every $A>0$ .

An important computational step in the proof of Lemma 4.1 is the following lemma which we will prove in Section 8.

#### Lemma 4.2.

Let $\varepsilon\in(0,1/100),\,\tau_{1}=\frac{16}{35}-\varepsilon$ and $\tau\in[\varepsilon,\tau_{1}]$ . Let $\beta_{1},\beta_{2},\beta_{3}\in[\varepsilon,\tau_{1}]$ with $\beta_{1}+\beta_{2}+\beta_{3}=1$ . For $\nu\geqslant 0$ , define

$$ \displaystyle H_{1,\tau}(\nu) \displaystyle:=\max\left\{0,\min\{\tau+2\beta_{1}(2\nu-1),\mathcal{K}(2\beta_{1},\nu;\tau)\}\right\} \displaystyle H_{2,\tau}(\nu) \displaystyle:=\min\{\mathcal{K}(\beta_{2},\nu;\tau),\mathcal{K}(2\beta_{2},\nu;\tau)\} \displaystyle H_{3,\tau}(\nu) \displaystyle:=\min\{\mathcal{K}(\beta_{3},\nu;\tau),\mathcal{K}(2\beta_{3},\nu;\tau)\}. $$

For $j\in\{1,2,3\}$ , define the function $P_{j,\tau}\colon[0,\tau]\to\mathbb{R}_{\geqslant 0}$ via

$$ P_{j,\tau}(t)=\inf\{\beta_{j}\nu\colon\nu\in[\varepsilon^{6},\varepsilon^{-1}],H_{j,\tau}(\nu)\geqslant t\}. $$

Then, for every $t\in[0,\tau]$ , we have

$$ P_{1,\tau}(t)+P_{2,\tau}(t)+P_{3,\tau}(t)>t+\varepsilon^{10}. $$

#### Proof of Lemma 4.1 assuming Lemma 4.2.

Notice first that by our assumption on the coefficients $a_{1}(n)$ (use e.g. [10, Lemma 3.9(i)] and partial summation), we have for every $A>0$ the bound

$$ \sup_{T_{0}\leqslant t\leqslant T_{1}}|A_{1}(1/2+it)|\ll\frac{X^{\beta_{1}/2}}{\log^{A}X}. $$

Combining the preceding bound with the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality and the mean value theorem gives, for every $A>0$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\int_{T_{0}}^{X^{\varepsilon}}|A_{1}(1/2+it)A_{2}(1/2+it)A_{3}(1/2+it)|\,\textnormal{d}t \displaystyle\ll_{A}\frac{X^{\beta_{1}/2}}{\log^{A}X}\left(\int_{T_{0}}^{X^{\varepsilon}}|A_{2}(1/2+it)|^{2}\,\textnormal{d}t\int_{T_{0}}^{X^{\varepsilon}}|A_{3}(1/2+it)|^{2}\,\textnormal{d}t\right)^{1/2} \displaystyle\ll_{A,B}\frac{X^{\beta_{1}/2}}{\log^{A}X}\left((X^{\varepsilon}+X^{\beta_{2}})(X^{\varepsilon}+X^{\beta_{3}})\right)^{1/2}\log^{O_{B}(1)}X. $$

Since $\beta_{2},\beta_{3}\geqslant\varepsilon$ and $\beta_{1}+\beta_{2}+\beta_{3}=1$ , the right-hand side is $\ll X^{1/2}/\log^{A}X$ for every $A>0$ .

Thus, by dyadic splitting, it suffices to show that, for every $T\in[X^{\varepsilon},T_{1}]$ and

$$ \mathcal{I}_{T}=[T,\min\{2T,T_{1}\}], $$

we have

$$ \int_{\mathcal{I}_{T}}|A_{1}(1/2+it)A_{2}(1/2+it)A_{3}(1/2+it)|\,\textnormal{d}t\ll_{A,B}\frac{X^{1/2}}{\log^{A}X}. $$

Let $C=C(B)$ be as in Lemma 2.3(ii) and let $\mathcal{I}_{T}=\mathcal{T}_{1}\sqcup\mathcal{T}_{2}$ , where $\mathcal{T}_{1}$ consists of those $t\in\mathcal{I}_{T}$ for which

$$ |A_{1}(1/2+it)|<\frac{X^{\beta_{1}/2}}{T}\log^{C}X $$

and $\mathcal{T}_{2}=\mathcal{I}_{T}\setminus\mathcal{T}_{1}$ .

By the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality and the mean value theorem (see e.g. [8, Theorem 9.1]) it follows that

$$ \displaystyle\int_{\mathcal{T}_{1}}|A_{1}(1/2+it)A_{2}(1/2+it)A_{3}(1/2+it)|\,\textnormal{d}t \displaystyle\ll\frac{X^{\beta_{1}/2}}{T}\log^{C}X\left(\int_{\mathcal{T}_{1}}|A_{2}(1/2+it)|^{2}\,\textnormal{d}t\int_{\mathcal{T}_{1}}|A_{3}(1/2+it)|^{2}\,\textnormal{d}t\right)^{1/2} \displaystyle\ll_{B}\frac{X^{\beta_{1}/2}}{T}\left((T+X^{\beta_{2}})(T+X^{\beta_{3}})\right)^{1/2}\log^{O_{B}(1)}X \displaystyle\ll_{B}\left(X^{\beta_{1}/2}+\frac{X^{(\beta_{1}+\beta_{2})/2}+X^{(\beta_{1}+\beta_{3})/2}}{T_{0}^{1/2}}+\frac{X^{(\beta_{1}+\beta_{2}+\beta_{3})/2}}{T_{0}}\right)\log^{O_{B}(1)}X \displaystyle\ll_{A,B}\frac{X^{1/2}}{\log^{A}X} $$

for every $A>0$ .

Thus it suffices to show that

$$ \int_{\mathcal{T}_{2}}|A_{1}(1/2+it)A_{2}(1/2+it)A_{3}(1/2+it)|\,\textnormal{d}t\ll_{A,B}\frac{X^{1/2}}{\log^{A}X}. $$

Write $T=X^{\tau}$ with $\tau\in[\varepsilon,\tau_{1}]$ . Note that, for $t\in\mathcal{T}_{2}$ , one has

$$ |A_{1}(1/2+it)|\geqslant\frac{X^{\beta_{1}/2}}{T}\log^{C}X. $$

We deduce from Lemma 2.3(i) and (ii) that, for every $\nu\geqslant 0$ ,

$$ \mathcal{N}_{A_{1}}(\nu;\mathcal{T}_{2})\ll X^{\max\left\{0,\min\{\tau+2\beta_{1}(2\nu-1),\mathcal{K}(2\beta_{1},\nu;\tau)\}\right\}+o(1)}. $$

Besides, for $j\in\{2,3\}$ and $\nu\geqslant 0$ , we have by Lemma 2.3

$$ \mathcal{N}_{A_{j}}(\nu;\mathcal{T}_{2})\ll\min\{X^{\mathcal{K}(\beta_{j},\nu;\tau)+o(1)},X^{\mathcal{K}(2\beta_{j},\nu;\tau)+o(1)}\}. $$

The desired estimate now follows from Proposition 3.2 and Lemma 4.2. This completes the proof. ∎

#### Remark 4.3.

The example $(\beta_{1},\beta_{2},\beta_{3})=(1/5,2/5,2/5)$ is a limiting case which shows that one cannot take $\tau_{1}=16/35$ in Lemma 4.2: Set $\nu=2/7$ and observe that then

$$ H_{1,\tau_{1}}\Big(\frac{2}{7}\Big)=\tau_{1}+2\beta_{1}(2\nu-1)=\tau_{1}-\frac{6\beta_{1}}{7}=2/7, $$

$$ H_{2,\tau_{1}}\Big(\frac{2}{7}\Big)=\tau_{1}+\beta_{2}(2\nu-1)=\tau_{1}-\frac{3\beta_{2}}{7}=2/7, $$

$$ H_{3,\tau_{1}}\Big(\frac{2}{7}\Big)=\tau_{1}+\beta_{3}(2\nu-1)=\tau_{1}-\frac{3\beta_{3}}{7}=2/7. $$

Hence, taking $t=2/7$ it follows that $P_{j,\tau_{1}}(2/7)\leqslant 2\beta_{j}/7$ for each $1\leqslant j\leqslant 3$ , and thus

$$ P_{1,\tau_{1}}\Big(\frac{2}{7}\Big)+P_{2,\tau_{1}}\Big(\frac{2}{7}\Big)+P_{3,\tau_{1}}\Big(\frac{2}{7}\Big)\leqslant\frac{2}{7}=t, $$

so (4.2) does not hold.

In more classical language, these computations correspond to the fact that with current understanding of the large values of Dirichlet polynomials, we cannot rule out the scenario that

$$ \displaystyle\left|\sum_{n\sim X^{\beta_{j}}}\frac{a_{j}(n)}{n^{1/2+it}}\right|\geqslant X^{\beta_{j}(1/2-2/7)}\qquad j=1,2,3 $$

for $\gg X^{2/7}$ one-separated points $t\in[-X^{\tau_{1}},X^{\tau_{1}}]$ , where $a_{1}(n)=1$ and $|a_{j}(n)|\ll d_{B}(n)$ for $j=2,3$ and some fixed $B$ .

In order to obtain the exponent $19/35-\varepsilon$ in Theorems 1.4, 1.5, 1.6 and 1.7, we would need to essentially have the bound

$$ \int_{X^{\varepsilon}}^{X^{\tau_{1}+\varepsilon}}\left|\sum_{n\sim X^{1/5}}\frac{1}{n^{1/2+it}}\right|^{5}\,\textnormal{d}t\ll\frac{X^{1/2}}{\log^{A}X}, $$

and it is the above-mentioned scenario which prevents us from obtaining this.

## 5. A Baker–Harman–Pintz type trilinear estimate

We now prove a trilinear estimate for Dirichlet polynomials in the spirit of the work of Baker, Harman, and Pintz (see [5, Lemma 7.3]).

#### Lemma 5.1 (Baker–Harman–Pintz trilinear estimates).

Let $\varepsilon>0$ and $B\geqslant 1$ . Let

$$ 1\leqslant T_{1}\leqslant X^{2/5-\varepsilon} $$

and $\mathcal{T}\subseteq[-T_{1},T_{1}]$ . Let $\beta_{1},\beta_{2},\beta_{3}\in[\varepsilon,1/2]$ be such that $\beta_{2}\leqslant\beta_{3}\leqslant\beta_{1}$ and $\beta_{1}+\beta_{2}+\beta_{3}=1$ . For $j\in\{1,2,3\}$ , let

$$ \displaystyle A_{j}(s)=\sum_{X^{\beta_{j}}<n\leqslant 2X^{\beta_{j}}}a_{j}(n)n^{-s}, $$

where

$$ |a_{j}(n)|\ll_{B}d_{B}(n)\log^{B}X $$

and

$$ \sup_{|t|\leqslant T_{1}}|A_{2}(1/2+it)|\ll_{A}\frac{X^{\beta_{2}/2}}{\log^{A}X} $$

for every $A\geqslant 1.$

Then

$$ \int_{\mathcal{T}}|A_{1}(1/2+it)A_{2}(1/2+it)A_{3}(1/2+it)|\,\textnormal{d}t\ll_{A,B}\frac{X^{1/2}}{\log^{A}X} $$

for every $A\geqslant 1.$

An important computational step in the proof of Lemma 5.1 is the following lemma which we will prove in Section 8.

#### Lemma 5.2.

Let $\varepsilon,\varepsilon_{0}>0$ , $\tau\in[\varepsilon,\frac{2}{5}-\varepsilon]$ , and, for $\beta\geqslant\varepsilon$ , define the function $H_{\beta,\tau}\colon\mathbb{R}_{\geqslant 0}\to[0,\tau]$ via

$$ \displaystyle H_{\beta,\tau}(\nu) \displaystyle:=\min_{k\in\{1,2\}}\mathcal{K}(k\beta,\nu;\tau) $$

and the function $P_{\beta,\tau}\colon[0,\tau]\to\mathbb{R}_{\geqslant 0}$ via

$$ P_{\beta,\tau}(t)=\inf\{\beta\nu\colon\nu\in[\varepsilon^{6},\varepsilon^{-1}],H_{\beta,\tau}(\nu)\geqslant t\}. $$

Then, for every $\beta_{1}\in[2/5,1/2]$ and $\beta_{2},\beta_{3}\in[1/5,1/3]$ with $\beta_{1}+\beta_{2}+\beta_{3}=1$ and every $t\in[0,\tau]$ , we have

$$ P_{\beta_{1},\tau}(t)+P_{\beta_{2},\tau}(t)+P_{\beta_{3},\tau}(t)>t+\varepsilon^{10}. $$

#### Proof of Lemma 5.1 assuming Lemma 5.2.

By the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality, the mean value theorem for Dirichlet polynomials (see e.g. [8, Theorem 9.1]), and the pointwise hypothesis (5.2),

$$ \displaystyle\int_{\mathcal{T}\cap[-2X^{\varepsilon},2X^{\varepsilon}]}|A_{1}(1/2+it)A_{2}(1/2+it)A_{3}(1/2+it)|\,\,\textnormal{d}t \displaystyle\leqslant\sup_{|t|\leqslant T_{1}}|A_{2}(1/2+it)|\left(\int_{-2X^{\varepsilon}}^{2X^{\varepsilon}}|A_{1}(1/2+it)|^{2}\,\,\textnormal{d}t\right)^{1/2}\left(\int_{-2X^{\varepsilon}}^{2X^{\varepsilon}}|A_{3}(1/2+it)|^{2}\,\,\textnormal{d}t\right)^{1/2} \displaystyle\ll_{A,B}\frac{X^{1/2}}{\log^{A}X} $$

for any $A\geqslant 1$ . By dyadic splitting and symmetry (using complex conjugates of coefficients), it is enough to prove (5.3) with $\mathcal{T}$ replaced by

$$ \mathcal{T}_{T}=\mathcal{T}\cap[T,2T],\qquad[T,2T]\subseteq[X^{\varepsilon},T_{1}]. $$

Suppose first that $\beta_{1}-\beta_{3}\leqslant 1/5$ . The Dirichlet polynomial Baker–Harman–Pintz parallelogram estimate in [5, Lemma 7.3], in the form used in the proof of [10, Lemma 3.5(i)], applies with $\theta=3/5$ , since

$$ |\beta_{1}-\beta_{3}|\leqslant\frac{1}{5}=2\theta-1,\qquad 1-\beta_{1}-\beta_{3}=\beta_{2}\leqslant\frac{1}{3}<\frac{2}{5}=4\theta-2, $$

and its pointwise hypothesis for the factor corresponding to $\beta_{2}$ is precisely (5.2). This gives

$$ \int_{\mathcal{T}_{T}}|A_{1}(1/2+it)A_{2}(1/2+it)A_{3}(1/2+it)|\,\,\textnormal{d}t\ll_{A,B}\frac{X^{1/2}}{\log^{A}X}. $$

It remains to consider $\beta_{1}-\beta_{3}>1/5$ . Since $\beta_{3}=1-\beta_{1}-\beta_{2}$ , the ordering of the $\beta_{j}$ shows that the closure of this region is the triangular region with $(\beta_{1},\beta_{2},\beta_{3})\in\mathfrak{T}_{\triangle}$ , where

$$ \mathfrak{T}_{\triangle}\coloneqq\operatorname{conv}\left\{\left(\frac{7}{15},\frac{4}{15},\frac{4}{15}\right),\left(\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{4},\frac{1}{4}\right),\left(\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{5},\frac{3}{10}\right)\right\}, $$

where $\operatorname{conv}$ denotes the convex hull. In particular, this triangle is contained in the compact region

$$ \beta_{1}\in\left[\frac{2}{5},\frac{1}{2}\right],\qquad\beta_{2},\beta_{3}\in\left[\frac{1}{5},\frac{3}{10}\right]; $$

see Figure 1.

*Figure 1. Trilinear exponent region. The green region is covered by the Baker–Harman–Pintz parallelogram estimate; the triangular region is the remaining region.*

Write $T=X^{\tau}$ with $\tau\in[\varepsilon,2/5-\varepsilon]$ . By Lemma 2.3, for any $\nu\geqslant 0$ and $j\in\{1,2,3\}$ ,

$$ \mathcal{N}_{A_{j}}(\nu;\mathcal{T}_{T})\ll X^{\min_{k\in\{1,2\}}\mathcal{K}(k\beta_{j},\nu;\tau)+o(1)}. $$

Now Proposition 3.2 and Lemma 5.2 give the required estimate on $\mathcal{T}_{T}$ . Summing the dyadic blocks completes the proof. ∎

#### Remark 5.3.

By extending the proof of Lemma 5.2 to a wider region of $\beta_{1},\beta_{2},\beta_{3}$ (allowing larger $k$ in (5.4)) we could avoid appealing to the Baker–Harman–Pintz parallelogram estimate. However, now we emphasise the new region we needed to cover.

#### Remark 5.4.

The instance $(\beta_{1},\beta_{2},\beta_{3})=(1/2,1/4,1/4)$ is a limiting case and shows that one cannot take $\tau=2/5$ in Lemma 5.2. Indeed, set $\nu=3/10$ and observe that then

$$ \displaystyle H_{\beta_{1},\tau}(3/10) \displaystyle=2\beta_{1}\nu=3/10, \displaystyle H_{\beta_{3},\tau}(3/10)=H_{\beta_{2},\tau}(3/10) \displaystyle=\min\Big(\tau+\beta_{2}(2\nu-1),4\beta_{2}\nu\Big)=\min(3/10,3/10)=3/10 $$

Hence, taking $t=3/10$ it follows that $P_{\beta_{j},\tau}(3/10)\leqslant 3\beta_{j}/10$ for each $1\leqslant j\leqslant 3$ , and hence

$$ P_{\beta_{1},\tau}(3/10)+P_{\beta_{2},\tau}(3/10)+P_{\beta_{3},\tau}(3/10)\leqslant\frac{3}{10}=t, $$

in which case (5.5) does not hold.

In a more classical language, these computations correspond to the fact that with current understanding of the large values of Dirichlet polynomials, we cannot rule out the scenario that, for bounded coefficients $a_{j}(n)$ ,

$$ \left|\sum_{n\sim X^{\beta_{j}}}\frac{a_{j}(n)}{n^{1/2+it}}\right|\geqslant X^{\beta_{j}(1/2-3/10)} $$

for $\gg X^{3/10}$ one-separated points $t\in[-X^{\tau},X^{\tau}]$ .

In order to obtain the exponent $3/5-\varepsilon$ in Theorem 1.1, we would need to essentially have, for $T=X^{O(1)}$ , the bound

$$ \int_{X^{\varepsilon}}^{X^{\tau+\varepsilon}}\left|\sum_{n\sim X^{1/4}}\frac{1}{n^{1/2+it+iT}}\right|^{4}\,\textnormal{d}t\ll\frac{X^{1/2}}{\log^{A}X}, $$

and it is the above-mentioned scenario which prevents us from obtaining this — the coefficients $a_{j}(n)=n^{-iT}$ prevent us from using type I information once $T$ is a largish power of $X$ .

## 6. Higher order uniformity in short intervals

The purpose of this section is to prove the nilsequence discorrelation estimates for $\mu$ and $\Lambda-\Lambda_{X}^{\sharp}$ given in Theorem 1.2. As stated before, we use the same nilsequence terminology as in [10, Section 2.3].

Before deducing Theorem 1.1 from Theorem 1.2, we state a result that allows us to reduce that theorem to the range $H\leqslant X^{1-\varepsilon}$ (cf. also [15, Section 7]).

#### Lemma 6.1 (Gluing Gowers norms on adjacent intervals).

Let $s\in\mathbb{N}$ . Let $a\in\mathbb{R}$ and $H\geqslant 2L\geqslant 4$ , and write $I=(a,a+H]$ . Then, for every $f\colon\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{C}$ ,

$$ \|f\|_{U^{s}(I)}\ll_{s}\max_{\begin{subarray}{c}I^{\prime}\subseteq I\text{ an interval}\\
L/2<|I^{\prime}|\leqslant L\end{subarray}}\|f\|_{U^{s}(I^{\prime})}. $$

#### Proof.

Set

$$ m=\left\lceil\frac{H}{L}\right\rceil,\qquad\ell=\frac{H}{m}. $$

Then $L/2<\ell\leqslant L$ . Partition $I$ into the consecutive intervals

$$ I_{j}=(a+j\ell,a+(j+1)\ell],\qquad 0\leqslant j<m, $$

and write $f_{j}=f\mathbf{1}_{I_{j}}$ .

For a tuple $\boldsymbol{i}=(i_{\omega})_{\omega\in\{0,1\}^{s}}$ , with each $i_{\omega}\in\{0,\ldots,m-1\}$ , set

$$ \Lambda_{\boldsymbol{i}}=\sum_{x,h_{1},\ldots,h_{s}\in\mathbb{Z}}\prod_{\omega\in\{0,1\}^{s}}\mathcal{C}^{|\omega|}f_{i_{\omega}}(x+\omega_{1}h_{1}+\cdots+\omega_{s}h_{s}). $$

By multilinearity, we have

$$ \|f\mathbf{1}_{I}\|_{U^{s}(\mathbb{Z})}^{2^{s}}=\sum_{\boldsymbol{i}}\Lambda_{\boldsymbol{i}}. $$

We first count the tuples $\boldsymbol{i}$ for which $\Lambda_{\boldsymbol{i}}$ can be nonzero. Suppose that such a tuple $\boldsymbol{i}$ is fixed and let $x,h_{1},\ldots,h_{s}$ be such that $\prod_{\omega\in\{0,1\}^{s}}\mathcal{C}^{|\omega|}f_{i_{\omega}}(x+\omega_{1}h_{1}+\cdots+\omega_{s}h_{s})\neq 0$ . Writing, for $\omega\in\{0,1\}^{s}$ ,

$$ n_{\omega}=x+\omega_{1}h_{1}+\cdots+\omega_{s}h_{s}, $$

we have

$$ n_{\omega}=(1-|\omega|)n_{\boldsymbol{0}}+\sum_{r=1}^{s}\omega_{r}n_{\boldsymbol{e}_{r}}. $$

The condition $n_{\omega}\in I_{i_{\omega}}$ gives

$$ i_{\omega}=(1-|\omega|)i_{\boldsymbol{0}}+\sum_{r=1}^{s}\omega_{r}i_{\boldsymbol{e}_{r}}+O_{s}(1). $$

Therefore, once

$$ i_{\boldsymbol{0}},i_{\boldsymbol{e}_{1}},\ldots,i_{\boldsymbol{e}_{s}} $$

have been chosen, there are only $O_{s}(1)$ possibilities for every remaining $i_{\omega}$ . Hence at most $O_{s}(m^{s+1})$ tuples $\boldsymbol{i}$ contribute.

For each such tuple, the Gowers–Cauchy–Schwarz inequality gives

$$ |\Lambda_{\boldsymbol{i}}|\leqslant\prod_{\omega\in\{0,1\}^{s}}\|f_{i_{\omega}}\|_{U^{s}(\mathbb{Z})}. $$

Writing

$$ \eta=\max_{\begin{subarray}{c}I^{\prime}\subseteq I\text{ an interval}\\
L/2<|I^{\prime}|\leqslant L\end{subarray}}\|f\|_{U^{s}(I^{\prime})}, $$

we have

$$ \|f_{j}\|_{U^{s}(\mathbb{Z})}\leqslant\eta\|\mathbf{1}_{I_{j}}\|_{U^{s}(\mathbb{Z})}\ll_{s}\eta\ell^{(s+1)/2^{s}}. $$

Combining this with (6.2) yields

$$ |\Lambda_{\boldsymbol{i}}|\ll_{s}\eta^{2^{s}}\ell^{s+1}. $$

Summing over the $O_{s}(m^{s+1})$ possible tuples $\boldsymbol{i}$ that contribute non-trivially to (6.1), we obtain

$$ \|f\mathbf{1}_{I}\|_{U^{s}(\mathbb{Z})}^{2^{s}}\ll_{s}\eta^{2^{s}}m^{s+1}\ell^{s+1}=\eta^{2^{s}}H^{s+1}. $$

Finally,

$$ \|\mathbf{1}_{I}\|_{U^{s}(\mathbb{Z})}^{2^{s}}\asymp_{s}H^{s+1}. $$

Dividing (6.3) by (6.4) and taking $2^{s}$ -th roots proves the claim. ∎

#### Proof of Theorem 1.1 assuming Theorem 1.2.

Let $\eta=\min\{\varepsilon/2,1/10\}$ . For $H\leqslant X^{1-\eta}$ , the result follows from Theorem 1.2, with $\eta$ in place of $\varepsilon$ , by the inverse theorem for the Gowers norms and the transference argument in [10, Proof of Theorem 1.5 in Section 9], with just $5/8$ replaced by $3/5$ .

Suppose now that $H>X^{1-\eta}$ and set $L=X^{1-\eta}/2$ . By Lemma 6.1, it suffices to show that whenever $I^{\prime}=(Y,Y+H^{\prime}]\subseteq(X,X+H]$ is an interval with

$$ L/2<H^{\prime}\leqslant L, $$

we have

$$ \|\Lambda-\Lambda_{X}^{\sharp}\|_{U^{s}(I^{\prime})}=o_{s}(1). $$

Now $X\leqslant Y\leqslant 2X$ and, for all sufficiently large $X$ ,

$$ Y^{3/5+\eta}\leqslant H^{\prime}\leqslant Y^{1-\eta}. $$

The first part of the proof, applied with base point $Y$ , therefore gives

$$ \|\Lambda-\Lambda_{Y}^{\sharp}\|_{U^{s}(I^{\prime})}=o_{s,\varepsilon}(1). $$

Let $w=w(X)$ tend to infinity sufficiently slowly and let $\Lambda_{w}$ be as in [10, Section 9]. The argument proving [10, (9.17)], using [10, Lemma 9.6(i) and Remark 9.2], is uniform in the sieve level permitted there. Applied with base point $Y$ to the sieve levels defining $\Lambda_{X}^{\sharp}$ and $\Lambda_{Y}^{\sharp}$ , it gives

$$ \|\Lambda_{X}^{\sharp}-\Lambda_{w}\|_{U^{s}(I^{\prime})}+\|\Lambda_{Y}^{\sharp}-\Lambda_{w}\|_{U^{s}(I^{\prime})}=o_{s,\varepsilon}(1) $$

uniformly for such $I^{\prime}$ . The triangle inequality now gives (6.5), and thus Theorem 1.1 follows. ∎

### 6.1. Combinatorial decomposition

The following elementary lemma is the combinatorial decomposition needed after applying Heath-Brown’s identity.

#### Lemma 6.2 (Type I, Type $\mathrm{I}_{2}$ , Type II trichotomy).

Let $k\geqslant 1$ and let $\alpha_{1},\ldots,\alpha_{k}\geqslant 0$ with $\sum_{j\leqslant k}\alpha_{j}=1$ . For $J\subseteq\{1,\ldots,k\}$ write $\alpha_{J}=\sum_{j\in J}\alpha_{j}$ . At least one of the following alternatives holds.

- (i) $\alpha_{j}\geqslant 2/5$ for some $j$ .

- (ii) $\alpha_{j}+\alpha_{\ell}\geqslant 3/5$ for some distinct $j,\ell$ .

- (iii) There is a subset $J^{*}$ with $2/5\leqslant\alpha_{J^{*}}\leqslant 3/5$ , and there is a partition $\{1,\ldots,k\}=J_{1}\sqcup J_{2}\sqcup J_{3}$ such that $\alpha_{J_{r}}\in[1/10,1/2]$ for $r=1,2,3$ .

#### Proof.

We assume that both (i) and (ii) fail and will show that case (iii) must hold. We begin by finding a set $J^{*}$ such that $2/5\leqslant\alpha_{J^{*}}\leqslant 3/5$ . Without loss of generality, suppose $\alpha_{1}\geqslant\alpha_{2}\geqslant\cdots\geqslant\alpha_{k}\geqslant 0$ .

If $\alpha_{2}\geqslant 1/5$ , then we set $J^{*}=\{1,2\}$ and the desired bound follows from $\alpha_{1}\geqslant\alpha_{2}$ and the assumption that $\alpha_{1}+\alpha_{2}<3/5$ .

Otherwise, let $j^{*}$ be the least index such that $\sum_{1\leqslant j\leqslant j^{*}}\alpha_{j}\geqslant 2/5$ and set $J^{*}=\{1,2,\dots,j^{*}\}$ . Since we are not in case (i), we have $j^{*}\geqslant 2$ , and hence $\alpha_{j^{*}}\leqslant\alpha_{2}<1/5$ . Therefore,

$$ \frac{2}{5}\leqslant\alpha_{J^{*}}=\sum_{1\leqslant j<j^{*}}\alpha_{j}+\alpha_{j^{*}}<\frac{2}{5}+\frac{1}{5}=\frac{3}{5}. $$

Therefore, such a set $J^{*}$ exists in both cases.

Set $J_{1}=J^{*}$ if $\alpha_{J^{*}}\leqslant 1/2$ , and otherwise set $J_{1}=(J^{*})^{c}$ . Then $2/5\leqslant\alpha_{J_{1}}\leqslant 1/2$ and $1/2\leqslant\alpha_{J_{1}^{c}}\leqslant 3/5$ . Moreover, $|J_{1}^{c}|\geqslant 2$ , since we are not in case (i). It remains to partition $J_{1}^{c}$ into two sets $J_{2}$ and $J_{3}$ satisfying the required bounds. First suppose that there exists $j^{\prime}\in J_{1}^{c}$ such that $\alpha_{j^{\prime}}\geqslant 1/10$ . Then set $J_{2}=\{j^{\prime}\}$ and $J_{3}=J_{1}^{c}\backslash J_{2}$ . In this case $1/10\leqslant\alpha_{J_{2}}<2/5$ , since we are not in case $(i)$ , and

$$ 1/10<\alpha_{J_{3}}=\alpha_{J_{1}^{c}}-\alpha_{J_{2}}\leqslant 1/2. $$

Otherwise, $\alpha_{j}<1/10$ for all $j\in J_{1}^{c}$ . Choose $J_{2}\subset J_{1}^{c}$ minimally such that $\sum_{j\in J_{2}}\alpha_{j}\geqslant 1/10$ and set $J_{3}=J_{1}^{c}\backslash J_{2}$ . Then $\alpha_{J_{2}}<1/5$ and hence

$$ 3/10<\alpha_{J_{3}}=\alpha_{J_{1}^{c}}-\alpha_{J_{2}}\leqslant 1/2. $$

This proves that case (iii) always occurs when $(i)$ and $(ii)$ fail. ∎

#### Definition 6.3.

We call $a\colon\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{R}$ an admissible trilinear component if there exist exponents $\gamma_{1},\gamma_{2},\gamma_{3}\in[1/10,1/2]$ and functions $\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2},\alpha_{3}\colon\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{R}$ such that the following conditions hold.

- (i) We have (6.6)

$$ \frac{1}{10}\leqslant\gamma_{2}\leqslant\gamma_{3}\leqslant\gamma_{1}\leqslant\frac{1}{2},\qquad\gamma_{1}+\gamma_{2}+\gamma_{3}=1. $$

and

$$ a=\alpha_{1}*\alpha_{2}*\alpha_{3}. $$

- (ii) The functions $\alpha_{j}$ are such that, for some $Z\asymp X$ , we have

$$ \operatorname{supp}(\alpha_{j})\subseteq[Z^{\gamma_{j}},2Z^{\gamma_{j}}]. $$

Moreover, each $\alpha_{j}$ has the form

$$ \alpha_{j}(n)=\mathbf{1}_{I_{j}}(n)(b_{j,1}*\cdots*b_{j,\ell_{j}})(n),\qquad I_{j}\subseteq[Z^{\gamma_{j}},2Z^{\gamma_{j}}], $$

where $I_{j}$ is an interval, $\ell_{1}+\ell_{2}+\ell_{3}\leqslant 20$ , every $b_{j,r}$ is one of

$$ \mathbf{1}_{J},\qquad(\log\cdot)\mathbf{1}_{J},\qquad\mu\mathbf{1}_{J} $$

for an interval $J\subseteq(N,2N]$ , at most one of all the elementary factors is logarithmically weighted, and a Möbius factor has $N\ll Z^{1/10}$ .

We now use Heath-Brown’s identity to reduce the Möbius and von Mangoldt functions to Type I, $\mathrm{I}_{2}$ and II sums, in the sense of [10, Definition 4.1].

#### Proposition 6.4 (Heath-Brown reduction).

Each of the functions $\mu$ and $\Lambda$ admits a representation on $(X,X+H]$ as a linear combination of $O(\log^{O(1)}X)$ sums with coefficients satisfying $|a(n)|\ll d_{20}(n)\log X$ of the following forms.

- (a) (Type I sums) We have $a=\alpha*\beta$ , where

$$ \operatorname{supp}(\alpha)\subset[1,X^{3/5}\log^{O(1)}X],\qquad\sum_{n\leqslant A}|\alpha(n)|^{2}\ll A\log^{O(1)}X $$

for every $A\geqslant 1$ , and the factor $\beta$ is a dyadic $1$ -weighted or logarithmically weighted factor, and $\|\beta\|_{\TV(\mathbb{N})}\ll\log^{O(1)}X$ .

- (b) (Type $I_{2}$ sums) We have $a=\alpha*\beta_{1}*\beta_{2}$ , where

$$ \operatorname{supp}(\alpha)\subset[1,X^{2/5}\log^{O(1)}X]\qquad\sum_{n\leqslant A}|\alpha(n)|^{2}\ll A\log^{O(1)}X, $$

for every $A\geqslant 1$ , and

$$ \|\beta_{1}\|_{\TV(\mathbb{N})}+\|\beta_{2}\|_{\TV(\mathbb{N})}\ll\log^{O(1)}X. $$

- (c) (Type II sums) We have $a=\alpha*\beta$ , where $\textnormal{supp}(\alpha)\subseteq(M,2M]$ , $\textnormal{supp}(\beta)\subseteq(N,2N]$ and

$$ M,N\in[X^{2/5}\log^{-O(1)}X,X^{3/5}\log^{O(1)}X], $$

and moreover the coefficient sequences satisfy $\sum_{M<n\leqslant 2M}|\alpha(n)|^{2}\ll M\log^{O(1)}X$ and $\sum_{N<n\leqslant 2N}|\beta(n)|^{2k}\ll N\log^{O(1)}X$ for $k=1,2$ . Furthermore, every Type II component may be taken to be an admissible trilinear component.

Furthermore, if we define

$$ \Lambda_{X,\mathrm{I}}^{\sharp}(n)\coloneqq\frac{\mathcal{P}(R)}{\varphi(\mathcal{P}(R))}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}d\leqslant X^{3/10}\\
d\mid(n,\mathcal{P}(R))\end{subarray}}\mu(d), $$

then this function has a Type I representation as above and

$$ \sum_{X<n\leqslant X+H}\left|\Lambda_{X}^{\sharp}(n)-\Lambda_{X,\mathrm{I}}^{\sharp}(n)\right|\ll H\exp\bigl(-c\log^{1/20}X\bigr). $$

#### Proof.

Apply the Heath-Brown identities for $\Lambda$ and $\mu$ in [10, Lemma 2.16], with $L=10$ , and subdivide every factor dyadically. That lemma gives at most $20$ factors, each of type $\mathbf{1}_{J}$ , $(\log\cdot)\mathbf{1}_{J}$ , or $\mu\mathbf{1}_{J}$ , with at most one logarithmic factor and with every Möbius factor of length $\ll X^{1/10}$ . Lemma 6.2, applied to the resulting support exponents and followed by a dyadic subdivision of each of the three grouped product variables, produces respectively the Type I alternative in Proposition 6.4(a), the Type $\mathrm{I}_{2}$ alternative in Proposition 6.4(b), and the admissible trilinear alternative in Definition 6.3, with the moment estimates following from the standard divisor bounds, while the assertion concerning $\Lambda_{X,\mathrm{I}}^{\sharp}$ and its error is [10, (4.7)–(4.8)]. ∎

### 6.2. Trilinear sums

The new arithmetic input leading to our improvement is the following trilinear estimate.

#### Proposition 6.5 (High frequency trilinear major arcs at the $3/5$ scale).

Let $A,B\geqslant 1$ and $\varepsilon>0$ be fixed. Let

$$ X^{3/5+\varepsilon}\leqslant H\leqslant X^{1-\varepsilon}, $$

and let $a_{n}$ be any admissible trilinear component arising from Proposition 6.4(c). There is a constant $C_{A}=C(A,B,\varepsilon)>0$ such that, uniformly for

$$ \frac{X}{H}\log^{C_{A}}X\leqslant|T|\leqslant X^{B}, $$

one has

$$ \left\lvert\sum_{X<n\leqslant X+H}a_{n}n^{iT}\right\rvert^{\,*}\ll_{A,B,\varepsilon}\frac{H}{\log^{A}X}. $$

#### Proof.

Let $P=\{b_{0}<n\leqslant b_{0}+L:n\equiv a\,(\mathrm{mod}\,q)\}\subseteq[X,X+H]$ be a progression on which the supremum in (1.10) is attained for (6.8). It suffices to show that

$$ \Big|\sum_{n\in P}a_{n}n^{iT}\Big|\ll_{A,B,\varepsilon}\frac{H}{\log^{A}X}. $$

By the divisor bound, $a_{n}\ll_{\varepsilon}X^{\varepsilon/4}$ , so that

$$ \sum_{n\in P}|a_{n}|\ll_{A,B,\varepsilon}X^{\varepsilon/4}\left(\frac{L}{q}+1\right). $$

This gives (6.9) unless $L\geqslant HX^{-\varepsilon/2}$ and $q\leqslant X^{\varepsilon/2}$ .

Write $d=(a,q)$ , $q=dq^{\prime}$ and $a=da^{\prime}$ , so that $(a^{\prime},q^{\prime})=1$ . Shiu’s bound [13, Theorem 1], applied after $n=dm$ , gives

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{n\in P}|a_{n}|\ll\left(\frac{L}{d\varphi(q^{\prime})}+1\right)d_{20}(d)\log^{O(1)}X\ll\frac{L}{q^{1/2}}\log^{O(1)}X. $$

It follows, on taking $A_{1}$ sufficiently large in terms of $A,B,\varepsilon$ , that (6.9) holds if $L<H\log^{-A_{1}}X$ or $q>\log^{A_{1}}X$ . We may therefore assume that

$$ L\geqslant H\log^{-A_{1}}X\quad\text{ and }\quad q\leqslant\log^{A_{1}}X. $$

By the orthogonality of Dirichlet characters, we have

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}b_{0}<n\leqslant b_{0}+L\\
n\equiv a\,(\mathrm{mod}\,q)\end{subarray}}a_{n}n^{iT} \displaystyle=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}b_{0}<n\leqslant b_{0}+L\\
d\mid n\\
\frac{n}{d}\equiv a^{\prime}\,(\mathrm{mod}\,q^{\prime})\end{subarray}}a_{n}n^{iT} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{\varphi(q^{\prime})}\sum_{\chi\,(\mathrm{mod}\,q^{\prime})}\overline{\chi(a^{\prime})}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}b_{0}<n\leqslant b_{0}+L\\
d\mid n\end{subarray}}a_{n}\chi(n/d)n^{iT}. $$

Write $u_{0}=\lfloor b_{0}\rfloor+1/2$ and $v_{0}=\lfloor b_{0}+L\rfloor+1/2$ , and let $T_{1}\coloneqq\frac{X}{H}\log^{B_{1}}X$ with $B_{1}$ sufficiently large. The truncated Perron formula then gives

$$ \displaystyle\begin{aligned} \sum_{n}a_{n}\mathbf{1}_{d\mid n}\chi(n/d)n^{iT}\mathbf{1}_{[u_{0},v_{0}]}(n)&=\frac{1}{2\pi i}\int_{1/2-iT_{1}}^{1/2+iT_{1}}\frac{v_{0}^{s}-u_{0}^{s}}{s}\sum_{n}a_{n}n^{-s+iT}\mathbf{1}_{d\mid n}\chi(n/d)\,\textnormal{d}s\\
\quad&+O\left(\frac{X}{T_{1}}\log^{O(1)}X+X^{o(1)}\right),\end{aligned} $$

where the error bound follows from Shiu’s bound after a dyadic subdivision by distance from the half-integer endpoints. Note that

$$ \frac{v_{0}^{1/2+it}-u_{0}^{1/2+it}}{1/2+it}\ll\frac{L}{X^{1/2}}. $$

Fix a representation $a=\alpha_{1}*\alpha_{2}*\alpha_{3}$ and parameters $Z,\gamma_{1},\gamma_{2},\gamma_{3}$ as in Definition 6.3. For each factorisation $d_{1}d_{2}d_{3}=d$ , set

$$ \displaystyle r_{j} \displaystyle=\frac{d}{d_{1}\cdots d_{j}}, \displaystyle\mathcal{M}_{j}(s) \displaystyle=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}d_{j}\mid n\\
(n/d_{j},r_{j})=1\end{subarray}}\alpha_{j}(n)\chi(n/d_{j})n^{-s+iT},\qquad 1\leqslant j\leqslant 3. $$

Note that the number of factorisations is $O(\log^{O_{A_{1}}(1)}X)$ . Splitting the convolution variables successively according to $d_{1}=(n_{1},d)$ and $d_{2}=(n_{2},d/d_{1})$ yields

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{d\mid n}a_{n}\chi(n/d)n^{-s+iT}=\sum_{d_{1}d_{2}d_{3}=d}\mathcal{M}_{1}(s)\mathcal{M}_{2}(s)\mathcal{M}_{3}(s). $$

The polynomials $\mathcal{M}_{j}(s)$ have supports on $[Z^{\gamma_{j}},2Z^{\gamma_{j}}]$ with the exponents in (6.6). Thus, returning to (6.12), we reduce matters to the normalised Dirichlet polynomial estimate, for some $A_{2}$ sufficiently large in terms of $A_{1}$ , namely

$$ \int_{-T_{1}}^{T_{1}}\left\lvert\mathcal{M}_{1}(1/2+it)\mathcal{M}_{2}(1/2+it)\mathcal{M}_{3}(1/2+it)\right\rvert\,\textnormal{d}t\ll_{A,B,\varepsilon}\frac{Z^{1/2}}{\log^{A_{2}}X}, $$

uniformly for all Dirichlet characters $\chi\pmod{q^{\prime}}$ and all divisor allocations. If $C_{A}>B_{1}+2$ , then for $|t|\leqslant T_{1}$ ,

$$ Z^{\varepsilon/3}\leqslant|t-T|\leqslant Z^{B+1}. $$

Recall that each $\alpha_{j}$ is a Dirichlet convolution of a bounded number of indicator sequences of intervals, or logarithmically weighted such indicators, or copies of Möbius function. We open the elementary convolutions in the shortest factor $\mathcal{M}_{2}$ . We distribute the divisibility condition among the elementary variables by the same successive gcd decomposition and remove the resulting coprimality conditions by Möbius inversion. This introduces only a polylogarithmic loss. One of the boundedly many factor polynomials has length $Z^{c+o(1)}$ for some $c=c(\varepsilon)>0$ ; after the other variables are fixed, it remains an interval sum with coefficient $1$ , $\mu$ or $\log$ and a character of polylogarithmic modulus. Applying e.g. [10, Lemma 3.9(i),(ii)] with $X=2Z^{B+1}$ (and partial summation for $\log$ ) to that factor, and the trivial bound to the others, gives

$$ \sup_{t\in[-T_{1},T_{1}]}\left\lvert\mathcal{M}_{2}(1/2+it)\right\rvert\ll_{A,B,\varepsilon}Z^{\gamma_{2}/2}\log^{-A^{\prime}}X $$

for every $A^{\prime}>0$ . Moreover, $T_{1}\leqslant Z^{2/5-\varepsilon/3}$ for sufficiently large $X$ , and the support and coefficient hypotheses of Lemma 5.1 hold. Hence that lemma applies with $Z$ in place of $X$ . Taking $A^{\prime}$ sufficiently large gives (6.13). This completes the proof. ∎

### 6.3. Proof of Theorem 1.2

We first observe that the argument in [10, Theorems 3.1 and 4.2] reduces the nilsequence discorrelation problem in the range $X^{3/5+\varepsilon}\leqslant H\leqslant X^{1-\varepsilon}$ to an abelian Type II obstruction.

#### Proposition 6.6 (Nilsequence discorrelation up to an abelian Type II obstruction).

Let $\varepsilon>0$ and $d,D,A\geqslant 1$ . Suppose that

$$ 2\leqslant X^{3/5+\varepsilon}\leqslant H\leqslant X^{1-\varepsilon}. $$

Let $G/\Gamma$ be a filtered nilmanifold of degree at most $d$ , dimension at most $D$ , and complexity at most $\log^{A}X$ . Let $F\colon G/\Gamma\to\mathbb{C}$ have zero mean and satisfy

$$ \|F\|_{\mathrm{Lip}}\leqslant\log^{A}X, $$

let $g:\mathbb{Z}\to G$ be polynomial, and let

$$ f\in\{\Lambda-\Lambda_{X}^{\sharp},\mu\}. $$

Then

$$ \left|\sum_{X<n\leqslant X+H}f(n)F(g(n)\Gamma)\right|^{*}\ll_{d,D,A,\varepsilon}\frac{H}{\log^{A}X}, $$

unless the following exceptional alternative holds.

There exist $A_{1}=C(d,D,A,\varepsilon)>0$ , an admissible trilinear component $h$ arising from Proposition 6.4(c) and a real number

$$ |T|\leqslant(X/H)^{d+1}\log^{A_{1}}X $$

such that

$$ \displaystyle\left|\sum_{X<n\leqslant X+H}f(n)n^{iT}\right|^{*} \displaystyle\gg_{d,D,A,\varepsilon}H\log^{-A_{1}}X, \displaystyle\left|\sum_{X<n\leqslant X+H}h(n)n^{iT}\right|^{*} \displaystyle\gg_{d,D,A,\varepsilon}H\log^{-A_{1}}X. $$

#### Proof.

We argue by induction on the dimension of $G/\Gamma$ . The zero-dimensional case is immediate, since a function with mean zero on a one-point nilmanifold vanishes.

Choose $C_{0}=C_{0}(d,D,A,\varepsilon)$ sufficiently large. On enlarging $C_{0}$ , we may assume that it dominates all logarithmic powers in Proposition 6.4. Moreover, we may assume that

$$ \sum_{X<n\leqslant X+H}|f(n)|\ll H\log^{C_{0}}X. $$

Indeed, for $f=\mu$ this is immediate, while for $f=\Lambda-\Lambda_{X}^{\sharp}$ it follows from Shiu’s bound and the definition of $\Lambda_{X}^{\sharp}$ . Let $A_{1}$ be sufficiently large in terms of $d,D,A,\varepsilon,C_{0}$ to absorb any logarithmic losses that follow.

Choose $E>A+C_{0}+10$ . By the Fourier decomposition of [10, Proposition 2.9], we have

$$ F=\sum_{\xi\in\Xi}F_{\xi}+O(\log^{-E}X),\qquad|\Xi|+\max_{\xi\in\Xi}\|F_{\xi}\|_{\mathrm{Lip}}\ll\log^{O_{d,D,A,E}(1)}X, $$

where $F_{\xi}$ oscillates with central frequency $\xi$ . For each $\xi\in\Xi$ , define

$$ m_{\xi}=\int_{G/\Gamma}F_{\xi},\qquad F_{\xi}^{0}=F_{\xi}-m_{\xi}. $$

Then $F_{\xi}^{0}$ has mean zero; if $\xi\neq 0$ , Haar invariance gives $m_{\xi}=0$ , while the zero-frequency component factors through the quotient by the centre. The error term is controlled by (6.17), the constants $m_{\xi}$ by the major arc estimate of [10, Theorem 3.1(i)], and every component invariant under a positive-dimensional central subgroup by the induction hypothesis on the corresponding quotient. Consequently, after enlarging $A_{1}$ , we may assume, unless the exceptional alternative has already occurred, that $\dim Z(G)=1$ and that $F$ oscillates with a non-zero central frequency.

By Proposition 6.4, the function $f$ can be represented as a linear combination of $O(\log^{O(1)}X)$ functions $h$ of the following forms:

- (i) $h$ is a $(\log^{-A_{1}}X,X^{3/5+\varepsilon/5})$ type I sum;

- (ii) $h$ is a $(\log^{-A_{1}}X,X^{2/5+\varepsilon/5})$ type I2 sum;

- (iii) $h$ is a $(\log^{-A_{1}}X,A_{II}^{-},A_{II}^{+})$ type II sum satisfying (6.18) $\displaystyle X^{2/5}\log^{-O(1)}X\ll A_{II}^{-}\leqslant A_{II}^{+}\ll X^{3/5+\varepsilon/5}.$

For $f=\Lambda-\Lambda_{X}^{\sharp}$ , the $L^{1}$ error in the last sentence of Proposition 6.4 is smaller than every required logarithmic loss. If the claimed discorrelation estimate fails, we have

$$ \left|\sum_{X<n\leqslant X+H}f(n)F(g(n)\Gamma)\right|^{*}\gg\frac{H}{\log^{A+1}X}. $$

Then the triangle inequality and the number of components give one function $h$ of one of the above types for which

$$ \displaystyle\left|\sum_{X<n\leqslant X+H}h(n)F(g(n)\Gamma)\right|^{*}\gg\frac{H}{\log^{A+O(1)}X}. $$

We apply [10, Theorem 4.2] to this component. In the Type I and Type $I_{2}$ cases, and in the non-abelian Type II case, it gives one of the following alternatives:

- Case 1: a non-trivial horizontal character $\eta:G\to\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}$ of Lipschitz norm $O_{d,D}(\log^{O_{d,D,A,A_{1}}(1)}X)$ satisfies (6.21) $\displaystyle\|\eta\circ g\|_{C^{\infty}[X,X+H]}\ll_{d,D}\log^{O_{A_{1}}(1)}X;$

- Case 2: the component $h$ is Type II and the nilmanifold is abelian.

The size alternative in [10, Theorem 4.2(i),(ii),(iv)] cannot occur. Indeed, the corresponding quantities in the three cases satisfy

$$ X^{3/5+\varepsilon/5}=o(H),\qquad X^{1/3}(X^{2/5+\varepsilon/5})^{2/3}=X^{3/5+2\varepsilon/15}=o(H), $$

and, by (6.18),

$$ \max\{A_{II}^{+},X/A_{II}^{-}\}\ll X^{3/5+\varepsilon/5}\log^{O(1)}X=o(H). $$

In Case 2, since $\dim Z(G)=1$ , the group $G$ is one-dimensional. The single-frequency property therefore gives

$$ F(g(n)\Gamma)=b\,e(P(n)) $$

for some $b\in\mathbb{C}$ and some polynomial $P:\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{R}$ of degree at most $d$ . The original failed correlation (6.19) and the component correlation (6.20) give now

$$ \displaystyle\left|\sum_{X<n\leqslant X+H}f(n)e(P(n))\right|^{*} \displaystyle\gg_{d,D,A,\varepsilon}H\log^{-A_{1}}X, \displaystyle\left|\sum_{X<n\leqslant X+H}h(n)e(P(n))\right|^{*} \displaystyle\gg_{d,D,A,\varepsilon}H\log^{-A_{1}}X. $$

After normalising by $b$ , [10, Theorem 4.2(iii)] gives an integer $q\ll\log^{O_{A_{1}}(1)}X$ and a number $|T|\leqslant(X/H)^{d+1}\log^{O_{A_{1}}(1)}X$ such that

$$ \displaystyle\|e(P(n))n^{-iT}\|_{\mathrm{TV}((X,X+H]\cap\mathbb{Z};q)} \displaystyle\ll_{d,D,A,\varepsilon}\log^{O(A_{1})}X, $$

By [10, Lemma 2.2(iii)], combining (6.22) and (6.23) with (6.24) and enlarging $A_{1}$ give (6.15) and (6.16). This is the exceptional alternative in the statement.

Therefore, it remains to consider the case in which (6.21) holds. As in [10, Section 4.2], we apply [10, Lemma 2.11] to factor $g\in\Poly(\mathbb{Z}\to G)$ as $g=\varepsilon g^{\prime}\gamma$ , where $\varepsilon$ is smooth, $\gamma$ is rational and $g^{\prime}\in\Poly(\mathbb{Z},\ker\eta)$ . Freezing $\varepsilon$ and $\gamma$ incurs an error of $O(H\log^{-A-1}X)$ and splits $(X,X+H]$ into $O(\log^{O_{A_{1}}(1)}X)$ arithmetic progressions $P_{j}$ , as in [10, Section 4.2]. On each $P_{j}$ , we are therefore reduced to a nilsequence $F_{j}(g_{j}(n)\Gamma_{j})$ on a proper rational subnilmanifold $G_{j}/\Gamma_{j}$ satisfying $\dim G_{j}<\dim G$ .

With the constants in this factorisation fixed, choose $B^{\prime}$ sufficiently large in terms of $A_{1},A,d,D,\varepsilon$ to absorb the number of progressions and all other logarithmic losses. If the induction hypothesis, applied to the mean-zero part of some $F_{j}$ on the original interval $(X,X+H]$ , yields its exceptional alternative, then it gives (6.15) and (6.16), together with the required bound for $T$ , with a possibly larger logarithmic exponent. We enlarge the final value of $A_{1}$ to that exponent. Otherwise, after subtracting the mean of $F_{j}$ , the major arc estimate and the induction hypothesis, both applied with saving exponent $B^{\prime}$ , give

$$ \Big|\sum_{n\in P_{j}}f(n)F_{j}(g_{j}(n)\Gamma_{j})\Big|^{*}\ll\frac{H}{\log^{B^{\prime}}X}. $$

Intersecting an arbitrary arithmetic progression with the $P_{j}$ and summing the resulting estimates gives

$$ \Big|\sum_{X<n\leqslant X+H}f(n)F(g(n)\Gamma)\Big|^{*}\ll\frac{H}{\log^{A}X}, $$

as claimed. This completes the induction and hence the proof. ∎

#### Proof of Theorem 1.2.

Let $f\in\{\mu,\Lambda-\Lambda_{X}^{\sharp}\}$ . Subtracting the mean of $F$ , the constant part is bounded by [10, Theorem 3.1(i)]; thus we may suppose that $F$ has mean zero. The Lipschitz norm of the new $F$ is at most $2/\delta$ . Fix a sufficiently large $M=M(A,d,D)$ , and write

$$ A^{\prime}=\max\{A,M+1\}. $$

If $\delta<\log^{-M}X$ , the trivial estimate

$$ \left|\sum_{X<n\leqslant X+H}f(n)\overline{F(g(n)\Gamma)}\right|^{*}\ll\delta^{-1}H\log X $$

is at most $\delta^{-O_{d,D}(1)}H\log^{-A}X$ once the exponent implicit in $O_{d,D}(1)$ is chosen sufficiently large. If $\delta\geqslant\log^{-M}X$ , the complexity of $G/\Gamma$ is at most $\log^{M}X$ . We apply Proposition 6.6 to $\overline{F}$ with $A^{\prime}$ in place of $A$ . We reach

$$ \left|\sum_{X<n\leqslant X+H}f(n)\overline{F(g(n)\Gamma)}\right|^{*}\ll_{d,D,A,\varepsilon}\frac{H}{\log^{A^{\prime}}X}\ll\frac{H}{\log^{A}X}, $$

unless the alternative of that proposition holds.

It remains to rule out the alternative of Proposition 6.6. Let $h,T$ and $A_{1}$ be as there. We apply Proposition 6.5 with $A_{1}+10$ and $d+2$ in place of $A$ and $B$ and let $C_{2}=C_{2}(A_{1}+10,d+2,\varepsilon)$ be the constant denoted $C_{A}$ there. If

$$ \frac{X}{H}\log^{C_{2}}X\leqslant|T|\leqslant\left(\frac{X}{H}\right)^{d+1}\log^{A_{1}}X, $$

then $|T|\leqslant X^{d+2}$ for all sufficiently large $X$ , and Proposition 6.5 gives

$$ \left|\sum_{X<n\leqslant X+H}h(n)n^{iT}\right|^{*}\ll\frac{H}{\log^{A_{1}+10}X}, $$

contradicting (6.16).

Suppose instead that

$$ |T|<\frac{X}{H}\log^{C_{2}}X. $$

Then

$$ \|n^{iT}\|_{\mathrm{TV}((X,X+H]\cap\mathbb{Z})}\ll 1+\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}X<n\leqslant X+H\end{subarray}}|(n+1)^{iT}-n^{iT}|\ll 1+|T|\frac{H}{X}\ll\log^{C_{2}}X. $$

Combining this with (6.15) and [10, Lemma 2.2(iii)], we obtain

$$ \left|\sum_{X<n\leqslant X+H}f(n)\right|^{*}\gg\frac{H}{\log^{A_{1}+C_{2}}X}. $$

The major arc estimate of [10, Theorem 3.1(i)], applied with saving exponent $A_{1}+C_{2}+1$ , contradicts this. Hence the alternative in Proposition 6.6 cannot occur, and the theorem follows. ∎

## 7. Sums of the Möbius function over short intervals

The aim of this section is to prove Theorem 1.4. Let us first give the relevant combinatorial decomposition lemma.

#### Lemma 7.1 (Type I, Type II, Type I/II trichotomy).

Let $\tau\in(0,1/2)$ , let $0\leqslant\eta<1-2\tau$ , and let $k\geqslant 1$ . Let $\alpha_{1},\ldots,\alpha_{k}\geqslant 0$ , write $S=\sum_{j\leqslant k}\alpha_{j}$ , and suppose that $|S-1|\leqslant\eta$ . For $J\subset\{1,\ldots,k\}$ write $\alpha_{J}=\sum_{j\in J}\alpha_{j}$ . Then at least one of the following alternatives holds.

- (i) There is an index $j_{0}\in\{1,\dotsc,k\}$ such that $\alpha_{j_{0}}>\tau$ .

- (ii) There is a partition $\{1,\dotsc,k\}=J_{1}\sqcup J_{2}$ with $\alpha_{J_{1}},\alpha_{J_{2}}\in[\tau,S-\tau].$

- (iii) There is an index $j_{0}\in\{1,\dotsc,k\}$ and a partition $\{1,\dotsc,k\}=\{j_{0}\}\sqcup J_{1}\sqcup J_{2}$ such that $S-2\tau<\alpha_{j_{0}}\leqslant\tau$ and, for $r\in\{1,2\}$ , we have

$$ S-2\tau<\alpha_{J_{r}}<\tau. $$

#### Proof.

Assume that (i) and (ii) fail. After discarding zero terms, choose maximal disjoint sets $J_{1},J_{2}\subseteq\{1,\dotsc,k\}$ such that $\alpha_{J_{1}},\alpha_{J_{2}}<\tau$ . Write $J_{0}=\{1,\dotsc,k\}\setminus(J_{1}\cup J_{2})$ .

Let us first show that $|J_{0}|=1$ . Since $S\geqslant 2\tau$ , we have $J_{0}\neq\emptyset$ . Assume for contradiction that there exist distinct $r_{1},r_{2}\in J_{0}$ . By maximality,

$$ \alpha_{J_{1}\cup\{r_{1}\}},\alpha_{J_{2}\cup\{r_{2}\}}\geqslant\tau. $$

Since we are not in case (ii), neither sum lies in $[\tau,S-\tau]$ , so both exceed $S-\tau$ . But then

$$ S\geqslant\alpha_{J_{1}\cup\{r_{1}\}}+\alpha_{J_{2}\cup\{r_{2}\}}>2(S-\tau)\geqslant S, $$

which is a contradiction. Hence $|J_{0}|=1$ , so $J_{0}=\{j_{0}\}$ for some $j_{0}\in\{1,\ldots,k\}$ .

Since case (i) fails, $\alpha_{j_{0}}\leqslant\tau$ . Moreover, neither $J_{1}$ nor $J_{2}$ is empty, since otherwise $S<2\tau$ . We have

$$ \alpha_{j_{0}}=S-\alpha_{J_{1}}-\alpha_{J_{2}}>S-2\tau, $$

and, for $\{r,s\}=\{1,2\}$ ,

$$ \alpha_{J_{r}}=S-\alpha_{j_{0}}-\alpha_{J_{s}}>S-2\tau. $$

Thus if $(i)$ and $(ii)$ fail, we are indeed in case (iii). ∎

We prove Theorem 1.4 following the overall strategy of Matomäki–Teräväinen [11]. We spell out the reduction from the short interval Möbius sum to a comparison of Dirichlet polynomial components, since this is where the Heath-Brown – Iwaniec type estimate is used.

### 7.1. Ramaré extraction and comparison

Choose parameters

$$ P\coloneqq\exp(\log^{2/3+\eta_{0}}X),\qquad Q\coloneqq X^{1/(\log\log X)^{2}}, $$

where $\eta_{0}>0$ is chosen sufficiently small in terms of $\varepsilon$ , and satisfies $\eta_{0}<\min\{1/40,\varepsilon/2\}$ . Employing a Ramaré-type identity [11, Lemma 3.1] with $2\eta_{0}$ in place of $\varepsilon$ , we obtain, uniformly for $X^{2\eta_{0}}\leqslant H\leqslant X$ ,

$$ \sum_{X<n\leqslant X+H}\mu(n)=-\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}X<prn\leqslant X+H\\
P<p\leqslant Q\\
r\leqslant X^{\eta_{0}}\end{subarray}}a_{r}\mu(n)+O\left(H\frac{\log P}{\log Q}\right), $$

with coefficients satisfying $|a_{r}|\leqslant d(r)$ . With the choice (7.1), the error term in (7.2) is $\ll H(\log X)^{-1/3+2\eta_{0}+o(1)}$ , and is therefore $O(H\log^{-1/3+\varepsilon}X)$ by the choice of $\eta_{0}$ .

We next decompose the main term in (7.2). Apply Heath-Brown’s identity [8, (13.38)] to $\mu(n)$ with parameter $K=20$ , and then decompose all variables dyadically. The identity has $2j-1$ variables in its $j$ th summand, and after adjoining dummy variables equal to $1$ , this expresses the main term as a linear combination of $O(\log^{2K+2}X)$ sums of the following form:

$$ S_{\mathcal{I}}\coloneqq\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}prn_{1}\cdots n_{2K-1}\in\mathcal{I}\\
p\in(P_{1},2P_{1}],\,r\in(R,2R],n_{j}\in(N_{j},2N_{j}]\\
p\leqslant Q\end{subarray}}a_{r}\alpha_{1}(n_{1})\cdots\alpha_{2K-1}(n_{2K-1}), $$

where $P_{1}\in[P,Q],\,R\in[1/2,X^{\eta_{0}}],\,N_{j}\geqslant 1/2$ , and

$$ P_{1}RN_{1}\cdots N_{2K-1}\asymp X. $$

For $1\leqslant j\leqslant K-1$ , the coefficient $\alpha_{j}(n)$ is an interval indicator (or a dummy factor supported at $1$ , with $N_{j}=1/2$ ); for $K\leqslant j\leqslant 2K-1$ , it is the Möbius function restricted to an interval with $N_{j}\leqslant(2X)^{1/K}$ (or a dummy factor supported at $1$ , with $N_{j}=1/2$ ). In particular, every factor of length greater than $(2X)^{1/K}$ is a $1$ -weighted factor.

Finally, define

$$ Y\coloneqq X\exp\bigl(-3\log^{1/3}X\bigr). $$

For each dyadic component, we compare the summation over $(X,X+H]$ with the corresponding summation over $(X,X+Y]$ . The required comparison is provided by the following proposition.

#### Proposition 7.2.

Let $\varepsilon>0$ , $B_{0}>0$ , and $X^{19/35+\varepsilon}\leqslant H\leqslant Y$ . Let $S_{\mathcal{I}}$ be any dyadic component of the form (7.3). Then

$$ S_{(X,X+H]}=\frac{H}{Y}S_{(X,X+Y]}+O_{\varepsilon,B_{0}}\left(\frac{H}{\log^{B_{0}}X}\right). $$

The estimate is uniform in the dyadic parameters satisfying (7.4).

#### Proof of Theorem 1.4 assuming Proposition 7.2.

If $H>Y$ , the Vinogradov–Korobov estimate for the summatory Möbius function gives

$$ \left|\sum_{X<n\leqslant X+H}\mu(n)\right|\ll X\exp\bigl(-c\log^{3/5}X(\log\log X)^{-1/5}\bigr)\ll\frac{H}{\log^{100}X}, $$

so there is nothing to prove. We may therefore assume that $H\leqslant Y$ .

Choose $B_{0}=100$ in Proposition 7.2 to compensate for the $O(\log^{2K+2}X)$ dyadic components. Summing (7.6) and recombining Heath-Brown’s identity and (7.2) gives

$$ \sum_{X<n\leqslant X+H}\mu(n)=\frac{H}{Y}\sum_{X<n\leqslant X+Y}\mu(n)+O_{\varepsilon}\left(\frac{H}{\log^{1/3-\varepsilon}X}\right). $$

For some $c>0$ , the main term on the right-hand side is $\ll H\exp(-c\log^{3/5}X(\log\log X)^{-1/5})$ by the classical zero-free region for $\zeta(s)$ , so Theorem 1.4 follows. ∎

### 7.2. The Dirichlet polynomial estimate

We conclude this section with the proof of Proposition 7.2.

#### Proof of Proposition 7.2.

Fix $A>B_{0}$ sufficiently large in terms of $K=20$ to absorb the fixed logarithmic losses in this proof.

For $1\leqslant j\leqslant 2K-1$ , write

$$ \beta_{j}=\max\left\{\frac{\log N_{j}}{\log X},0\right\},\qquad\beta_{2K}=\max\left\{\frac{\log R}{\log X},0\right\},\qquad\rho=\frac{\log P_{1}}{\log X}, $$

and set $S=\sum_{j=1}^{2K}\beta_{j}$ . By (7.4),

$$ S=1-\rho+O(1/\log X),\qquad 0\leqslant\rho\leqslant\frac{1}{(\log\log X)^{2}}+O(1/\log X). $$

Thus, for $X$ sufficiently large, Lemma 7.1 applies to $\beta_{1},\dotsc,\beta_{2K}$ with

$$ \tau=\frac{16}{35}-\frac{\varepsilon}{4},\qquad\eta=\frac{2}{(\log\log X)^{2}}. $$

We split into cases.

Case 1: Lemma 7.1(i) holds. Now there is an index $j_{0}$ with $\beta_{j_{0}}>\tau.$ Since $\tau>2/K$ , $\alpha_{j_{0}}$ is an interval indicator. Write its supporting interval as $I_{j_{0}}=(u,v]$ . Putting the sum over $n_{j_{0}}$ inside, in this case we obtain, for some $|b_{m}|\leqslant d_{100}(m)$ ,

$$ S_{(X,X+H]}-\frac{H}{Y}S_{(X,X+Y]}=\sum_{m\leqslant 2X/N_{j_{0}}}b_{m}\left(\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}X/m<n_{j_{0}}\leqslant(X+H)/m\\
n_{j_{0}}\in(u,v]\end{subarray}}1-\frac{H}{Y}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}X/m<n_{j_{0}}\leqslant(X+Y)/m\\
n_{j_{0}}\in(u,v]\end{subarray}}1\right). $$

Now the difference in the parentheses is $O(1)$ unless

$$ X<mu\leqslant X+Y\qquad\text{or}\qquad X<mv\leqslant X+Y. $$

There are $O(Y/N_{j_{0}}+1)$ integers $m$ for which one of these holds, and for each of them the difference in the parentheses is $O(1+HN_{j_{0}}/X)=O(HN_{j_{0}}/X)$ . Shiu’s bound for the divisor bounded coefficients $b_{m}$ thus gives

$$ S_{(X,X+H]}-\frac{H}{Y}S_{(X,X+Y]}\ll\left(\frac{X}{N_{j_{0}}}+\frac{HY}{X}+\frac{HN_{j_{0}}}{X}\right)\log^{O(1)}X. $$

Since $N_{j_{0}}\in(X^{\tau},2X/P]$ , $H\geqslant X^{19/35+\varepsilon}$ , and $Y/X=\exp(-3\log^{1/3}X)$ , this is $\ll_{A,\varepsilon}H/\log^{A}X$ as claimed.

Case 2: Lemma 7.1(ii) or (iii) holds. By a standard reduction using Perron’s formula (see e.g. [5, Lemma 7.2]), it is enough to prove that, for every $A\geqslant 1$ ,

$$ \int_{T_{0}}^{T_{1}}\left|P_{1}(1/2+it)N_{2K}(1/2+it)\prod_{j=1}^{2K-1}N_{j}(1/2+it)\right|\,\textnormal{d}t\ll_{A}\frac{X^{1/2}}{\log^{A}X}, $$

where

$$ T_{0}=\exp(\log^{1/3}X),\qquad T_{1}=\frac{X^{1+\varepsilon/2}}{H}\leqslant X^{16/35-\varepsilon/2}, $$

and

$$ P_{1}(s)=\sum_{P_{1}<p\leqslant\min\{2P_{1},Q\}}p^{-s},\quad N_{2K}(s)=\sum_{R<r\leqslant 2R}a_{r}r^{-s},\quad N_{j}(s)=\sum_{N_{j}<n\leqslant 2N_{j}}\alpha_{j}(n)n^{-s} $$

for $1\leqslant j\leqslant 2K-1$ .

Case 2.1: Lemma 7.1(ii) holds. Let $J_{1}\sqcup J_{2}=\{1,\dotsc,2K\}$ be the partition in the lemma and set, for $\ell\in\{1,2\}$ ,

$$ A_{\ell}(s)=\prod_{j\in J_{\ell}}N_{j}(s), $$

and

$$ \beta_{J_{\ell}}\coloneqq\sum_{j\in J_{\ell}}\beta_{j}, $$

so that $A_{\ell}(s)$ has length $X^{\beta_{J_{\ell}}}$ .

Alternative (ii) of Lemma 7.1 gives

$$ \tau\leqslant\beta_{J_{1}},\beta_{J_{2}}\leqslant S-\tau. $$

Since $\tau=\frac{16}{35}-\frac{\varepsilon}{4}$ ,

$$ T_{1}\leqslant X^{16/35-\varepsilon/2}=X^{\tau-\varepsilon/4}\leqslant\min\{X^{\beta_{J_{1}}},X^{\beta_{J_{2}}}\}. $$

For every $B_{0}>0$ , by the zero-free region estimate in the form used in [11, Lemma 4.3], we have

$$ \sup_{T_{0}\leqslant|t|\leqslant T_{1}}|P_{1}(1/2+it)|\ll_{B_{0}}P_{1}^{1/2}\log^{-B_{0}}X. $$

The Cauchy–Schwarz inequality, followed by the mean-value theorem for Dirichlet polynomials (see e.g. [8, Theorem 9.1]), (7.10), and (7.4) yields

$$ \displaystyle\int_{T_{0}}^{T_{1}}|P_{1}(1/2+it)A_{1}(1/2+it)A_{2}(1/2+it)|\,\,\textnormal{d}t \displaystyle\ll_{B_{0}}P_{1}^{1/2}\log^{-B_{0}}X\left(\int_{T_{0}}^{T_{1}}|A_{1}(1/2+it)|^{2}\,\,\textnormal{d}t\right)^{1/2}\left(\int_{T_{0}}^{T_{1}}|A_{2}(1/2+it)|^{2}\,\,\textnormal{d}t\right)^{1/2} \displaystyle\ll P_{1}^{1/2}\log^{-B_{0}}X\left(T_{1}+X^{\beta_{J_{1}}}\right)^{1/2}\left(T_{1}+X^{\beta_{J_{2}}}\right)^{1/2}\log^{O(1)}X \displaystyle\ll P_{1}^{1/2}(X^{\beta_{J_{1}}+\beta_{J_{2}}})^{1/2}\log^{-B_{0}+O(1)}X\ll\frac{X^{1/2}}{\log^{B_{0}-O(1)}X} $$

Choosing $B_{0}$ sufficiently large therefore gives (7.8).

Case 2.2: Lemma 7.1(iii) holds. Let $\{1,\dotsc,2K\}=\{j_{0}\}\sqcup J_{1}\sqcup J_{2}$ be the partition in the lemma, and set $\beta_{J_{r}}=\sum_{j\in J_{r}}\beta_{j}$ . Then

$$ S-2\tau<\beta_{j_{0}},\beta_{J_{1}},\beta_{J_{2}}\leqslant\tau. $$

Moreover,

$$ S-2\tau=\frac{3}{35}+\frac{\varepsilon}{2}-\rho+O(1/\log X)>\frac{1}{K} $$

for sufficiently large $X$ . Hence $j_{0}\leqslant K-1$ , so $N_{j_{0}}(s)$ is an interval-indicator factor. Absorb $P_{1}(s)$ into either of the other two blocks and subdivide the two product supports into $O_{K}(1)$ dyadic pieces. For a fixed piece, write the product as $L(s)M(s)N(s)$ , with $L(s)=N_{j_{0}}(s)$ , let $L_{0},M_{0},N_{0}$ be the lengths of the polynomials, and set $\widetilde{X}=L_{0}M_{0}N_{0}\asymp_{K}X$ . Writing

$$ L_{0}=\widetilde{X}^{\gamma_{1}},\quad M_{0}=\widetilde{X}^{\gamma_{2}},\quad N_{0}=\widetilde{X}^{\gamma_{3}}, $$

we have $\gamma_{1},\gamma_{2},\gamma_{3}\in[\varepsilon/8,16/35-\varepsilon/8]$ with $\gamma_{1}+\gamma_{2}+\gamma_{3}=1$ . Furthermore, for sufficiently large $X$ ,

$$ T_{1}\leqslant\widetilde{X}^{16/35-\varepsilon/8},\qquad T_{0}\geqslant\exp(\log^{1/4}\widetilde{X}). $$

Lemma 4.1, applied with $\widetilde{X}$ in place of $X$ and $\varepsilon/8$ in place of $\varepsilon$ , now gives (7.8). ∎

## 8. Computational lemmas

In this section we prove Lemmas 4.2 and 5.2. Note that each of these is a claim about positivity of a piecewise linear function (of the shape $P_{1}(t)+P_{2}(t)+P_{3}(t)-t-\varepsilon^{10}$ ). A brute force approach would be to check the inequality at all the possible break-points of these functions. Here we provide different proofs, based on looking at slopes of the piecewise linear functions.

Before turning to the proofs of Lemmas 4.2 and 5.2, for $\beta\geqslant\varepsilon$ and $t\in[0,\tau]$ , we define and study the function

$$ \displaystyle\begin{aligned} R_{\beta,\tau}(t)&:=\beta\inf\{\nu\geqslant 0\colon\mathcal{K}(\beta,\nu;\tau)\geqslant t\}\\
&=\max\left\{0,\min\Bigl\{\frac{t}{2},\max\Bigl\{\frac{t-\tau+2\beta}{6},\min\Bigl\{\frac{t-\tau+\frac{8}{5}\beta}{4},\frac{t-\frac{\tau}{2}+\beta}{4}\Bigr\},\frac{t-\tau+\beta}{2}\Bigr\}\Bigr\}\right\}.\end{aligned} $$

Splitting into cases, we obtain the following explicit formulas. If $\varepsilon\leqslant\beta\leqslant\tau/2$ , then

$$ R_{\beta,\tau}(t)=\begin{cases}0,&\text{if $0\leqslant t\leqslant\tau-2\beta$,}\\
\frac{t-\tau+2\beta}{6},&\text{if $\tau-2\beta\leqslant t\leqslant\tau-\frac{4}{5}\beta$,}\\
\frac{t-\tau+\frac{8}{5}\beta}{4},&\text{if $\tau-\frac{4}{5}\beta\leqslant t\leqslant\tau-\frac{2}{5}\beta$},\\
\frac{t-\tau+\beta}{2},&\text{if $\tau-\frac{2}{5}\beta\leqslant t\leqslant\tau$}.\end{cases} $$

If $\tau/2\leqslant\beta\leqslant 5\tau/6$ , then

$$ \displaystyle R_{\beta,\tau}(t)=\begin{cases}\frac{t}{2},&\text{if $0\leqslant t\leqslant\beta-\frac{\tau}{2}$,}\\
\frac{t-\tau+2\beta}{6},&\text{if $\beta-\frac{\tau}{2}\leqslant t\leqslant\tau-\frac{4}{5}\beta$},\\
\frac{t-\tau+\frac{8}{5}\beta}{4},&\text{if $\tau-\frac{4}{5}\beta\leqslant t\leqslant\tau-\frac{2}{5}\beta$},\\
\frac{t-\tau+\beta}{2},&\text{if $\tau-\frac{2}{5}\beta\leqslant t\leqslant\tau$}.\end{cases} $$

If $5\tau/6\leqslant\beta\leqslant\tau$ , then

$$ \displaystyle R_{\beta,\tau}(t)=\begin{cases}\frac{t}{2},&\text{if $0\leqslant t\leqslant\beta-\frac{\tau}{2}$,}\\
\frac{t-\frac{\tau}{2}+\beta}{4},&\text{if $\beta-\frac{\tau}{2}\leqslant t\leqslant\frac{3\tau}{2}-\beta$},\\
\frac{t-\tau+\beta}{2},&\text{if $\frac{3\tau}{2}-\beta\leqslant t\leqslant\tau$}.\end{cases} $$

Finally, if $\beta>\tau$ , then

$$ R_{\beta,\tau}(t)=\frac{t}{2}. $$

#### Proof of Lemma 4.2.

First of all, we observe that $H_{j,\tau}(\nu)$ is nondecreasing in $\tau\in[\varepsilon,\tau_{1}]$ . As a consequence, $\{\nu:H_{j,\tau}(\nu)\geqslant t\}\subseteq\{\nu:H_{j,\tau_{1}}(\nu)\geqslant t\}$ . From the definition of $P_{j,\tau}$ in Lemma 4.2 we thus have for $\tau\in[\varepsilon,\tau_{1}]$ and $0\leqslant t\leqslant\tau$ that

$$ P_{j,\tau}(t)\geqslant P_{j,\tau_{1}}(t). $$

For convenience, set $P_{j}(t)=P_{j,\tau_{1}}(t)$ and $R_{\beta}(t)=R_{\beta,\tau_{1}}(t)$ . It then suffices to prove that

$$ \displaystyle F(t):=P_{1}(t)+P_{2}(t)+P_{3}(t)-t>\varepsilon^{10} $$

for all $0\leqslant t\leqslant\tau_{1}$ .

Since $\nu$ takes values in the interval $[\varepsilon^{6},\varepsilon^{-1}]$ , we can conclude the above inequality when $t$ is rather small. Indeed, for all $t\in[0,\tau_{1}]$ one has

$$ P_{1}(t)+P_{2}(t)+P_{3}(t)\geqslant(\beta_{1}+\beta_{2}+\beta_{3})\varepsilon^{6}=\varepsilon^{6}. $$

Thus, for $t\leqslant\varepsilon^{6}/2$ , we have

$$ F(t)\geqslant\frac{\varepsilon^{6}}{2}>\varepsilon^{10}. $$

Let us assume below that $\varepsilon^{6}/2<t\leqslant\tau_{1}$ . From the definition of $R_{\beta}(t)$ , it is immediate that if $\mathcal{K}(\beta_{2},\nu;\tau_{1})\geqslant t$ and $\mathcal{K}(2\beta_{2},\nu;\tau_{1})\geqslant t$ , then $\beta_{2}\nu\geqslant R_{\beta_{2}}(t)$ and $2\beta_{2}\nu\geqslant R_{2\beta_{2}}(t)$ . Thus it follows from the definitions of $P_{2}(t)$ in Lemma 4.2 and $R_{\beta}(t)$ in (8.1) that

$$ \displaystyle P_{2}(t)\geqslant\max\left\{R_{\beta_{2}}(t),\frac{1}{2}R_{2\beta_{2}}(t)\right\}. $$

Similarly,

$$ \displaystyle P_{3}(t)\geqslant\max\left\{R_{\beta_{3}}(t),\frac{1}{2}R_{2\beta_{3}}(t)\right\},\qquad P_{1}(t)\geqslant\max\left\{\frac{t-\tau_{1}+2\beta_{1}}{4},\frac{1}{2}R_{2\beta_{1}}(t)\right\}. $$

We shall prove (8.6) for $t\in[\varepsilon^{6}/2,\tau_{1}]$ using these piecewise-linear lower bounds.

We first make a preliminary reduction. By (8.8), (8.7) and (8.1), we have, for $\beta_{2},\beta_{3}\leqslant\tau_{1}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle P_{1}(t)+P_{2}(t)+P_{3}(t) \displaystyle\geqslant\frac{t-\tau_{1}+2\beta_{1}}{4}+\min\left\{\frac{t}{4},\frac{t-\tau_{1}+2\beta_{2}}{4}\right\}+\frac{t-\tau_{1}+\beta_{3}}{2} \displaystyle=\min\left\{t-\frac{3}{4}\tau_{1}+\frac{\beta_{1}+\beta_{3}}{2},\frac{1}{2}+t-\tau_{1}\right\}. $$

The second term in the minimum is $t+3/70+\varepsilon>t+\varepsilon^{10}$ . The first term is strictly greater than $t+\varepsilon^{10}$ if

$$ \beta_{1}+\beta_{3}>\frac{3}{2}\tau_{1}+2\varepsilon^{10}\iff\beta_{2}<1-\frac{3}{2}\tau_{1}-2\varepsilon^{10}. $$

Thus, using also the symmetry between $\beta_{2}$ and $\beta_{3}$ , we may restrict ourselves to the case

$$ \beta_{2},\beta_{3}\in\left[1-\frac{3}{2}\tau_{1}-2\varepsilon^{10},\tau_{1}\right]\subseteq[11/35+\varepsilon,\tau_{1}]. $$

In particular, after interchanging $\beta_{2}$ and $\beta_{3}$ if necessary, we assume from now on that

$$ \frac{11}{35}+\varepsilon\leqslant\beta_{2}\leqslant\beta_{3}\leqslant\tau_{1}. $$

Since $\varepsilon\in(0,1/100)$ , we have $11/35+\varepsilon\geqslant\tau_{1}/2$ , so $\beta_{2},\beta_{3}\geqslant\tau_{1}/2$ in this range. When $\beta\geqslant\tau_{1}/2$ let

$$ \displaystyle p(\beta)=\beta-\tau_{1}/2 $$

denote the first breakpoint of (8.3) and (8.4), thus the end of the initial slope- $1/2$ segment. Similarly let

$$ \displaystyle r(\beta)=\begin{cases}\tau_{1}-2\beta/5,\qquad&\text{ if }\beta\leqslant 5\tau_{1}/6;\\
3\tau_{1}/2-\beta,&\text{ if }5\tau_{1}/6\leqslant\beta\leqslant\tau_{1},\end{cases} $$

denote the last breakpoint of (8.2), (8.3) and (8.4), thus the beginning of the final slope- $1/2$ segment. Then $r(\beta)$ is a continuous and non-increasing function in $\beta$ . Since $R_{\beta_{2}}(t)=R_{\beta_{3}}(t)=t/2$ whenever $0\leqslant t\leqslant p(\beta_{2})\leqslant p(\beta_{3})$ , we then have

$$ F(t)\geqslant P_{1}(t)\geqslant\beta_{1}\varepsilon^{6}\geqslant\varepsilon^{7}>\varepsilon^{10}, $$

as desired.

It therefore remains to consider the case $p(\beta_{2})\leqslant t\leqslant\tau_{1}$ . We divide the rest of the argument into two cases depending on whether $\beta_{1}\geqslant\tau_{1}/2$ or $\beta_{1}<\tau_{1}/2$ .

Case 1: $\beta_{1}\geqslant\tau_{1}/2$ . Define

$$ F_{+}(t)=R_{\beta_{2}}(t)+R_{\beta_{3}}(t)+\frac{t-\tau_{1}+2\beta_{1}}{4}-t. $$

From (8.7)–(8.8), it suffices to show that $F_{+}(t)>\varepsilon^{10}$ whenever $t\in[p(\beta_{2}),\tau_{1}]$ . We shall show that $F_{+}(t)$ attains its minimum at $t=r(\beta_{2})$ .

When $t\in[p(\beta_{2}),r(\beta_{2})]$ , the slope of $R_{\beta_{2}}$ is at most $1/4$ , and the slope of $R_{\beta_{3}}$ is at most $1/2$ . Therefore the slope of $F_{+}(t)$ is at most $0$ . On the other hand, when $t\geqslant r(\beta_{2})\geqslant r(\beta_{3})$ both $R_{\beta_{2}}$ and $R_{\beta_{3}}$ are on their final branches (noting $r(\beta)$ is non-increasing), hence both of them have slope $1/2$ . Thus in this range $F_{+}$ has slope

$$ 1/2+1/2+1/4-1=1/4\geqslant 0. $$

Consequently, $F_{+}$ attains its minimum at $r(\beta_{2})$ , and the minimum is

$$ \displaystyle F_{+}(r(\beta_{2})) \displaystyle=\frac{r(\beta_{2})-\tau_{1}+\beta_{2}}{2}+\frac{r(\beta_{2})-\tau_{1}+\beta_{3}}{2}+\frac{r(\beta_{2})-\tau_{1}+2\beta_{1}}{4}-r(\beta_{2}) \displaystyle=\frac{r(\beta_{2})}{4}-\frac{5}{4}\tau_{1}+\frac{1}{2}. $$

If $\beta_{2}\leqslant 5\tau_{1}/6$ , then $r(\beta_{2})=\tau_{1}-2\beta_{2}/5$ and therefore,

$$ F_{+}(r(\beta_{2}))=-\tau_{1}-\frac{\beta_{2}}{10}+\frac{1}{2}\geqslant\frac{1}{2}-\frac{13\tau_{1}}{12}>\varepsilon^{10}, $$

If instead $\beta_{2}>5\tau_{1}/6$ , then $r(\beta_{2})=\frac{3\tau_{1}}{2}-\beta_{2}$ . Using also $\beta_{2}\leqslant(1-\beta_{1})/2\leqslant 1/2-\tau_{1}/4$ , we obtain

$$ F_{+}(r(\beta_{2}))=\frac{1}{2}-\frac{7\tau_{1}}{8}-\frac{\beta_{2}}{4}\geqslant\frac{3}{8}-\frac{13\tau_{1}}{16}>\varepsilon^{10}. $$

This proves (8.6) in Case 1.

Case 2: $\beta_{1}<\tau_{1}/2$ . Define

$$ F_{-}(t)=R_{\beta_{2}}(t)+R_{\beta_{3}}(t)+R_{2\beta_{1}}(t)/2-t. $$

For $t\in[p(\beta_{2}),r(\beta_{2})]$ , the slopes of $R_{\beta_{2}}$ , $R_{\beta_{3}}$ , and $R_{2\beta_{1}}/2$ are at most $1/4$ , $1/2$ , and $1/4$ , respectively, so the slope of $F_{-}$ is $\leqslant 0$ in this interval. For $t\in[r(\beta_{2}),\tau_{1}]$ , the first two slopes equal $1/2$ and the slope of $R_{2\beta_{1}}$ is non-negative, so the slope of $F_{-}$ is $\geqslant 0$ in this interval. Therefore $F_{-}$ attains its minimum at $r(\beta_{2})$ , and the minimum is

$$ \displaystyle F_{-}(r(\beta_{2})) \displaystyle=\frac{r(\beta_{2})-\tau_{1}+\beta_{2}}{2}+\frac{r(\beta_{2})-\tau_{1}+\beta_{3}}{2}+\frac{R_{2\beta_{1}}(r(\beta_{2}))}{2}-r(\beta_{2}) \displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}-\frac{\beta_{1}}{2}-\tau_{1}+\frac{R_{2\beta_{1}}(r(\beta_{2}))}{2}. $$

Thus it suffices to show that

$$ \displaystyle R_{2\beta_{1}}(r(\beta_{2}))>2\tau_{1}+\beta_{1}-1+2\varepsilon^{10} $$

Consider this for a fixed $\beta_{1}<\tau_{1}/2$ . Now $R_{2\beta_{1}}(t)$ is increasing in $t$ while $r(\beta_{2})$ is decreasing in $\beta_{2}$ . Thus $R_{2\beta_{1}}(r(\beta_{2}))$ is minimal when $\beta_{2}$ is maximal. Since $\beta_{2}\leqslant\beta_{3}$ and $\beta_{1}+\beta_{2}+\beta_{3}=1$ , we have $\beta_{2}\leqslant(1-\beta_{1})/2$ . Thus it suffices to show (8.11) for $\beta_{2}=(1-\beta_{1})/2$ . For $\beta_{1}<\tau_{1}/2$ , we have $(1-\beta_{1})/2\geqslant 5\tau_{1}/6$ . Thus, by definition of $r(\beta)$ it suffices to show that

$$ H(\beta_{1}):=R_{2\beta_{1}}\left(\frac{3\tau_{1}}{2}+\frac{\beta_{1}-1}{2}\right)-(2\tau_{1}+\beta_{1}-1+2\varepsilon^{10})>0. $$

Looking carefully at (8.2), (8.3), (8.4), (8.5), we see that the slope of $H(\beta_{1})$ is $\leqslant 0$ when the argument of $R_{2\beta_{1}}$ is $<r(2\beta_{1})$ and $\geqslant 0$ when the argument of $R_{2\beta_{1}}$ is $\geqslant r(2\beta_{1})$ . Thus it suffices to consider the case

$$ \frac{3\tau_{1}}{2}+\frac{\beta_{1}-1}{2}=r(2\beta_{1}) $$

If we had $2\beta_{1}\leqslant 5\tau_{1}/6$ , it would follow that

$$ r(2\beta_{1})=\tau_{1}-\frac{4\beta_{1}}{5}. $$

In this case

$$ \frac{3\tau_{1}}{2}+\frac{\beta_{1}-1}{2}-r(2\beta_{1})=\frac{\tau_{1}}{2}-\frac{1}{2}+\frac{13}{10}\beta_{1}\leqslant\frac{25}{24}\tau_{1}-\frac{1}{2}<0. $$

Thus (8.13) does not have a solution with $2\beta_{1}\leqslant 5\tau_{1}/6$ and $H(\beta_{1})$ is non-increasing in this range.

For $2\beta_{1}>5\tau_{1}/6$ , by the definition of $r(\beta)$ ,

$$ \frac{3\tau_{1}}{2}+\frac{\beta_{1}-1}{2}=\frac{3\tau_{1}}{2}-2\beta_{1}\iff\beta_{1}=\frac{1}{5} $$

and

$$ R_{2/5}\left(\frac{3\tau_{1}}{2}+\frac{\frac{1}{5}-1}{2}\right)=\frac{\frac{3\tau_{1}}{2}-\frac{2}{5}-\tau_{1}+\frac{2}{5}}{2}=\frac{\tau_{1}}{4}. $$

Thus

$$ H(1/5)=\frac{\tau_{1}}{4}-(2\tau_{1}+\frac{1}{5}-1+2\varepsilon^{10})=-\frac{7\tau_{1}}{4}+\frac{4}{5}-2\varepsilon^{10}. $$

Recalling $\tau_{1}=16/35-\varepsilon$ , we see that $H(1/5)=\frac{7}{4}\varepsilon-2\varepsilon^{10}>0$ and the claim follows. ∎

#### Proof of Lemma 5.2.

Set $\tau^{*}=2/5-\varepsilon$ and, for convenience, set $P_{\beta}(t)=P_{\beta,\tau^{\ast}}(t)$ and $R_{\beta}(t)=R_{\beta,\tau^{\ast}}(t)$ . Arguing as in the beginning of the proof of Lemma 4.2, it suffices to show that

$$ \displaystyle F(t):=P_{\beta_{1}}(t)+P_{\beta_{2}}(t)+P_{\beta_{3}}(t)-t>\varepsilon^{10} $$

for all $t\in[\varepsilon^{6}/2,\tau^{\ast}]$ . Note that, for all $\beta\in\{\beta_{1},\beta_{2},\beta_{3}\}$ ,

$$ P_{\beta}(t)\geqslant\max\Big\{R_{\beta}(t),\frac{R_{2\beta}(t)}{2}\Big\}. $$

We may assume that $\beta_{2}\leqslant\beta_{3}$ . Since $\beta_{2}\geqslant 1/5$ and $\beta_{1}\geqslant 2/5$ , we have $\beta_{1},2\beta_{2}\geqslant\tau^{*}$ . We therefore deduce from (8.15) and the definition of $R_{\beta}(t)$ that

$$ P_{\beta_{1}}(t)\geqslant R_{\beta_{1}}(t)=\frac{t}{2}\qquad\text{ and }\qquad P_{\beta_{2}}(t)\geqslant\frac{R_{2\beta_{2}}(t)}{2}=\frac{t}{4}. $$

Therefore,

$$ P_{\beta_{1}}(t)+P_{\beta_{2}}(t)+P_{\beta_{3}}(t)-t\geqslant P_{\beta_{3}}(t)-\frac{t}{4}\geqslant R_{\beta_{3}}(t)-\frac{t}{4}. $$

The remaining task is to prove that for all $t\in[\varepsilon^{6}/2,\tau^{*}]$ we have

$$ \displaystyle R_{\beta_{3}}(t)-\frac{t}{4}>\varepsilon^{10}. $$

First of all, we notice that

$$ \beta_{3}\geqslant(1-\beta_{1})/2\geqslant 1/4\geqslant\tau^{*}/2. $$

If $R_{\beta_{3}}(t)=t/2$ , then (8.16) is immediate. In particular we can concentrate on the range $\beta_{3}\in[1/4,\tau^{\ast}].$ Looking at the slopes of $R_{\beta}(t)$ in (8.3) and (8.4), we see that the left-hand side of (8.16) is minimal when $t=r(\beta_{3})$ with

$$ \displaystyle r(\beta)=\begin{cases}\tau^{\ast}-2\beta/5,\qquad&\text{ if }\beta\leqslant 5\tau^{\ast}/6;\\
3\tau^{\ast}/2-\beta,&\text{ if }5\tau^{\ast}/6\leqslant\beta\leqslant\tau^{\ast},\end{cases} $$

and

$$ R_{\beta_{3}}(r(\beta_{3}))-\frac{r(\beta_{3})}{4}=\frac{r(\beta_{3})-\tau^{\ast}+\beta_{3}}{2}-\frac{r(\beta_{3})}{4}=\frac{r(\beta_{3})-2\tau^{\ast}+2\beta_{3}}{4}. $$

Now, for $\beta_{3}\in[5\tau^{\ast}/6,\tau^{\ast}]$ , we obtain

$$ R_{\beta_{3}}(r(\beta_{3}))-\frac{r(\beta_{3})}{4}=\frac{\beta_{3}-\tau^{\ast}/2}{4}\geqslant\frac{\tau^{\ast}}{12}>\varepsilon^{10}. $$

and for $\beta_{3}\in[1/4,5\tau^{\ast}/6]$ , we obtain

$$ R_{\beta_{3}}(r(\beta_{3}))-\frac{r(\beta_{3})}{4}=\frac{-\tau^{*}+8\beta_{3}/5}{4}\geqslant\frac{\varepsilon}{4}>\varepsilon^{10}, $$

which completes the proof. ∎

## 9. Multiplicative functions and almost primes in short intervals

In this section we shall briefly indicate how to prove Theorems 1.5, 1.6 and 1.7. In case $H\in[X^{0.98},X]$ we split the interval $(X,X+H]$ into intervals of length $X^{0.9}$ and apply the result with this $H$ for each subinterval. Hence we can assume that $H\in[X^{19/35+\varepsilon},X^{0.98}]$ .

We may assume that $\varepsilon\in(0,1/100)$ . The discussion in [11, Section 5.1] reduces the proofs of Theorems 1.5 and 1.6 to comparison estimates of the form (7.6). The resulting dyadic components contain a bounded number of factors with divisor-bounded coefficients, allowing fixed powers of $\log X$ . Every factor of length greater than $(2X)^{1/20}$ is an interval sum weighted by a Dirichlet character of bounded modulus, possibly with a logarithmic weight.

The proof of Proposition 7.2 extends to these components, since the extra short factors satisfy the same divisor moment bounds, and $S-2\tau>1/20$ guarantees that the singleton in case (iii) is a character-weighted interval factor. Case (i) uses periodicity and partial summation, case (ii) uses the character-weighted prime polynomial estimate, and case (iii) uses Lemma 4.1 with a character weight. This yields Theorems 1.5 and 1.6 whenever $X^{19/35+\varepsilon}\leqslant H\leqslant Y$ .

We now turn our attention to Theorem 1.7. Take $k=100$ and write $P=\exp((\log\log X)^{2})$ and $Q=X^{\varepsilon}$ . Note that, as will become transparent later, we deliberately chose a different $k$ from the one taken in [11, Section 5.2]. Consider

$$ P(s)=\sum_{P_{1}<p\leqslant\min\{2P_{1},Q\}}p^{-s},\ \ \ \ \ \ \ N_{i}(s)=\sum_{N_{i}<n\leqslant 2N_{i}}a_{i}(n)n^{-s}, $$

where $P_{1}N_{1}\ldots N_{2k}\asymp X$ , $P_{1}\in[P,Q]$ , $N_{i}\geqslant 1/2$ , and

$$ a_{i}(n)\equiv\begin{cases}1\ \text{ or }\log n\ \text{ or }1_{n=1},&\text{if }i\leqslant k,\\[4.0pt]
\mu(n)1_{n\leqslant(2X)^{1/k}}\ \text{ or }\ 1_{n=1},&\text{if }k+1\leqslant i\leqslant 2k.\end{cases} $$

The discussion in [11, Section 5.2] leading to equation (5.7) reduces matters to showing that

$$ \int_{T_{0}}^{T_{1}}\Big\lvert P\Big(\frac{1}{2}+it\Big)N_{1}\Big(\frac{1}{2}+it\Big)\ldots N_{2k}\Big(\frac{1}{2}+it\Big)\Big\rvert dt\ll_{A}\frac{X^{1/2}}{\log^{A}X}, $$

with

$$ T_{0}:=X^{0.01},\qquad T_{1}:=\frac{X^{1+\varepsilon/10}}{H}. $$

As was done in [11], we split the interval $[T_{0},T_{1}]$ into two parts, namely

$$ \mathcal{T}_{1}=\{t\in[T_{0},T_{1}]:\lvert P(1/2+it)\rvert>P_{1}^{1/2}\log^{-10A}X\} $$

and its complement $\mathcal{T}_{2}=[T_{0},T_{1}]\setminus\mathcal{T}_{1}$ .
